10023-there-s-pippins-and-cheese-to-come:
Charles S. Brooks's 1917 book of essays takes its title from the first piece, a noonday quest for food on a fine day. Brooks, author of Journeys to Bagdad and Chimney-Pot Papers, writes about buying old books, roads of morning, and the unknown reader.

His essays wander pleasantly from Chinese restaurants on second stories to dogs, sticks, and holiday moods, in a voice both learned and easy. Illustrated by Theodore Diedricksen Jr., the book suits slow reading. Readers who like familiar essays will enjoy Brooks's habit of finding thought in lunch, a bookshop, or a morning road.
10268-patty-at-home:
Carolyn Wells published this girls' book in 1904, following Patty Fairfield as she sets up a home of her own. Debate and decision open the tale, then tea clubs, shopping, servants, and bills test Patty's taste and sense. The book belongs to a series loved for its bright, domestic humor.

A caller, a pleasant evening, a successful play, a sailing party, and more cousins fill Patty's busy days. She learns to balance fun, manners, and money with grace. Readers get a cheerful, period story of a young woman learning to run a house and keep friends.
10393-making-the-house-a-home:
Edgar A. Guest published this memoir in 1922, telling how he and his wife built a home over fifteen years, starting with their marriage on June 28, 1906. Guest, then leaving night work as a police reporter for the Detroit Free Press, frames home as more than a house: a hall of contentment built slowly, page by page.

Smiles and tears, weal and woe, care and grief fill the record, which hopes later readers will not falter in belief. Guest writes in plain, rhymed and prose passages, warm and homely. Readers get a cheerful, sentimental story of marriage, work, and making a house into a home.
10464-a-child-s-anti-slavery-book-contai:
This child's anti-slavery book, with ten pictures, opens with a few words about American slave children and stories of slave life. Its pictures show a slave father sold from his family, a boy sold, whipping, hunting runaways, and waiting to be sold. The book was made to teach Northern children the cruelty of slavery in plain, moving terms.

Stories include Little Lewis, Mark and Hasty, Aunt Judy's story from real life, and a cry of never giving up. Each tale stresses family loss, courage, and faith. Readers get a powerful, historic abolitionist book for children, painful in subject but humane in purpose.
10979-footsteps-on-the-road-to-learning-:
An 1850 alphabet book in rhyme teaches children their letters through pictures and short verses. Each letter gets several words: A for ass, ape, and ark, B for boy, bat, and bark, C for cow, calf, and cart, and so on through X for Xerxes. Illustrations face the verses, helping beginners match sounds to images.

The rhymes are simple and memorable, with a child's voice at the start promising to read the fine picture book all through and show Mamma how well the ABCs are remembered. Though brief, the book is complete in its purpose: a first reader for the nursery. It shows mid-Victorian methods of teaching letters, before graded school readers took over.
11421-russell-h-conwell-founder-of-the-i:
Agnes Rush Burr's Russell H. Conwell, Founder of the Institutional Church in America, with an introduction by Floyd W. Tomkins, tells the work and the man behind Temple University and Grace Baptist Church. Dedicated to church members who built temple walls with self-sacrifice, the book includes Conwell's two famous lectures, Acres of Diamonds and Personal Glimpses of Celebrated Men and Women, as recently delivered. Tomkins measures greatness by helpfulness, not wealth, birth, or intellect.

Conwell's institutional church joined worship with education, hospitals, and social service. Burr's biography, published in 1905, is admiring and contemporary. For historians of American religion, it documents a model of church as community institution that spread widely in the twentieth century.
11574-master-skylark-a-story-of-shaksper:
John Bennett's story of Shakespeare's time follows Nicholas Attwood, a boy singer called Master Skylark, from his home through Coventry and the Warwick road to London. The Lord Admiral's Players, a master-player, and the Rose playhouse draw him into the theatre world.

Chapters carry him from a May-day play and disowning to a strange ride, a dash for freedom, and at last singing before Queen Elizabeth at Christmas. Carew, Cicely, and the Children of Paul's cross his path, and the book ends with a wayfaring home after a year of stage life.
1160-the-game:
Jack London tells of Joe Fleming, a young prizefighter who loves Genevieve, a girl who fears the ring, and who agrees to one last bout before marriage. The novel follows the fight in close, brutal detail, from the dressing room to the final blow, and then to its tragic aftermath.

London, who knew the fight game, writes the bout as both sport and fate: skill, courage, and luck decide in minutes. The love story frames the violence with tenderness. The book is short and hard, and it stands as London's finest study of the ring.
11758-baldy-of-nome:
Esther Birdsall Darling's Baldy of Nome follows a dog in Alaska, from the parting of the ways and a first step to the Solomon Derby and the great race. Chapters cover the woman, the racers, and others, a tragedy without a moral, and immortals of the trail.

Pictures show the racing team, Scotty Allan with Baldy, and the steamer Corwin at the ice edge five miles from shore. A later scene brings Nellie Silk's malamute pups, with a dog tunnelling under a manger to reach them, called the one scandal in the kennel. The book is a true-feeling tale of sled dogs, mushers, and the Nome trail.
11765-between-you-and-me:
Sir Harry Lauder's Between You and Me, published in New York in 1919, is dedicated to the fathers and mothers of boys who went to war and boys who prepared to go. A verse at the front speaks for one of the boys who went, imagining a return to Dover, money spent, and a thought kept: he was there.

Lauder writes in Scots voice about a bonny world worth saving, and about Britain's long unity against invaders from over the sea. Zeppelins and Gothas, he notes, were the first armed men on British soil in centuries. The book is a minstrel's wartime memoir, warm, patriotic, and plainspoken.
1216-reflections-on-the-decline-of-scien:
Charles Babbage invented the calculating engine, and he argues in this 1830 tract that English science had sunk into decay. The Royal Society rewarded rank over merit, jobs went to toadies, and real workers starved. He names names and proposes reforms, from fair pay to honest medals.

Babbage writes with a reformer's anger and an engineer's love of system, and his complaints helped spur the founding of the British Association. The book is both a polemic and a portrait of science as a profession being born. It still speaks to debates on how science is funded and judged.
12416-as-seen-by-me:
Lilian Bell published As Seen by Me in 1900, a travel book in letters from Europe, Russia, and the Near East. Bell, author of The Instinct of Step-Fatherhood, writes as an American woman abroad, observant and opinionated.

Chapters run from a first letter on the way through London, Paris, and a yacht called Hela, to Vilna, St. Petersburg, Moscow, Constantinople, Cairo, the Nile, Greece, Naples, and Rome. A mid-book worry concerns trunks lost off a train at Vilna and a week as guests without a change of clothes. Bell mixes hotel anecdotes with sights, including the Cleopatra relief at Denderah. The book is a lively Edwardian travelogue, personal rather than scholarly.
12607-you-can-search-me:
Hugh McHugh's 1905 comic sketches, You Can Search Me, illustrated by Gordon H. Grant, follow John Henry through a series of scrapes. Chapters promise John Henry gets a partner, a sufficiency, busy, a shock, excited, a setback and a surprise. Illustrations show a plain omelette and prunes, iron on an instep, a cream-coloured horse looking sadly, and a dropped egg.

Chapter one opens with wedding bells due in seven weeks for John Henry's pal Bunch Jefferson, who answers dolefully that he must dig up money. McHugh, author of the John Henry books, writes in slangy, first-person humour. The volume is light American comedy, best read as a string of tall tales about money, friends and marriage.
12833-what-dreams-may-come:
Gertrude Atherton, writing as Frank Lin, set this novel in Constantinople at the opening of the twentieth century. Golden domes, bazaars, palaces, and latticed streets frame a story of love, intrigue, and high-born society in the old Ottoman capital. The city itself, vast and beautiful, tires the senses with its splendour.

At the centre stands a proud, high-strung heroine and a man sure he can master both himself and any woman who loves him. Their contest of wills drives the plot through drawing rooms and gardens. The novel offers period romance with an exotic setting and a sharp eye for social power.
12967-memoirs-and-historical-chronicles-:
This volume gathers memoirs of Marguerite de Valois, Madame de Pompadour, and Catherine de Medici, queens and favourites of the French courts. Marguerite's letters trace her infancy, efforts to convert her to the new religion, confirmation in Catholicism, and court progresses broken by sudden confusion. A child Mozart playing for Pompadour fronts the book.

A later passage shows a loyal courtier promising Marguerite, at hazard of his life, to free her brother from arrest, with Scottish archers waiting on the stairs. Court intrigue, faith, and family loyalty drive the memoirs. The book offers vivid, first-person glimpses of Renaissance and Bourbon France.
1297-the-iron-puddler-my-life-in-the-rol:
James J. Davis, who rose from a Welsh immigrant boy in the Pittsburgh rolling mills to become Secretary of Labor, tells his life in this memoir. He puddled iron in heat and danger, learned the trade's pride and its toll, and climbed through union and public life to Washington.

Davis writes the mills with firsthand grit: the furnaces, the wages, and the men who worked them. His story is both labor history and an American success tale. The book gives a rare worker's view of the steel age, and it still reads as honest and vivid.
13194-the-rules-of-the-game:
Stewart Edward White's 1910 novel The Rules of the Game, illustrated by Lejaren A. Hiller, is set in Sierra country the author warns readers not to match to real folk. White states that Baker's power company and the character Plant have nothing to do with any real company or man. The novel's geography may be known, but its people are invented.

Bob, a mountain boy, faces Selwyn over Lucky Lands, where over eight hundred families settled and three in four made good. Selwyn defends the land, water, and price, while Bob doubts the methods behind the sale. Later, Bob trades jobs with a youth planting cedar posts, and rangers cook their own meals at camp. The novel is a western tale of land, water, and fair dealing.
13329-pe-lle-as-and-me-lisande-alladine-:
Maurice Maeterlinck's three plays, Pélléas and Mélisande, Alladine and Palomides, and Home, appear here in Richard Hovey's translation, Stone and Kimball, 1896, reprinted 1911. Maeterlinck's preface denies that the plays were written for marionettes, insisting that living actors kill poems. The plays are symbolist drama, dreamlike and still.

In Pélléas, little Yniold lifts a lamp to his weeping parents in the dark, while Golaud enters the courtyard. In Alladine, a palace grows too big for its dweller, with windows on the sea uncountable, corridors that turn without reason, and thirty doors pushed open before light is found. The volume is a key text of symbolist theatre.
1335-the-ancien-re-gime:
Charles Kingsley, the novelist and clergyman, lectures on the ancien régime, the old order of France before the Revolution: its kings, nobles, priests, and peasants, and the abuses that made revolt inevitable. The lectures trace how privilege rotted and how new ideas spread.

Kingsley writes with a reformer's zeal and a storyteller's pace, praising the Revolution's hopes while warning against its terrors. The book is short and vivid, if Victorian in its judgments. It suits readers who want a lively entry to pre-revolutionary France. Kingsley's lectures give a lively entry to pre-revolutionary France.
13442-henry-hudson-a-brief-statement-of-:
Thomas A. Janvier states Henry Hudson's aims and achievements in brief, then adds a newly discovered partial record of the trial of the mutineers who abandoned Hudson and others to death. No portrait of Hudson is known, Janvier warns, and the dapper man in a ruffed collar often reproduced as Hudson certainly is not him.

Hudson sought a short way to India, guided by Captain Smith's news from Virginia and by Davis's Straits, and sailed with the Half Moon into the river that bears his name. Janvier parallels Hudson's mutiny with Greely's Arctic expedition of 1883 to 1884, where twenty-five men set out and only seven were found alive, to show how close quarters breed grievance. The book defends Hudson's seamanship and fame.
13469-a-history-of-pantomime:
R. J. Broadbent, author of Stage Whispers, writes a history of pantomime from Liverpool in December 1901, hoping to give readers new information about an ancient entertainment neglected in stage histories. He dedicates the book to William Wade and traces pantomime through centuries of theatre.

Early chapters show actors excluded from church rites in the fourth century, with visitors to Sunday entertainments excommunicated and sacraments withheld save at death's door. Later pages follow patents, theatres, and the king's memory of two London theatres in Charles's time. Broadbent treats pantomime as a serious factor in theatrical history, not a mere Christmas trifle.
13843-libretto-la-bohe-me:
Giacomo Puccini's opera La Bohème appears here in libretto form, with text by Giuseppe Giacosa and Luigi Illica. An English version by W. Grist and P. Pinkerton accompanies the Italian. Characters include Rodolph the poet, Marcel the painter, Schaunard the musician, and Colline the philosopher. Mimi, Musetta, Benoit the landlord, and Alcindoro complete the cast.

Set in Paris about 1830, the opera follows young artists in an attic studio. Rodolph and Marcel joke about burning a manuscript and a painting, the Red Sea, for warmth. Love, poverty, illness, and friendship shape the four acts. The libretto lets readers follow Puccini's music with ease. It suits opera lovers and students of the work.
14066-everyday-foods-in-war-time:
Mary Swartz Rose, a nutrition teacher at Columbia, wrote this 1918 guide to eating well while saving food for war. Chapters take one staple at a time: milk in the home, cereals worth eating, meat worth saving, potatoes and their substitutes, fruits and vegetables, fat and vitamins, and sugar with spice. An appendix adds wartime recipes that put each principle to work.

Plain economics drives the advice. An apple a day may cost a cent or five, while a doctor's visit costs a hundred times more, so varied fruits and vegetables count as health insurance. Cornmeal must replace wheat bread, since white bread will vanish if cooks refuse substitutes. Rose warns against eating to be entertained in wartime: food must nourish first. Teachers and housewives found here a science of thrift, written in friendly, practical prose.
14083-tom-fairfield-s-pluck-and-luck-or-:
Allen Chapman's 1913 school story follows Tom Fairfield, a boarding-school boy accused of a wrong he did not commit. Football games, cross-country runs, and woodland mishaps fill the early chapters. Trouble sharpens when horses are poisoned and suspicion falls on Tom. Friends urge him to speak, but he holds his silence while he hunts for proof.

An empty bottle becomes the key clue. Tom tests what it once held, traces a ragged stranger, and faces down accusers in a tense pursuit. Loyalty, fair play, and steady nerve matter as much as speed on the field. Boys' adventure fiction of this era loved a hero who clears his name by deeds, and Tom fits the mold without losing his sense of humor.
14086-carry-on-letters-in-war-time:
Lieutenant Coningsby Dawson, a novelist serving in the Canadian Field Artillery, wrote these wartime letters home, published in 1917 with notes by his father. Poems open the book, asking what soldiers will crave when war ends: laughter, wind in sunlit trees, and lives gathered up to mend. Letters follow from the front, plain and immediate.

Danger arrives without gradual breaking-in. Guns to right, rear, and front are knocked out by direct hits, and an officer blown thirty feet into the air picks himself up and carries on. Dawson sits with his groom by a fire, dreams of British Columbia, and walks No Man's Land within seventy yards of the enemy. Exaltation mixes with hardship throughout, and the letters read as a young writer learning, under fire, what courage and homesickness truly cost.
1438-no-name:
Wilkie Collins's sensation novel follows Magdalen and Norah Vanstone, sisters left nameless and penniless when a flaw in their parents' marriage voids their inheritance. Norah bears the loss quietly, but Magdalen, the younger and bolder sister, plots to win back her fortune by guile, disguise, and a daring marriage scheme.

Told in scenes separated by intervals, the novel moves from a country house to London stages and seaside lodgings, with secrets, forged letters, and a villainous captain along the way. Collins's plotting is at its most intricate here. It is a gripping tale of law, identity, and a woman's fight for a name.
14540-when-william-came:
Saki, pen name of H. H. Munro, published this satirical invasion novel in 1914, imagining Britain conquered by Germany and ruled from London by a German emperor. The story opens with Cicely Yeovil at home, watching a young pianist.

Yeovil, returning from abroad, finds his country altered: German officers, new rules, and English society adapting, resisting, or collaborating. Saki's wit is cool and merciless, aimed at complacency and fashion as much as at the invader. The novel reads as a warning dressed as comedy, written months before the real war began.
14594-cassell-s-vegetarian-cookery-a-man:
A. G. Payne wrote Cassell's Vegetarian Cookery as a manual of cheap and wholesome food, published with advertisements for gas kitcheners and household books. The volume teaches meatless cooking for ordinary households.

Recipes cover rice with cheese, stewed vegetables with butter, pepper, salt, and nutmeg, and many dishes using milk, eggs, and cheese rind to save money. Payne gives proportions in teacups and breakfast cups, and notes standing times. The book reflects late Victorian vegetarian reform, practical rather than preachy, and useful for historians of diet. Cassell's series aimed at thrifty housekeepers across Britain.
1468-the-history-of-england-from-the-acc:
Thomas Babington Macaulay's first volume opens his great history with a sweeping survey of England from Roman and Saxon times to the reign of James II. Chapter by chapter he traces conquest, church, law, and the slow blending of peoples into one nation, before the narrative proper begins in 1685.

Macaulay writes with vigour and confidence, judging kings, parliaments, and parties in a Whig spirit that favours liberty under law. The volume sets the stage for the Glorious Revolution to come. It remains a landmark of Victorian history, admired for its sweep even where later scholars dispute its verdicts.
15072-marjorie-s-maytime:
Carolyn Wells's 1911 children's book follows Marjorie Maynard through a spring of small adventures, opening with a May party. A new pet, a trial trip, a camp visit, and a picnic follow, with grandmothers, cousins, and school friends along the way. Marjorie jumps downstairs two steps at a time, noisy and glad.

Later chapters take her to Boston, a circus, and a festival, with jokes, parties, and childish scrapes in between. Wells writes in a bright, easy style for young girls. The book's charm lies in its everyday joys: May air, open doors, and a child who finds play in every corner of her world.
15172-the-ceremonies-of-the-holy-week-at:
Monsignor Baggs, Bishop of Pella, wrote this guide to Holy Week in Rome, in a third edition sold in Rome in 1854. It gives directions for seeing the ceremonies, from Palm Sunday at St. Peter's to Tenebrae, Holy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday. An appendix adds Jerusalem's peculiar Holy Week rites.

Practical notes tell visitors what book to carry, what dress to wear, and which tickets to seek from the papal household. Chapters explain the Mass and each day's office in clear order. Travelers and students of Catholic ritual will find the guide both useful and evocative of Rome in the 1850s.
15335-madame-chrysanthe-me:
Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème, translated by Laura Ensor, is the diary of a summer in Japan, offered to a duchess with a note on taste and propriety. Loti says he changed nothing, not even dates, and that the three true figures are himself, Japan, and the effect Japan had on him. Chrysanthème herself plays a leading, if elusive, role.

Through a temporary marriage, Japanese streets, houses, and customs unfold in lyrical, observant prose. The book made Japan vivid for Western readers, though modern eyes will note its colonial gaze. As travel literature, it remains beautiful, melancholy, and historically telling.
15603-one-man-in-his-time:
Ellen Glasgow published this novel in 1922, with an epigraph from Shakespeare: one man in his time plays many parts. A note insists no character was drawn from any actual person, past or present. Twenty-four chapters run from the shadow and Gideon Vetch through Corinna of the old print shop, the tribal instinct, and Margaret to magic and Corinna going to war.

Later chapters follow the world and Patty, September roses, Patty and Corinna, and old walls against the rising tide. A journey into mean streets, Corinna wondering, and a little light on human nature lead to the fear of life and Corinna facing life. Dance music, the night, and the dawn close in the victory of Gideon Vetch. Chapter one opens in Capitol Square at winter twilight, under a bronze Washington. Glasgow writes a Virginia novel of ambition, love, and changing times.
15855-the-man-from-home:
A play in novel form by Booth Tarkington and Harry Leon Wilson, issued by Harper and Brothers in 1908. Pictures from stage scenes join the text, with the original cast listed at the front. Liebler and Company managed the stage production. The comedy sends a plain American abroad, where old-world manners meet new-world candour.

The man from home, direct and loyal, upsets polished plots with honest talk. Love, money, and reputation tangle around him in foreign rooms. Tarkington and Wilson keep the dialogue brisk and the satire kind. The book preserves a hit of the Edwardian stage: America abroad, laughing at itself and at Europe in turn.
15927-the-vehement-flame:
A 1922 novel by Margaret Deland, author of Dr. Lavendar's People and Old Chester Tales. Deland dedicates the book to Lorin, with whom she planned the story seven or eight years before. Lorin's criticism helped the first chapters, then Deland went on alone, urged by memory of his interest. Her epigraph from the Song of Songs warns that love is strong as death.

Jealousy, cruel as the grave, burns through the novel like coals of fire. A marriage, a past love, and a fierce pride test the heroine's faith and will. Deland writes with moral seriousness and deep sympathy. The novel stands as a study of passion in later life: love that heals, and jealousy that destroys.
16006-lha-dhu-or-the-dark-day-the-works-:
A short Irish tale by William Carleton, Lha Dhu, or The Dark Day, in his collected works. Carleton opens with praise of Ireland's scenery, sweetly diversified, with wavy outlines melting into each other. Valleys, glens, meadows, and hamlets lie scattered over the green island. Their people feel mirth and sorrow in equal measure.

Each valley and pleasant hamlet, Carleton warns, bears some tearful remembrance of humble calamity the world never hears. Proud nobility know little of the fair and still sorrows below them. The Dark Day brings that sorrow into light. The tale stands as a brief Irish lament: beauty above, grief beneath, told with a patriot's heart.
16265-riley-songs-of-home:
James Whitcomb Riley's Songs of Home, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1910 with pictures by Will Vawter, gathers the Hoosier poet's homeliest verse. Contents run from the old trundle-bed and the mulberry tree to the old guitar, a feel in the Christmas air, his room, and dancin' days now over. Uncles, boys, guitars, and Christmas mornings crowd the pages in Riley's warm dialect.

Dedicated to George A. Carr, the volume celebrates farm kitchens, childhood, and small-town Indiana with humor and sentiment. Riley, America's beloved homespun poet, writes to be read aloud by the fire. Readers who like nostalgic American verse will find this a comfortable, musical collection.
16387-pinnock-s-improved-edition-of-dr-g:
William C. Taylor of Trinity College, Dublin, prepared this improved edition of Goldsmith's History of Rome, in a thirty-fifth American printing from the twenty-third English edition, published in Philadelphia in 1851. Its preface credits Niebuhr and other German scholars with new light on Roman history, revealing the true constitution of the republic that once ruled the known world. Their discoveries, Taylor notes, had previously reached few readers.

The volume retells Rome from kings and republic to empire, with literature and laws whose influence still shapes modern states. Pinnock's school edition made that history clear for students. Readers will find a solid, old-style survey of Roman greatness and decline.
16403-led-astray-and-the-sphinx-two-nove:
Octave Feuillet pairs two short French novels in this 1891 volume from Street and Smith. Led Astray opens as a letter from a young man staying at a flour mill in Lower Normandy, where the plain, flour-dusted miller's wife upends all his fine ideas of romance. The tale is told with light irony, as the writer's grand fancies keep meeting dull, real life.

The second tale, The Sphinx, follows Raoul de Trecoeur, a gifted and rich young man whose promise fades into idle pleasure. Both stories turn on love, vanity, and bad choices, and both end with a sharp moral sting. Together they show Feuillet's gift for short, polished tales of French social life.
16650-the-complete-home:
Clara E. Laughlin edited this 1907 home-making guide from D. Appleton, with a frontispiece of a thirty-four-hundred-dollar house. Oliver R. Williamson opens with choosing a place to live: renting, buying, or building, city or country, schools, churches, transport, and the butcher, baker, and candlestick maker. Floors, walls, and windows follow.

Later chapters, by various hands, cover the whole house in practical detail. The book aimed at families planning a home with taste and thrift. Readers of domestic history will find a rich picture of Edwardian housekeeping, from lot choice to living room.
16667-young-folks-history-of-rome:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this 1880 history of Rome for young readers, issued by Estes and Lauriat in Boston. It runs from early Italy and Aeneas, through the founding of Rome, kings, republic, and empire, down to Charles the Great as head of the new Western Empire. Chapters stay short and full of tale-like detail.

Yonge keeps the story brisk, with heroes, wars, laws, and fables such as Menenius Agrippa's tale. She writes to hold a young mind, not to drown it in dates. The book still serves as a friendly first Rome history for school-age readers, and as a sample of how the 1800s taught the past to children.
16908-once-upon-a-time:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this 1912 book of stories, issued by Scribner's in New York and dedicated to Gouverneur Morris. Contents run from A Question of Latitude and The Spy, through The Messengers, A Wasted Day, A Charmed Life, The Amateur, The Make-Believe Man, and Peace Manoeuvres. Pictures show Schnitzel smiling, a puzzled young Andrews asking about a knife, and a striking woman in a room.

Davis writes with a reporter's eye and a storyteller's pace, mixing spies, soldiers, and society folk. Each story stands alone, full of talk, action, and a twist. Readers who like early 1900s short stories will find a bright, well-made collection, best read a story at a time for its verve and its period charm.
17180-the-riddle-of-the-frozen-flame:
Mary E. and Thomas W. Hanshew's 1929 Cleek novel opens with Superintendent Maverick Narkom of Scotland Yard at his wits' end over a case he cannot make out. Cleek, the man of forty faces, takes the riddle of the frozen flame. Victims, a spectre at the feast, a shot in the dark, and a watcher in the shadow lead to a gruesome find at the Pig and Whistle. An inquest, prisoners, and a web of circumstance follow.

The Hanshews write in brisk, popular detective style, with twists at each chapter turn. Cleek's disguises and logic carry the tale to its solving toward morning. Mystery fans will enjoy a classic late Cleek case, full of fog, fear, and a final, satisfying reveal.
17226-emily-fox-seton-being-the-making-o:
Frances Hodgson Burnett joins two Emily Fox-Seton tales in this 1901 volume: The Making of a Marchioness and The Methods of Lady Walderhurst. Part One opens on a wet London morning as Emily, in a tailor-made suit worn a full year, steps from a twopenny bus and guards its folds from splashes. Her honest hazel eyes watch shop windows for new skirt shapes she cannot afford.

Emily, a poor, kind, hardworking woman, rises by goodness and sense into a marchioness, and the second part tests her new rank. Burnett writes with warmth and humor about class, dress, and worth. Fans of her children's books will enjoy this adult fairy tale, where kindness, not beauty or wealth, wins the day.
17273-an-exposition-of-the-last-psalme:
John Boys, Doctor of Divinity, preached this exposition of the last psalm at Paul's Cross on November 5, 1613, Gunpowder Treason Day, and printed it in 1615. Psalm 150, O praise God in his holiness, is his text, and he joins it to the festivals as a short defense of holy days in the Church of England. He dedicates the sermon to Sir William Monins, his kinsman.

Boys teaches two points: for what God is to be praised, and with what, from noble acts to every tool of praise. His old spelling and pulpit logic give the sermon its period flavor. Readers of early Anglican preaching will find a compact, learned defense of praise and holy days in Jacobean London.
17322-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Gaston Maspero's great ancient history, edited by A. H. Sayce and translated by M. L. McClure, reaches volume two, part A, in this Grolier text. Its theme is the political constitution of Egypt: king, queen, and royal princes, Pharaonic administration, feudalism, priesthood, military, and country people. Gizeh and Saqqara tombs, the Great Sphinx, and mastaba paintings help date the Memphite dynasties.

Maspero traces Pharaoh's double nature, titles, protocol, harem, children, and succession fights, with palace life beside. Over twelve hundred plates and pictures enrich the whole work. Students of ancient Egypt will find this volume a deep, classic guide to how the old kingdom was ruled and run.
17323-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
In the third volume of his great history, Gaston Maspero, professor at the College of France, covers Egypt, Chaldea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria. A. H. Sayce of Oxford edited it, and M. L. McClure translated it for the Grolier Society. Like its companion volumes it carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. The volume opens with ancient Chaldea, its creation stories, its deluge tale, and its gods.

Chapters then cover the country, its cities, its peoples, and its early dynasties, drawing on cuneiform records and on monuments. Readers get a grand, late Victorian survey of Mesopotamia before modern digging rewrote parts of the story. Its plates and its retelling of myth and history still give a vivid entry into the ancient Near East.
17324-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Volume four of Gaston Maspero's ancient history, edited by Sayce and translated by McClure, covers the first Chaldean empire and the Hyksos in Egypt. Syria's place in the ancient world opens the book: Lebanon, Damascus, the coast, and the Jordan valley, with Chaldean sway over Egyptian sway. Babylon's rise, Hammurabi's empire, canals, and buildings follow, with Elamite wars beside.

The Hyksos conquest of Egypt at the end of the period closes the volume. Maspero writes in full, learned detail, with plates and maps throughout the set. Readers of ancient Near East history will find a classic, orderly account of Babylon's first empire and Egypt's troubled age of foreign kings.
17325-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
The fifth volume of Maspero's great history, edited by A. H. Sayce of Oxford and translated by M. L. McClure for the Grolier Society, carries the story of Egypt, Chaldea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria forward. Gaston Maspero was professor at the College of France. As with its companion volumes, it carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. This volume continues the story of the Eighteenth Theban Dynasty.

Its opening sections treat Thutmosis III and the organisation of the Syrian provinces, then Amenophis III and the worshippers of Aton. Readers get a grand, late Victorian account of Egypt at the height of its empire, built on monuments and inscriptions. The plates and the narrative together still offer a vivid entry into New Kingdom Egypt.
17326-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Volume six of Maspero's history carries the close of the Theban empire, with Ramses III at its heart. Chapters describe manners, customs, population, and the rising power of Amon and his high priests. The Theban necropolis fills long pages: funerals, tombs, coffins, the harper's song, and the lives of draughtsmen, sculptors, and painters who worked among the dead.

Workmen's strikes, temple revenues, and priestly power under Ramses III's sons show an empire straining at its seams. Maspero's detail, drawn from tombs and temples, makes the age vivid. Egypt lovers will find this volume a rich, classic portrait of Thebes in decline, from funeral rites to palace politics.
17327-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Assyria's revival fills the seventh volume of Gaston Maspero's history of Egypt, Chaldea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria. A. H. Sayce of Oxford edited it, and M. L. McClure translated it for the Grolier Society, and Maspero was professor at the College of France. It carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures, in the pattern of the whole set. The volume's subject is the Assyrian revival and the struggle for Syria.

Assur-nazir-pal, who ruled from 885 to 860 before the common era, and Shalmaneser the second lead the narrative, as Assyria pushes west against Syrian states. Readers get a late Victorian survey of Assyrian power, drawn from palace records and monuments. Its plates and clear storytelling still make Assyria's rise easy to follow.
17328-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Volume eight of Maspero's history turns to Sennacherib, king of Assyria from 705 to 681 B.C., and his struggle with Judah and Egypt. Babylon revolts, Merodach-baladan seeks allies, and Kish falls in 703 B.C. Tyre's kings, Phoenician colonies, Hezekiah's reforms, and the siege of Jerusalem fill the middle, with Sennacherib camped before Lachish and disaster at Pelusium.

Renewed revolt, a fleet descent on Nagitu, and the destruction of Babylon close the volume's arc. Maspero's narrative, rich in names and dates, keeps empire politics clear. Readers of Assyrian and biblical history will find a classic, detailed account of a king whose wars shaped Judah, Egypt, and Babylon alike.
17329-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Persia's rise fills the ninth volume of Gaston Maspero's history of Egypt, Chaldea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria. A. H. Sayce of Oxford edited it, and M. L. McClure translated it for the Grolier Society, and Maspero was professor at the College of France. It carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. The volume's theme is the Iranian conquest and the faiths of ancient Iran.

Cyrus in Lydia and at Babylon, Cambyses in Egypt, and Darius with the organisation of his empire form the spine of the story. Readers watch a new power take over the old kingdoms of the Near East and weld them into one realm. The book still serves as a readable, richly pictured survey of Persia's rise under its first great kings.
17496-elsie-at-home:
Martha Finley, author of Elsie Dinsmore and Elsie's Vacation, published this volume of the Elsie series in a special authorised edition, with copyright dated 1887. The book opens on a stormy March evening, with rain and sleet falling and a blustering northeast wind sweeping fields and gardens, while a hack lumbers along a wet road. That gloomy, homely opening suits a story of family life.

Readers rejoin Elsie at home, in the Christian domestic world that made Finley's heroine beloved by generations of young readers. The novel's pleasures are quiet ones: household cares, affection, and moral growth rather than wild adventure. It remains a window onto the kind of girls' fiction that shaped American parlours in the late nineteenth century.
17957-on-the-sublime:
Longinus, an ancient Greek critic, wrote On the Sublime on what lifts speech and verse to greatness, and this 1890 version was turned into English by H. L. Havell, with a preface by Andrew Lang. Macmillan printed it in London and New York, from a text shaped by German scholars.

Longinus asks what makes a line grand: high thought, strong feeling, fine figures, noble words, and a fit, lofty build. He draws on Homer, Plato, and the Bible for his cases, and he warns against swell and false fire. The book still stands as the first great work on literary grandeur, and a short, sharp guide for writers and readers.
1810-a-second-home:
The Rue du Tourniquet-Saint-Jean was once one of the darkest and most winding streets in Paris. A young woman named Caroline keeps rooms there that are not quite a home. Caroline, a young woman kept by a rich protector, sits for the famous hairdresser Plaisir, who praises her long, thick hair while she waits, out of patience, for her life to change.

The tale follows Caroline's second home — the rooms, the lovers, and the small economies by which a kept woman survives in Paris. Balzac writes it with sympathy and without preaching. The story's interest lies in its detail: a whole social world seen from a dressing table, where beauty is both a living and a trap.
18100-roads-from-rome:
Anne C. E. Allinson wrote Roads from Rome in 1922, published in New York by Macmillan, gathering essays that had run in part in The Atlantic Monthly. Allinson, who wrote Greek Lands and Letters with Francis Allinson, dedicates the book to her father, a lover of law and letters.

Essays run from The Estranger and A Poet's Toll to The Phrase-Maker, A Roman Citizen, and Fortune's Ledger. Catullus walks far from town to dull his grief, and Rome's roads lead the reader on. Allinson writes with grace and learning. It is a cultured, gentle book of travel and thought, best for lovers of Rome and Latin letters.
18151-time-crime:
H. Beam Piper's story, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in February and March 1955, follows the Paratime Police. Their task is to police the countless parallel timelines, and here they hunt a gang hiding on one line among billions. The blurb in the magazine calls the hunt a real headache for the police.

The opening places readers on a plantation timeline, where clerks count gold coins and a manager haggles over the price of enslaved workers. The police must conform to local custom while they search, even when it sickens them. The story mixes police work, time travel, and moral strain, as a small team tracks criminals who can vanish into another world.
18204-stamp-collecting-as-a-pastime:
Edward J. Nankivell wrote Stamp Collecting as a Pastime in 1902, printed in London by Stanley Gibbons, as one of the firm's philatelic handbooks. Nankivell, a journalist and member of the Philatelic Society of London, defends his hobby with wit and lore.

Chapters run from the charm and permanence of collecting to its geography, history, great rarities, romance, and worth as an investment. Nankivell holds that a pastime lets time slip by unnoticed, and that stamps do just that. The book is a charming, old guide for beginners, and a window on the golden age of stamp collecting.
18267-we-philologists-complete-works-of-:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote this short work in the autumn of 1874, and it appeared only after his death. It stands as volume eight of the first complete English version of his works, edited by Oscar Levy and translated by J. M. Kennedy in 1911. Its subject is the classical scholar, the philologist, and the training that shapes such a person.

Nietzsche argues that chance rules most choices of a calling. Few people, he says, truly fit the work they take up, and many waste years in posts that do not suit them. The essay asks what a scholar is for, and whether the study of old texts serves life or only itself. It is a sharp, brief attack on academic habit.
18304-american-adventures-a-second-trip-:
Julian Street wrote this 1917 travel book as a second trip abroad at home, with pictorial sidelights by Wallace Morgan. Street and his companion set out to learn America by dwelling a while in each city and town, rather than rushing past. An opening plate calls Charleston the last stronghold of a unified American upper class, where Madeira, port, and noblesse oblige still held sway.

Chapters move through the borderland, Baltimore, Harpers Ferry and John Brown, the Virginias and the Washingtons, Charlottesville and Monticello, and fox-hunting in Virginia. Street notes idioms, manners, and sectional misunderstandings, such as you-all. Readers get a witty survey of an America that was changing fast, seen town by town in the years before the First World War.
18316-notable-women-of-olden-time:
The American Sunday-School Union published this 1852 book of lives for young readers. Each chapter retells the story of a woman from the Old Testament, with a plain moral title. Sarah is The Wife, Hagar is The Wife Unloved, and Rebekah is The Partial and Intriguing Mother. Leah and Rachel appear as The Rival Sisters.

Later chapters give Miriam the affectionate sister, Deborah the prophetess, Jezebel the artful woman, Athaliah the ambitious woman, and Esther the orphan queen. The book opens with Abraham called to leave his kindred for a strange land. Readers get Bible stories told as character lessons, with each woman held up as a warning or an example for the young.
18420-the-bobbsey-twins-at-home:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Bobbsey Twins book, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York in 1916. The twins at home begin with Tommy Todd's story, told on a train as a little fellow asks his mother how many more stations before home. His golden-haired sister sits beside him, and the journey home sets the book's domestic frame.

Chapters follow a sudden stop, Snap and Snoop, home again, Tommy's troubles, school days, the school play, and Nan baking a cake. Later chapters bring the lumber yard, a queer play-house, the first frost, chestnuts, a storm, the first snow, Bert's snowshoes, and being lost in a storm. Young readers get the Bobbseys at home and at school: pets, play, weather, and small scrapes, told in short, cheerful chapters.
18459-hypnerotomachia-the-strife-of-loue:
Francesco Colonna wrote this dream romance, here in the English Experience facsimile of the London 1592 edition, published by Da Capo Press and Theatrum Orbis Terrarum in 1969. The facsimile reproduces the Bodleian Library's copy, with the publishers' thanks to the library's curators.

The work tells of a lover's dream, full of strange buildings, gardens, and allegorical figures, in the ornate prose of the English Renaissance. It is a landmark of early printed romance, valued for its strange beauty and its lasting place in the history of the book, rather than for a plain story told straight.
18564-the-religion-of-ancient-rome:
Cyril Bailey, fellow and tutor of Balliol College, Oxford, published this short study at London in 1907. He seeks the native religion of early Rome before Greek books and eastern cults reshaped it, using old calendars, inscriptions, and rites kept in later writers. His chapters move from the religion of Numa through farm life to worship of the household, the fields, and the state.

Later chapters cover auguries and auspices, then close on religion and morals. Bailey warns that classical literature alone misleads, since later layers hide the early faith. The book is a compact, scholarly guide to Roman religion at its roots.
19073-cocoa-and-chocolate-their-history-:
Arthur W. Knapp, research chemist to Cadbury Brothers, wrote this 1920 history of cocoa and chocolate from plantation to consumer. It moves from early history to growing, harvest, markets, and the planter's life, with notes on chief producing areas. The aim is to join science, trade, and taste in one account.

Knapp recalls Cortes in Mexico in 1519, where Montezuma drank chocolate from golden goblets, frothy with vanilla and spice. From Aztec tribute lists to modern factories, the bean's path is traced step by step. Readers get a rich, informed history of a food that moved from royal drink to daily treat.
19208-vitality-supreme:
Bernarr Macfadden wrote this health book on vitality supreme, covering posture, breathing, food, sleep, bathing, and the mind as master force for health or disease. Chapters promise power through functional activity, a straight spine, clean bowels, strong lungs, and a daily regimen. The laugh cure and singing as a tonic also get chapters.

Macfadden explains how blood feeds organs, how lungs take in oxygen and cast out carbonic acid gas, and how kidneys clean the system. Sound lungs and steady breathing, he argues, sustain every other function. Readers get a vigorous early fitness manual, confident, practical, and very much of its era.
1927-elinor-wyllys-or-the-young-folk-of-:
Susan Fenimore Cooper, daughter of James Fenimore Cooper, writes Elinor Wyllys, a tale of the young folk of Longbridge, in this first volume. Elinor, a sensible heroine, moves among friends, suitors, and village society. Cooper published Elinor Wyllys in 1846, as her first novel, under her own name.

Cooper writes domestic fiction with a moral eye, praising duty, kindness, and good sense. The novel gives a picture of American village life in the 1840s, and of a woman writer finding her own voice. Longbridge, a thin veil for Cooperstown, gives the tale its village truth.
1928-elinor-wyllys-or-the-young-folk-of-:
Susan Fenimore Cooper continues Elinor Wyllys in this second volume, carrying the young folk of Longbridge through further trials of love, friendship, and reputation. Elinor's steadiness remains the story's anchor. The second volume resolves love plots begun in the first, with Elinor's judgment at the centre.

New complications test the village circle, and Cooper resolves them with moral warmth rather than sensation. Read with the first volume, the tale gives a full picture of American domestic life in the 1840s. Cooper's village society, with its calls and church, gives the romance its social frame.
19313-the-silk-hat-soldier-and-other-poe:
Richard Le Gallienne wrote this war-time verse book, The Silk-Hat Soldier and Other Poems in War Time. It follows his many earlier volumes on Stevenson, Kipling, Meredith, and the Golden Girl. The poems speak for small peoples under great powers. They speak for soldiers and for lands pressed into cruel wars. The tone is lyrical and indignant.

One poem cries that a mighty hand would add so small a land to its land. A boy might conquer bees or ants in the same spirit. The poem asks what gain comes from binding peoples and driving them to sing underground in whispers. The Czech, Pole, Finn, and Schleswig Dane are named. Readers get First World War verse of protest and pity.
19400-history-of-egypt-chald-a-syria-bab:
Gaston Maspero wrote this great History of Egypt, Chaldea, Syria, Babylonia, and Assyria, edited by A. H. Sayce and translated by M. L. McClure, with over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. Volume one, part A, opens with an editor's preface praising Maspero as a master of Egyptian science, ancient Oriental history, and archaeology. The Grolier Society published it in London.

Maspero weighs new finds as sheets pass through the press, from a king Samas-natsir linked with Sargon of Accad, to de Morgan's vast temple at Kom Ombo and twelfth-dynasty jewellery at Dahshur. Readers get a rich, old-style survey of the ancient Near East, built on texts, tombs, and digs.
19651-key-out-of-time:
Andre Norton wrote this science fiction novel, published in Cleveland in the early nineteen sixties. Ross, a time castaway, deals with sea rovers, dolphin allies, and a leader named Vistur, weighing whether to let foes believe his force is larger than it is.

Chapters carry him from a lotus world and the lair of Mano-Nui through storm menace, time wreck, and battle tests. Norton, a master of young adult adventure, mixes time travel with sea lore, and the book remains a favorite of her long shelf. Ross and Loketh hide supply containers by a cave wall, weighting them down so they sink out of sight.
19943-the-hippodrome:
Rachel Hayward's The Hippodrome, dated 1913, is a novel of the music-hall world. Its manager counts women only for their money or brains, the narrator observes. If women had cash to spend, that was a different matter. Brains and energies that could be used counted too. As women themselves, they did not count in his career. The cold eye of that portrait drives the book.

The Hippodrome was a famous London variety theater's name. Hayward sets ambition and exploitation under its lights. Performers, managers, and hangers-on fill her stage. The novel treats show business as business first. Its cynicism feels modern beside period romance. It survives as a sharp theatrical novel.
20116-the-belief-in-immortality-and-the-:
J. G. Frazer wrote The Belief in Immortality and the Worship of the Dead, a vast study of faith. This volume deals much with beliefs in Australia, among other lands. It lists what Queensland peoples held about the soul and the dead. Some held that the dead are born again in new bodies.

Others held that the dead go to the sky or a far land. Frazer sorts such beliefs from reports sent from across the world. His method compares customs side by side on a huge scale. Readers get a landmark of early anthropology, rich in detail and bold claims.
20133-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-at-:
Laura Lee Hope published Bunny Brown and His Sister Sue at Aunt Lu's City Home in 1916. Bunny wakes and laughs as he rubs his sleepy eyes awake. He jokes that Sue thinks they are back on grandpa's farm. Their mother stands smiling at the two children in the hall.

City life gives Bunny and Sue new sights at every turn. Aunt Lu's home brings traffic, shops, and crowds unlike their small town. The Bunny Brown books follow the pair through mild scrapes and bright days. Young readers get gentle fun, family warmth, and a child's view of the city.
20293-a-popular-history-of-the-art-of-mu:
W. S. B. Mathews wrote A Popular History of the Art of Music. He aims to cover the same span that fills far larger histories. Naumann, Ambros, and Fétis used three to ten times the space. Mathews grants that competent judges will differ on his success.

Specimens of music and many engravings help the reader hear and see. The book runs from the earliest times to the composer's own day. It made music history plain to students and keen amateurs alike. Readers get a brisk, well-stocked tour of Western music in one volume.
20464-a-journey-through-france-in-war-ti:
Joseph G. Butler, Jr. toured France in 1917 as part of an American commission, and his book reports what he saw. The chapters move from the front to hospitals and cities. Photographs show the commissioners and a typical French soldier in uniform.

Later chapters describe the Carrel method of treating wounds. Another follows a city caught in an army's path. The contents run to twenty-six chapters in all. Butler closes with his impressions of France and the French people. The book gave American readers a businessman's eyewitness account of their new ally at war.
20559-r-holmes-co-being-the-remarkable-a:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote R. Holmes and Co. as a comic answer to Sherlock Holmes and the gentleman thief Raffles. His hero, Raffles Holmes, is the son of Holmes and the daughter of Raffles. He solves cases with a thief's talents and a detective's brain, and keeps the profits vague.

The narrator suffers through a New York heat wave. Even the radiators, cold all winter, now hiss at the touch of a moistened finger. Enough cooling drinks to float an ocean liner have passed into him, with no effect. Bangs's parodies were best sellers in their day.
2059-the-little-shepherd-of-kingdom-come:
John Fox Jr. sets a Kentucky novel in the mountains and the Bluegrass, following Chad, a mountain boy who runs away, finds a home, and grows into a gentleman. School, a tournament, a trial, and college mark his rise. Fox wrote of Kentucky mountains he knew well, and his dialect gives the tale its local sound.

The Civil War then splits his world, putting brother against brother and testing his loyalties to home, to Margaret and Melissa, and to Morgan's men. Fox writes the border country with affection, and the book blends romance with the costs of war. Chad's path from shepherd boy to soldier mirrors Kentucky's own split loyalties in the war.
20632-molly-brown-s-orchard-home:
Nell Speed's Molly Brown's Orchard Home, published in 1915, belongs to her Molly Brown series for girls. Molly and her friends plan a stay at an orchard home, away from their usual college and Kentucky scenes. The trip begins under a cloud, as Molly explains in her letter home.

Our going is not quite so happy as we meant it to be. Kent cannot come with us as we had planned. He will have to stay in Louisville for some months, and may not be able to leave at all this winter. Some complication of their affairs keeps him. The girls go on without him.
20907-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Sages from all Greece stream to Sardis at its height in this classic prose piece. Solon of Athens stands among them before rich King Croesus of Lydia. The Best of the World's Classics gathers such peaks of prose in one set.

Henry Cabot Lodge edited this ten-volume store of great writing in 1909. Herodotus here tells how Solon warned Croesus not to call any man happy till death. Tales, essays, speeches, and histories span the whole set. It served homes that wanted the world's best prose, well chosen and handsomely bound, within one shelf's reach.
21038-a-dog-with-a-bad-name:
Dry rot eats Bolsover College from within in A Dog with a Bad Name. Years of slow decay, Reed writes, have left patching near hopeless there. Boys expelled and masters resigned mark the school's vain tries at cure.

A boy with a bad name, fairly or not, stands at the tale's sore centre. School honour, false blame, and grit fill Reed's plot with real stakes. He asks how a name sticks and what it costs to clear one. Among his school tales, this one cuts deepest, a story of reputation in a world where boys judge fast and forgive slow.
21227-shenac-s-work-at-home:
Margaret Murray Robertson opens with sorrow in a Scottish district long ago, when many families were driven from homes held for generations. Most chose to cross the ocean and build new homes in a strange world beyond the sea. Shenac's story grows from that leaving of Scotland.

The emigrants left kirks, graves, and kin behind, facing weeks or months on the water with little knowledge of the land ahead. Robertson follows what such families made of Canada, and how a young woman like Shenac could work for her home from inside it. Faith, endurance, and household duty carry the tale, as in her other Scottish Canadian stories.
21345-a-wounded-name:
Captain Charles King was a career army officer and prolific novelist of the frontier army. He opens in a dust cloud on the alkali flats, as a stagecoach lurches toward Sancho's ranch. Sancho keeps a dinner ranch and watches through a fine binocular for passengers, with the boy Pedro announcing every cloud of dust. A disgraced officer's arrival starts the tale.

The title quotes Shakespeare: poor wounded name, my bosom as a bed shall lodge thee. King builds his plot on an officer's ruined reputation and its slow repair among soldiers, prospectors, and ranch folk in the West. His own service at West Point and on campaign gave his army tales their easy authority.
21562-the-gulf-and-inland-waters-the-nav:
A. T. Mahan tells the naval war on the Gulf and the rivers in The Gulf and Inland Waters, copyrighted in 1883. The book is volume three of The Navy in the Civil War. Mahan, a serving captain, built his tale chiefly on official reports.

Where reports left gaps, he wrote to men who had been there and asked. River fleets, blockade work, and the taking of ports fill the narrative. New Orleans, Mobile, and the Mississippi campaigns stand at its heart. Mahan later won world fame for his books on sea power, and this crisp, early history shows the mind at work.
21625-play-the-game:
Honor Carmody likes the boys, and owns it, in Ruth Comfort Mitchell's Play the Game! The book was copyrighted in 1920 and issued in book form by Appleton. Honor's mother and stepfather plan to send her to Marlborough school in Los Angeles.

Honor is aghast, sure she could not bear a girls' school. Mrs Lorimer, her friend's mother, is lovely and girlish at forty-one, with six children. She warns against letting a girl be queer, in the talk of the day. Mitchell, who also wrote verse tales, builds a bright tale of school, sport, and young love.
21629-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Volume two of The Best of the World's Classics, restricted to prose, treats Rome from 234 B.C. to 180 A.D. Henry Cabot Lodge leads the editing, with Francis W. Halsey as his partner. Portraits of Marcus Aurelius, Caesar, Cicero, and Seneca front the book, issued in 1909.

Cato the Censor opens with rules for running a Roman farm. Cicero follows with essays on old age, friendship, and duty, and a letter on his daughter's death. Notes explain each writer's life and place. The ten-volume set aimed to give home readers the cream of world prose in sound translations.
21679-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Volume three of The Best of the World's Classics, restricted to prose, covers Great Britain and Ireland from 1281 to 1745. Henry Cabot Lodge and Francis W. Halsey edit the set, issued in 1909. Milton, Bacon, Chaucer, and Shakespeare stand pictured at the front.

Richard de Bury opens with In Praise of Books, from his Philobiblon. De Bury, bishop of Durham and chancellor of England, founded a library at Oxford. Mandeville's travels and Wyclif's gospel rendering follow, then Chaucer on riches. Notes give each writer's life and place, in a home library of the world's best prose.
21877-woodrow-wilson-and-the-world-war-a:
America under Wilson is chronicled in Charles Seymour's Woodrow Wilson and the World War, a 1921 volume in the Yale Chronicles of America series. Seymour begins on March 4, 1913, when Wilson entered the White House as the first Democratic president elected in twenty years. No one, he says, could have guessed the part Wilson would play. Chapters follow neutrality, the submarine crisis, plots and preparedness, and America's decision for war.

The home front and the fighting front each get their due before the path to peace. The peace conference, the League of Nations fight, and the Senate's rejection of the treaty close the tale. Seymour wrote as a scholar close to events. The book remains a clear, early history of America's Great War years.
21890-the-path-to-home:
Home, fathers, and small daily kindnesses fill Edgar A. Guest's The Path to Home, a book of poems published in 1919. Guest was America's best-loved newspaper poet, author of Just Folks and A Heap o' Livin'. The index alone maps his world: Daddies, His Dog, The Cookie-Lady, Bread and Jam, and Becoming a Dad. Even the famous It Couldn't Be Done is here.

Guest writes in plain rhyme about mothers at doorways, children at gates, and asters along the fence. War touches the book too, in An Apple Tree in France and At the Peace Table. His secret was simple: he praised the ordinary home as the best place on earth. Millions of readers agreed, and cut his verses from the papers to keep.
22102-the-hills-of-home:
Alfred Coppel wrote The Hills of Home as a pulp science fiction adventure. His hero Jimmy shifts a heavy Martian pistol to his left hand and checks his harness. He is well armed, and he has no fear of the Plant Men. Barefoot, he turns upstream toward the shallows where he can cross the river.

Beyond the crossing lies his search along the base of the Golden Cliffs. A phonograph's sound floats over the water from the enemy side. Coppel mixes Mars, jungle peril, and a boyish hero in the magazine manner. The tale is pure pulp: quick scenes, strange creatures, and a young Earthman at home in an alien wilderness.
22153-pagan-and-christian-rome:
Rodolfo Lanciani, the great archaeologist of Rome, wrote Pagan and Christian Rome, issued in English in 1892. Lanciani had directed excavations across the city for years. His book moves between two Romes that share the same streets. One plate shows the graves found around the tomb of St. Peter, drawn from a rare engraving by the Pope's master mason.

Lanciani describes temples turned into churches, martyrs' shrines, and catacombs. He writes as a digger who knew the soil layer by layer. Tourists and scholars both used his books as guides to the ruins. This volume remains a vivid record of Rome's archaeology in its heroic age.
22184-more-tales-in-the-land-of-nursery-:
More Tales in the Land of Nursery Rhyme continues a series that sends children into the country where rhymes live. In this scene, delicate foreign birds have been sheltered in a barn through bad weather. The home birds despise them as foreigners. The strangers crouch shyly in a corner, silent unless spoken to, while a cold English winter beats outside.

Around such episodes the tales weave Mother Goose figures into small adventures. The land of nursery rhyme works like a storybook map: every rhyme a place to visit. Ada M. Marzials and her collaborators made the series for children who already knew the rhymes by heart. This volume adds fresh tales to the first collection's world.
22193-an-englishwoman-s-home:
An Englishwoman's Home, published in 1918, is a novel in letters from the last year of the Great War. It opens with a cedar wood box: the writer can see her friend's puzzled brows over so simple a note. Why should opening a box count as a wartime event? The letters answer slowly, through the small happenings of a home under war's shadow.

Domestic detail carries the book: houses, servants, rationed comforts, and news from the front. The writer chronicles a private world the war keeps shaking. Letter novels suited such intimate records well. This one preserves an Englishwoman's home front in 1918 from inside the household itself.
22374-caw-caw-or-the-chronicle-of-crows-:
Caw Caw, or the Chronicle of Crows, tells a spring-time tale in verse. Its subjects are a patient pair of crows. For many weeks, the poem says, they seek no other occupation.

One crow sits and looks around the woods. The other makes the woods resound with loud cawings. He brings worms, seeds, and other good things home. Kindly, he feeds his brooding mate from early morning to late evening. The poem watches nest life with fond, comic care. Readers get a gentle animal story in rhyme. It turns two common birds into a devoted pair worth following through spring.
22381-myths-and-legends-of-ancient-greec:
Myths and Legends of Ancient Greece and Rome retells the old gods' stories for general readers. Its second portion paints a picture of old Greek life. Customs, superstitions, and princely hospitalities fill that part of the work.

Those Greek-life chapters run longer than is usual in such books. The writer thought daily life deserved room beside the myths. Readers thus get tales plus the world that told them. Feasts, homes, and beliefs stand behind the gods and heroes. The book served schools and homes as a first mythology. It still gives a clear, story-first entry into Greek and Roman legend, with manners attached.
22654-the-doctor-of-pimlico-being-the-di:
The Doctor of Pimlico, subtitled Being the Disclosure of a Great Crime, is a crime novel by William Le Queux, the popular writer of thrillers and spy tales. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its title promises a respectable London district hiding a dark secret, a Le Queux specialty.

The sample shows four men walking together: a sharp, grey-haired general with many war ribbons, a tall staff captain in Gordon Highlanders tartan, and two civilians in shooting jackets. Soldiers and sportsmen side by side hint at the military circle the crime will touch. The book delivers period melodrama: hidden guilt, careful disguises, and a slow disclosure. It suits readers of early British crime fiction.
22716-the-book-hunter-at-home:
The Book Hunter at Home is a companion volume of essays on book collecting and the pleasures of the hunt. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its hunter has grown older since his earlier adventures among London's shops, and now writes from his own shelves.

It is a sad truth, the book opens, that bargains come oftener in youth than in age. The sophist may argue that age breeds philosophy, and philosophy scorns worldly things. Yet the book-hunter, among the most philosophical of beings, hunts bargains until his career's very end. Anecdotes of finds, prices, and fellow collectors fill the pages. The tone is club-room mellow, written for readers who measure wealth in shelf feet.
22916-left-at-home:
Mary L. Code sets Left at Home in a pleasant room on a winter's evening. Frost shines clear and cold outside while a bright fire blazes within, lighting the crimson carpet and curtains. On the snowy table-cover stand preparations for tea, of the kind Arthur usually appreciates at this hour. The subtitle calls the tale the heart's resting-place.

Domestic fiction of this kind built its drama from absence, duty, and reunion at the fireside. Someone has been left at home, and the story weighs what home asks of those who keep it. Code writes in the warm, moral register her readers expected. The result is a quiet period tale, best read for its household detail and its faith in ordinary affection.
22960-among-the-pines-or-south-in-secess:
Edmund Kirke travels Among the Pines, in the South in secession time, with a colonel and the colonel's servant Jim. Jim, about thirty, was born and raised in his master's family. The party journeys by day where possible, stopping at night at convenient resting places, the colonel, Jim, and the narrator in the same or adjoining rooms.

Kirke, the pen name of James Roberts Gilmore, wrote to show Northern readers the wartime South from inside. Plantations, poor whites, and enslaved people all enter his sketches, filtered through a Union man's eyes. The book's scenes of travel carry its politics quietly. It remains a vivid, arguable piece of wartime reporting, best read as one witness's South rather than the whole of it.
23117-the-island-home:
A sailor's song opens The Island Home. The opening song praises a following breeze, a full white sail, and a mast bending bravely under it. Our palace is the stout wooden ship, the chorus boasts, and our inheritance the open sea.

Behind the song stands a tale of the sea and of home made on an island, in the tradition of the Robinsonade. Richard Archer's island story, as it is often credited, sends its company through wreck, settlement, and return. Sea songs like the opening set the book's weather, hearty and homesick at once. Readers who like castaway industry, huts raised and gardens planted against the wild, will find the familiar pleasures honestly served.
23127-julian-home:
Prize day glitters in Julian Home. Harton families spend the morning touring school and village. Mothers and sisters wander in delight while their young escorts point out the sights with pride. Some cross the cricket field, others take the pleasant path down toward the bathing place.

Frederic William Farrar wrote Julian Home as a tale of college life, the university answer to his famous school story Eric. Undergraduates, examinations, friendships, and temptations fill its terms. The prize-day opening shows the world at its sunniest, families touring the ground their sons must make good in. Farrar's earnestness governs the whole, a Victorian clergyman's view of youth, affectionate and forever on the watch for the first wrong step.
23264-the-settlers-at-home:
The Settlers at Home opens by placing its scene with care. The land in question is not an island in the sea, the book explains. It is part of Lincolnshire: a tract hilly at its centre and ringed by rivers on most sides.

The Trent runs along its east side. Smaller rivers once ran round the rest and met the Humber northward. That ring of water shapes the settlers' world: cut off, yet connected. Readers get a story of home settlement in the Lincolnshire fens, where water, land, and isolation decide how a community lives.
23276-the-white-rose-of-langley-a-story-:
The White Rose of Langley is a story of the olden time, about a woman worn down by her life. Hard work and exposure have marked her, and sorrow may have marked her too. She sits up and looks wearily over the winter scene spread out before her.

Her voice holds none of a child's querulous complaint. Instead there is the dull, sullen apathy of hopeless endurance. That tone sets the tale's mood at once. Readers get a historical story of endurance under hardship, where winter, labour, and quiet suffering stand in for speeches about fate.
23329-le-monsieur-de-la-petite-dame:
Frances Hodgson Burnett set this short French tale in a theatre box, where a young beauty takes her seat in jewels and bright bloom. Beside her sits her husband, a small, plain man who bears her fan and wrap and keeps to the shade, while the grand Madame de Castro watches from the box across.

The tale turns on looks and rank: the wife draws every eye, the husband draws pity, and Paris talk does the rest. Burnett follows the pair through drawing rooms and social calls, where charm, pride, and cash shape what people see. The story asks, with wit, whether a marriage can hold when the world rates the two partners so far apart.
23408-far-from-home:
J. A. Taylor wrote this science fiction tale of a space flight gone wrong, with pictures by Emsh. A service lift rocket, Able Jake Four, lifts cleanly and reports no faults, but a flaw in its tracking radar keeps it from meeting Space Station One at its set hour.

News hounds crowd the trail within an hour, while the harassed Controller, long steeped in secrets and classified files, hedges over facts that popular science magazines have printed for years. Taylor plays the gap between official silence and public hunger for news, as a routine flight turns into a tense search far from home. The tale suits readers who like early space age drama, brisk and wry about red tape.
23430-rollo-in-rome:
Jacob Abbott wrote this eighteen fifty eight travel tale for young readers, following Rollo on his tour in Europe to Rome. A diligence office, a journey, an arrival, a ramble, and a getting lost chapter set the pace, before the Colosseum, the gladiator, the Tarpeian Rock, and a trip to Ostia.

The Vatican by torchlight, shown in the frontispiece, crowns the visit, with mosaic shops, marshes, ruins, and penance scenes along the way. Abbott teaches as he tells, pausing to explain sights, customs, and history in clear, boy friendly prose. Young travellers and armchair readers alike will enjoy Rollo's Roman days, a gentle guide to a great city in story form.
24268-the-desert-home:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this adventure book, one of the first he wrote, set in the great desert of the interior of North America. Some travelers setting out across that central desert lose their way, until they spot the light of a farmhouse, knock, and receive hospitality. Their kind hosts then explain their life there, and how lovely the place is.

Much of the rest of the book tells of encounters with animals and the uses of many trees and shrubs, in short chapters that hold attention well. The first chapter measures the desert itself, some 1,500 miles long and 1,000 wide, near a million square miles. Readers get a family adventure of desert life, told with naturalist detail.
2439-the-history-of-england-from-the-acc:
Thomas Babington Macaulay's History of England, in this volume from the accession of James II, tells the story of the Glorious Revolution and its aftermath. Macaulay follows James's fall, William's landing, and the settlement of a constitutional monarchy, with his famous narrative sweep and Whig confidence. The prose moves like a novel, with battles, debates, and vivid characters.

The history's partisanship is open, and modern scholars correct its judgments, but its storytelling remains superb. Readers of English history will find a foundational, if dated, classic. The volume stands as a monument of Victorian historiography.
24395-the-winds-of-time:
James H. Schmitz wrote this science fiction story, with pictures by Brotman. Its blurb tells the setup: a man contracts for a charter trip, but his hirer is not quite a man, and wants more than service. Pilot Gefty Rammer, owner of Rammer Spacelines, walks the passages of the Silver Queen between control compartment and staterooms. He tries to trade a haggard look for self-assurance, lest his passengers suspect he was just a step from gibbering.

In Mr. Maulbow's stateroom, Maulbow lies pale and unconscious on a couch, knocked out when unknown forces batted the Queen about as never before in eighteen years. Kerim Ruse, Maulbow's secretary, kneels beside her employer checking his pulse, and asks Gefty what he found. Gefty shrugs: the ship is undamaged, a tough tub, but what he saw from the escape hatch matches the screens. Readers get a charter trip gone strange.
24740-the-battle-of-spring-hill-tennesse:
Captain John K. Shellenberger read this paper to the Missouri Commandery of the Loyal Legion on February 2, 1907. He had fought at Spring Hill himself and spent more than twenty-five years gathering reports, letters, and talks with officers on both sides. His subject is the missed chance of November 1864, when Confederate forces let a Union army slip past them in the night.

Shellenberger walks the reader over the ground, fence corner by fence corner, and weighs who bore blame for the failure, naming Cheatham, Stewart, and Bate. He quotes generals freely and revisits the field twice. Civil War readers will find a close, soldier's-eye account of one of the war's strangest nights.
24918-hollowdell-grange-holiday-hours-in:
George Manville Fenn wrote Hollowdell Grange, one of his earliest books, about a London boy who spends a holiday with cousins in the country. The change from city streets to Lincolnshire lanes challenges him at every turn: farm animals, village characters, and country ways all feel strange and new.

Country scenes fill the book. A hot midsummer day at Hollowdell station shows the porter asleep and the dog snapping at flies. Later come a near drowning and a final failed rescue of a drowning lad trapped in a beach sluice. Lincolnshire speech runs through the talk. Fenn tells a warm, lively story of a town boy learning country life.
25292-in-nesting-time:
Olive Thorne Miller's In Nesting Time, published in 1893 with copyright 1888, is a book of bird sketches from careful observation. Miller opens with Jean Ingelow's rebuke of studying wild creatures by shooting them first, and promises instead live individuals in feathers, honestly observed.

Sketches follow baby birds, purple crow blackbirds, redwings, yellow-throated warblers, and Baltimore orioles. A pair kept in her room shows courtship manners: waiting turns at the bath, sitting on one perch, and tender calls when one strays. Miller's book helped teach American readers to watch birds alive rather than collect them dead.
25303-the-bad-boy-at-home-and-his-experi:
Walter T. Gray's Bad Boy at Home, published in 1885, is a comic diary by a boy who has just returned from Europe and decided to become an editor. He rejects school, he says, because schoolboys learn nothing but baseball and prize fighting, and he plans to make New York howl from the top rung of the ladder.

Written in cheerful misspelling, the book follows his Daily Buster prospectus and his midnight war with bedbugs. The enemy army, under Major General Bloodsucker, scales the walls while the boy defends his chair with wash basins for a moat. The title calls it the funniest book of the age, and it aims to earn the boast.
25396-dotty-dimple-at-home:
Sophie May's Dotty Dimple at Home, published in Boston in 1870, is the second volume of the Dotty Dimple Stories. Dotty, a small girl of large feelings, moves through chapters called The Lion and the Lamb, Fire, Playing Hindoo, Running Wild, and Johnny's Revenge.

A sailing adventure in a bowl shows May's comic touch. Solly, Lina, Dotty, and a deaf and dumb boy rock fearfully as wind drives them from a shore so near and yet so far. A new home, a surprise, and a sad story round out the book. May's tales charmed a generation of young readers.
25552-milk-for-you-and-me:
Winifred Randell, formerly of the Laboratory School at the University of Chicago, writes this short picture book for small children, issued by the National Dairy Council and revised in 1958. Its refrain tells the story in one line: it is milk for you and me.

Cows eat green grass in a sunny pasture, give milk every day, and are milked in a clean barn with clean hands and a clean machine. A truck then carries the cold, clean milk from farm to dairy. Simple sentences and pictures trace each step from pasture to table.
2577-the-ancient-regime:
Hippolyte Taine opens his great history, The Origins of Contemporary France, with this volume on the old order before the Revolution. Taine examines the structure of French society, the origin of noble privilege, and the public and local services owed by the privileged classes.

Later books in the volume study drawing room life, its habits, its charms, and its hidden costs, and the spirit and doctrines that grew within it. Taine writes as a stern analyst, piling detail upon detail. The book remains a classic portrait of a society that glittered at the top while its foundations cracked below.
26088-a-son-of-hagar-a-romance-of-our-ti:
Hall Caine's romance follows two brothers, Hugh and Paul, divided by a woman who leaves them both and takes the veil. Paul learns she is in the Catholic convent at Westminster, and the brothers' meeting turns bitter, each blaming the other for her loss.
