The tale opens with a glossary of Cumbrian words and a preface recalling Caine's earlier novel.

Caine sets the story in the present day, with the brothers' quarrel, the woman's choice, and the weight of a past misdeed driving the plot. The dedication to R. D. Blackmore frames the book as a bid for the deep, tranquil strength Caine admired in his elder. It is a novel of guilt, rivalry, and a love closed off by the convent door.
2612-the-history-of-england-from-the-acc:
Thomas Babington Macaulay continues his History of England in this third volume, covering chapters eleven through sixteen. William and Mary are proclaimed in London, rejoicings spread through England and Holland, and clergy, army, Tories, and Whigs each take their temper.

Macaulay follows ministerial arrangements, with William acting as his own minister for foreign affairs, and the new regime finding its feet. His prose drives forward with famous energy, judging men and measures in bold strokes. The volume remains a classic of narrative history, admired for style even where scholars now qualify its verdicts.
26198-south-africa-and-the-transvaal-war:
Louis Creswicke's South Africa and the Transvaal War, volume two of six, covers the war from its start to the Battle of Colenso on December 15, 1899. Published at Edinburgh in 1900, with maps and pictures, it opens with crisis at home and the occupation of Dundee. Battles at Glencoe, Elandslaagte, and Reitfontein follow, with the disaster at Nicholson's Nek.

Later chapters treat the sieges of Ladysmith, Mafeking, and Kimberley, the invasion of Cape Colony, and fights at Belmont, Graspan, and Modder River. The volume closes at Colenso, after Magersfontein, and it prints a facsimile of Rudyard Kipling's war poem The Absent-Minded Beggar. A frontispiece shows the Black Watch after Magersfontein.
26310-my-new-home:
Mrs. Molesworth's 1894 children's novel, with pictures by L. Leslie Brooke, follows Helena Charlotte Naomi Wingfield, fourteen past, to a new home. Helena introduces herself at Windy Gap, names her two sisters, and sets out the move that shapes the book. Chapters promise new friends and a plan, a happy day, a house called Waving View, and the beginning of troubles.

Later come two letters, a great change, number 29 Chichester Square, an arrival, and a catastrophe. Harry, Kezia's counsel, and a cousin Cosmo rushing uphill all play their parts. Helena also watches the Nestor family, whose father's illness weighs on her conscience. The book treats moving house as a child's great adventure, full of loss and fresh hope.
2642-back-home:
Eugene Wood dedicated this memoir to the memory of the woman he knew back home as My Ma Mag, and wrote it for readers who remember small town America. Chapters recall the old red schoolhouse, the Sabbath school, the revolving year, and the swimming hole.

Firemen's tournaments, devouring elements, and neighborhood characters fill the pages with warmth and humor. Wood writes as a man looking back with affection, not bitterness, at a vanished boyhood. The book charms as a gentle American remembrance, full of local color and quiet feeling. The dedication gives the book its tender key, and the chapters keep returning to it.
26517-mary-jane-s-city-home:
Clara Ingram Judson's 1920 children's book, illustrated by Thelma Gooch, follows Mary Jane and her sister Alice to a new city home. The story opens on a Pullman car, where late sun falls on a map spread between the seats and Mary Jane asks about a wiggly line of water. Their father explains the map as the train carries them toward the city.

Chapters follow neighbors around the corner, visits with Betty, sand castles at the beach, a beach supper, shopping, and a bus ride. A birthday luncheon, a lost doll cart, a trip to the zoo, days in the parks, and school beginning fill the year, closing with Christmas in Chicago and a summer home. The book charms through small, everyday adventures.
26742-the-chautauqua-girls-at-home:
Pansy, author of Four Girls at Chautauqua, published this sequel with William Briggs at Toronto, with Montreal and Halifax agents. It follows the girls home after the revelation of Chautauqua, opening on the last Sabbath of August, their first Sabbath at home since that summer. The world looks made over new, and their First Church, finest in choir, organ, carpets, and floral display, becomes the visible temple of the invisible God.

Ruth Erskine sits in her father's pew in delicate summer silks, laces about her white throat, looking unchanged while her heart sings for joy. Chapters follow Flossy beginning, burdens, Colonel Baker's Sabbath evening, new music, prayer-meeting and tableaux, Dr. Dennis's study, and looking for work. A revival meeting brings a solemn hush, with ladies standing, including volatile Flossy Shipley, in a story of faith carried into daily life.
26919-the-new-education-a-review-of-prog:
Scott Nearing, of the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, published this review of progressive movements with Row, Peterson and Company in 1915. An introduction on the old education carries harsh words from inside and a word from Huxley and Spencer. It leads to a new basis grounded in social change, city life, and the early home. Later chapters ask whether child or subject matter should come first, and attack the fallacious average.

Nearing visits kindergartens, model English lessons, and school shops. He follows the high school's effort to keep in step with life. He reports higher education at Lowville, a great city school system, the Oyler School of Cincinnati, and rural education. One experiment stands out. At Newton, seventy pupils of fifteen or more, forty girls and thirty boys, moved from seventh and eighth grades into high school without examination, to test whether they would thrive.
26982-with-haig-on-the-somme:
D. H. Parry's 1917 boys' war story sends Dennis to the Somme with Haig's army, in the thick of the First World War fighting. The chapters run from an uncensored letter read aloud and his first time under fire to dispatch riding, a sniper's lair, and a daring dash behind enemy lines.

Dennis meets a French pilot, Claude Laval, escapes from enemy hands, and learns the soldier's trade in dugouts, trenches, and gun positions. Written while the war still raged, the book mixes adventure with a young reader's first picture of what the Western Front demanded.
27528-rules-and-regulations-governing-ma:
The California State Board of Charities and Corrections compiled and published these rules in September 1922, from offices in San Francisco and Los Angeles. The booklet prints the law that governs maternity hospitals and homes, with the board's own regulations for licensing and supervision.

That law is chapter 69 of the Statutes of 1913, approved 23 April 1913 and in effect 10 August 1913. It covers maternity hospitals and lying-in asylums, where women are received during pregnancy, delivery, or after delivery. It also covers institutions, boarding houses, and homes for the reception and care of children. Violations carried a penalty under the act. The board watched each place named in the law.
27771-once-on-a-time:
A. A. Milne wrote this 1922 fairy-tale novel, decorated by Charles Robinson and published by Grosset and Dunlap by arrangement with G. P. Putnam's Sons. It is set in the invented kingdoms of Euralia and Barodia, with Araby far distant.

The King of Euralia, the Princess Hyacinth, Prince Udo, and the Countess move through twenty-two chapters of court comedy, wizards who may not exist, and whiskers dropped as a habit. Playful and ironic, the book shows Milne's lighter fantasy voice before Winnie-the-Pooh made him famous. Illustrations include a map of Euralia and Barodia, kings nursing bent whiskers, and armies returning to find majesties asleep.
27873-the-spirit-of-rome:
Vernon Lee wrote The Spirit of Rome, leaves from a diary, recording returns to Rome across the years from 1895 to 1905. Lee, brought up in Rome, discovered the city anew for herself after many years away, and dedicated the book to friends living and dead who made Rome what it is to her.

Entries visit the Sistine Chapel, the Pantheon, Villa Madama, the Alban Hills, the catacombs, and the Rione Monti, with seasons marked spring by spring. The diary blends art, history, and personal feeling, and it remains a classic of literary travel writing about Rome.
27887-wild-animals-at-home:
Ernest Thompson Seton published Wild Animals at Home with Doubleday, Page and Company in 1923, after a 1913 copyright, with over one hundred and fifty sketches and photographs by the author. Seton, head chief of the Woodcraft Indians, had already written Wild Animals I Have Known and Two Little Savages.

Contents cover the coyote, the prairie-dog and his kin, famous fur-bearers such as fox, marten, beaver, and otter, and horned and hoofed animals from blacktail deer to moose. Written from field observation, the book teaches natural history through stories of individual animals.
28101-the-van-dwellers-a-strenuous-quest:
Albert Bigelow Paine's The Van Dwellers, published in 1901, is a comic memoir of hunting for a home in New York City. Paine and his wife move from flat to flat, try a boarding house, and meet landlords, movers, and servants who test their patience. He dedicates the book, with a wink, to all who have lived in flats.

Each chapter reports a fresh failure or small win, from a first home in the city to a gilded flat that proves too grand. The humour comes from plain facts: thin walls, steep stairs, and rent that never quite fits. It remains a lively picture of city renting at the turn of the century.
28512-what-s-his-name:
George Barr McCutcheon's What's-His-Name, published by Grosset & Dunlap in March 1911 with illustrations by Harrison Fisher, makes its hero an unnoticed man. Two actors outside the Empire Theatre on Broadway spot him and name him as Nellie Duluth's husband. He ambles through life unseen, even by people whose business is noticing everything.

Chapters titled Our Hero, Miss Nellie Duluth, Mr. Fairfax, Luncheon, Christmas, The Revolver, The Lawyer, and Blakeville follow his marriage and troubles. Fairfax, Phoebe, and the stage world around Nellie sharpen the comic contrast. Readers get a light novel about fame's shadow and the man beside it.
28864-a-new-subspecies-of-microtus-monta:
E. Raymond Hall and Keith R. Kelson wrote this 1951 natural history paper naming a new subspecies of the montane vole from Montana. In 1949, John A. White collected two voles in the Bitterroot Valley for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History that fit no named subspecies. The authors compared them with Montana specimens in the United States National Museum, some earlier reported as Microtus nanus canescens.

Their study finds that animals from the Bitterroot and Flathead valleys form a heretofore unrecognized subspecies, named Microtus montanus pratincolus. The type is an adult female from six miles east of Hamilton, at thirty-seven hundred feet, taken August 14, 1949. Readers get a short, exact piece of mammal taxonomy, with measurements and comparisons.
28874-comments-on-the-taxonomy-and-geogr:
E. Raymond Hall and Keith R. Kelson wrote this 1951 paper on the taxonomy and geographic range of some North American rabbits. While preparing maps of lagomorph distribution, they found conflicting statements in the literature about the Florida cottontail and the Audubon cottontail. They examined specimens, mostly from the Biological Surveys collection of the Fish and Wildlife Service, with help from a Navy research contract.

The paper opens with the Florida cottontail in Nebraska, where confusion had grown over its subspecific identity. Hall and Kelson sort the names, dates, and specimens with museum care. Readers interested in mammal science get a short, technical correction to the record, showing how range maps are built from specimens, not guesses.
28936-in-the-morning-of-time:
Charles G. D. Roberts wrote this 1922 novel of the morning of time, when the world had no men. Its chapters follow a long-necked beast in teeming estuary waters and a king of the triple horn. They move on to the finding of fire, the children of the shining one, and the puller-down of trees. Later chapters bring the battle of the brands, the rescue of A-ya, and the bending of the bow.

Roberts, author of The Kindred of the Wild, imagines early human life through animal eyes and primitive struggle, with fire, fear, and the dark as great powers. The book blends natural history with romance, in prose that lingers on beasts and landscapes. Readers get a poetic prehistory, written before modern paleontology, but full of wonder at life's first mornings.
29143-pius-ix-and-his-time:
The Reverend Æneas MacDonell Dawson wrote this 1880 life, Pius IX and His Time, printed by Thos. Coffey in London. Dawson argues that Pius IX's pontificate was eventful beyond all others, with doctrines once open to discussion now pronounced in accord with all preceding Christian ages. The church extended the place of her tent vastly, and Pius himself lived longer than any predecessor, not even Peter attaining his length of days.

Yet the pontiff and the Catholic people beheld the loss of the patrimony of St. Peter, though the papacy, more ancient than its temporal power, still survives in undiminished vigor. The book opens with John Mary Count Mastai Ferreti, born at Sinigaglia on May 13, 1792. Readers get a Catholic biography of the longest-reigning pope, reverent in tone and rich in nineteenth-century church history.
292-beauty-and-the-beast-and-tales-of-ho:
Bayard Taylor retells Beauty and the Beast as a story of old Russia, borrowed from the author Petjerski. Beauty and the Beast and Tales of Home opens by softening the Russian original's sharp outlines with color and sentiment. A merchant's daughter meets a beast who is more than he seems.

Other tales follow: The Strange Friend, Jacob Flint's Journey, Twin-Love, and Eli's Daughter. Miss Bartram's Trouble and Mrs. Strongitharm's Report close the set. Taylor's domestic stories mix fancy with American home life. The volume shows a popular Victorian storyteller at work.
29261-animaduersions-uppon-the-annotacio:
Francis Thynne wrote these animadversions, or critical notes, on the annotations and corrections of some imperfections in printed editions of Chaucer's works. This text follows the 1865 Early English Text Society edition, edited by G. H. Kingsley, with features adopted from the 1876 Chaucer Society re-edition. Thynne, a Tudor antiquary, worked from manuscripts against faulty print.

Thynne lists his works, corrects readings, and argues over words and lines, showing how early editors tried to restore Chaucer. The notes preserve period spelling in the original, with modern editorial marks for supplied letters. Readers get a founding document of English textual criticism, valuable for Chaucer scholars and for anyone curious how old books were first put right.
29293-priestess-of-the-flame:
Sewell Peaslee Wright published this story in Astounding Stories in June 1932, with Commander John Hanson recounting the extraordinary story of Liane, Priestess of the Flame. Hanson, narrator of Wright's Special Patrol Service tales, opens by answering protests about his comments on women. Most protests, he notes with amusement, came from young men.

Hanson says he has suggested that women, in his experience, show a sad lack of ability with mechanical contrivances, though a careful search finds few uncomplimentary remarks. Liane's story then takes over, with flame, power, and a priestess whose authority is absolute where she rules. Readers get a pulp space tale of a formidable woman, told by a narrator whose views she promptly outshines.
29410-the-end-of-time:
Wallace West's short tale, printed in Astounding Stories in March 1933, opens with a little chemist's startling claim: time itself will end at six o'clock that morning. His guest, Jack Baron, a young radio engineer working at the Rothafel Radio laboratories, laughs it off as a yarn fit for the movies. The chemist insists that something is paralyzing humanity's time-sense, and that the final stroke will fall about daybreak.

West plays the idea for dread rather than mere spectacle: by millions, Earth's creatures slow and drop as their sense of time fails. Baron must learn that clocks and stars have nothing to do with the inner sense that orders life. Fans of early science tales will enjoy a tense, original story built on a single strange premise.
29418-the-man-from-time:
Frank Belknap Long's science tale follows Moonson, a daring man of the far future who bears a proud name yet fears to speak it aloud. The story's puzzle is plain and vast: how can one man be pinpointed in the whole of eternity? Long's answer turns on a simple human quality, found by a mind of great perception, that proves most effective even in solving time and space.

Moonson tries to conquer fear by laughing at every sin that ever was and doing as he pleases, a phrase the tale traces back to the Elizabethan age. Watching a green land in golden sunlight restores his purpose by its calm alone. Fans of classic science fiction will enjoy a thoughtful, strange tale of fear, courage, and time.
2951-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Childhood and adolescence in Venice begin the complete memoirs. Machen's translation of the rare 1894 London edition opens with Casanova at Dux. An editor's note warns that the memoirs were not written for children and may outrage readers offended by Chaucer, La Fontaine, Rabelais, and the Old Testament. Arthur Symons contributes an unpublished chapter on Casanova at Dux. The young Casanova's apprenticeship in adventure begins early, and a scene with Bettina's mother, begging him to come down because her daughter is dying, shows his mix of revenge and alarm.

Bettina lies writhing with convulsions in her father's bed. The volume establishes the voice that carries through the whole memoirs, candid, comic, and unashamed.
2952-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
A young Casanova serves as a cleric in Naples in this Venetian-years volume. Arthur Machen translated the rare unabridged London text of 1894, with chapters added from Arthur Symons's discoveries. Casanova's chapter headings recall misfortunes in Chiozza, Father Stephano, the lazaretto at Ancona, a Greek slave, and a pilgrimage to Our Lady of Loretto. The narrative follows the young adventurer on foot from Rome to Naples to meet a bishop, then on to Martorano and back.

An ambassador's retinue, styled grand, proves to consist of a Milanese steward named Carcinel and a handful of followers. The volume shows Casanova already trading on charm, luck, and nerve across Italy.
2953-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
A cassock gives way to a uniform in this Military Career volume. Casanova renounces the church, watches Therese leave, and takes an ensign's commission. He goes to Venice, where he is appointed ensign in the army of his native country. He embarks for Corfu and lands at Orsera for a walk. Careful to avoid notice, he takes a small inn at Bologna and sends letters to Therese and a French officer before buying linen.

A later passage weighs whether seeing a beautiful woman named Zelmi would dazzle him into passion and spoil the purity of his decision. The volume shows the young adventurer trading a cassock for a uniform.
2954-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Back in Venice after service abroad, Casanova gives up the army to become a fiddler. Machen's translation of the rare 1894 London edition carries the story. The chapters open with a fearful misfortune, cooling love, and a departure from Corfu, followed by giving up the army to become a fiddler. A wound heals while Madame F prepares to leave her bed and resume her usual life. Casanova joins a governor's review at Gouyn, traveling by galley on orders to meet his patron the next day.

The volume's confessions turn candid about his conduct, admitting that a life spent supplanting rivals and pleasing only himself was certain to be disliked. It shows the adventurer at his most self-aware, between soldiering and music.
2955-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Milan and Mantua receive Casanova after slight misfortunes drive him from Venice. Charles and his lovely wife visit on Low Sunday. On Low Sunday, Charles visits with his lovely wife, whose powdered hair pleases Casanova less than Christine's raven locks and country dress. Husband and wife bear the stamp of happiness, whatever their finery. Casanova reads a letter in secret, catching the word Cesena, a village name.

He turns it into a plan to buy a sheath on credit, asking a friend to endorse his letters of exchange. The volume moves through Milanese and Mantuan society with the usual mix of gallantry, debt, and improvisation. It shows the adventurer rebuilding his fortunes town by town.
2956-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Paris opens this Casanova volume, subtitled To Paris and Prison. The adventurer arrives from Bologna by way of Reggio and Parma, in Machen's rendering of the 1894 text. Casanova leaves Bologna a happy man, parts from a captain at Reggio after a delightful night with Henriette, and reaches Parma, where Henriette resumes women's dress and the pair enjoy mutual felicity. Relatives appear whom he chooses not to recognize.

The change from disguise to open life strikes him as sudden as a pantomime transformation, and the short sentence Come to Parma proves a fortunate catastrophe. Later chapters follow him through Parisian society, jealous guardians, and amorous schemes. The volume captures Casanova in his element, moving between cities, lovers, and new identities.
29563-geographic-variation-in-the-harves:
J. Knox Jones, Jr., and B. Mursaloglu wrote this 1961 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History, on geographic variation in the harvest mouse, Reithrodontomys megalotis, on the central Great Plains and in adjacent regions. Printed July 24, 1961, as volume fourteen, number two, pages nine to twenty-seven, with one figure in the text, it treats a small mammal across a wide range.

Earlier work by Hoffmeister and Warnock in 1955 had studied western harvest mice from Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, judging one subspecies sound. Jones and Mursaloglu test that judgment with new material. Students of mammalogy will find a careful, technical study of how one mouse varies from place to place.
2957-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Vienna at twenty-eight opens this Venice volume of To Paris and Prison. Casanova arrives well dressed but short of money, awaiting a letter of exchange. He arrives in the Austrian capital well provided with clothes but short of money, curtailing expenses until a letter of exchange drawn on M. de Bragadin arrives. His only recommendation comes from the Dresden poet Migliavacca to an illustrious patron. Casanova's Venetian chapters mix gifts, kisses, and scruples.

A charming young woman takes off shoes and stockings to try pairs he gave her, and he finds her innocence a check on his designs. The volume shows him balancing gallantry with a conscience he cannot quite silence. Vienna and Venice frame a young man's education in Europe.
2958-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
A nun becomes Casanova's lover in the Convent Affairs volume. Machen's translation tells how astonishment under the spell of her beauty nearly undid his wit. Countess Coronini, a lover's pique, a reconciliation, and a first meeting frame the chapters, with a philosophical parenthesis in between. Casanova admits he feared giving a poor opinion of his intelligence, so rambling might his answers have been.

The memoir lingers on small, charged details, including a diamond brooch unfastened from a ruffle and sensations he claims years cannot weaken. The convent setting heightens both the risk and the romance. The volume shows Casanova the storyteller at his most intimate, turning a forbidden courtship into a sustained narrative.
2959-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
A casino supper with the French ambassador opens this False Nun volume. Casanova feels pleased with his party, yet gambling anxiety torments him. A proposal from his companion follows, with consequences Casanova accepts, and his mistress proves unfaithful without giving him ground to complain. The supper pleases him, yet anxiety torments him.

The anxiety comes from his fatal habit of gambling, a passion so rooted that to live and to play seem two names for one thing. A later figure, Condulmer, sixty years old, passes for a saint while lending money and loving women, gaming, and gain. The volume shows Casanova's pleasures and his ruinous habit side by side.
2960-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Under the Leads locks Casanova in the Venetian prison beneath the Doge's palace roof. The volume recounts his arrest, his earthquake, and his long wait for judgment. The chapters open with an earthquake under the leads and the dread word tribunal, which turns Casanova to stone, leaving him only passive obedience. His desk stands open, papers on the table where he writes, and he hands them to the agent of the tribunal.

Casanova sits motionless as a statue, waiting for the storm without fear, yet overwhelmed by the uselessness of his pains and contrivances. He lifts his soul to God without repentance for what he has done. The volume gives the most famous prison narrative in the memoirs, tense, detailed, and oddly calm at its center.
2961-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
March 1757 brings a letter from Madame Manzoni to open this Paris and Holland volume. Count Tiretta, Abbe Coste, and the pope's niece soon fill the chapters. Count Tiretta of Trevisa, Abbe Coste, and Lambertini, the pope's niece, fill the early chapters, with talk by the fireside, the punishment of Damien, and Tiretta's mistake. Anger from Madame and a reconciliation follow. Casanova's happiness with Mademoiselle de la Meure turns to despair and jealousy when she marries, then to a change for the better.

A convent-bred girl and Tiretta's lodgings, where he likes his keeper's cleanliness and feeling more than her face, show the memoir's odd tenderness. The volume moves between Paris salons and Dutch counting houses with ease.
2962-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Holland and France hold Casanova's fortunes in this Return to Paris volume. He trades on reputation among financiers, oracles, and countesses, with Machen as translator. Letters await him from the comptroller-general, reporting twenty millions in government securities placed with M. d'Afri, who must not go beyond a loss of eight percent. His patron M. de Bernis advises him to do his best and assures him the ambassador will stand behind him.

Casanova moves among financiers, oracles, and countesses, quoting Pico della Mirandola on the stars, which influence but do not compel. The Comte d'Eigreville introduces him to his sister, the Comtesse du Remain, eager to meet the famous oracle. The volume shows Casanova as a financial adventurer, trading on reputation as much as on coin.
2963-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Duels, forgeries, and cabala fill this Holland and Germany volume of The Eternal Quest. A pretended countess, a forged bill, and a faithless lover drive the plot. A pretended Countess Piccolomini, a quarrel and duel, Esther and her father M. D'O, and Piccolomini's forged bill of exchange drive the chapters. Casanova is fleeced, threatened with assassination, and drawn into debauch with two Paduan girls.

Esther offers money to soothe his grief, writing that a large sum beyond what her father owes might make her his doctor and her happy in the cure. The rascally St. Germain flees after Casanova baits him, and Manon Baletti proves faithless, announcing her marriage by letter. The volume shows the adventurer's fortunes at their most precarious.
2964-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Swiss towns, monasteries, and inns carry Casanova through this volume of The Eternal Quest. He nearly becomes a monk, then changes his mind with reasons given. He resolves to become a monk, goes to confession, waits a fortnight, meets Giustiniani the Capuchin apostle, and then alters his mind, giving his reasons with candor. Pranks at an inn and dinner with an abbot follow.

The abbot tells cock-and-bull stories with such coolness that Casanova struggles not to laugh, restrained only by the holiness of the place and politeness. Later, a woman named Dubois amuses him till midnight with philosophy, admiring Locke and doubting that thought proves spirit. The volume mixes devotion, doubt, and comedy across Switzerland.
2965-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Voltaire himself receives Casanova in this volume of The Eternal Quest. The pupil of twenty years meets his master, and their talk turns to Ariosto. Casanova tells Voltaire that this is the happiest moment of his life, having been Voltaire's pupil for twenty years. Voltaire answers by asking him to attend his course for twenty more and bring his fees. Their discussions take up Ariosto, the Duc de Villars, and the syndic's three girls.

A dispute with Voltaire follows, and the narrative moves to Aix-en-Savoie and the Marquis Desarmoises. Gambling scenes show a marquis staking three hundred sequins, then breaking the bank on fifty Portuguese crowns. The volume pairs philosophy with gaming, the two tables where Casanova felt most at home.
2966-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Leaving Switzerland, Casanova heads for France and Italy with a cash box others covet. He leaves the Marquis de Prie and his company coveting his cash box. He changes horses at Chamberi, then finds his Grenoble lodging not to his liking and drives to the post office in his carriage. Horoscopes and the doorkeeper's daughters fill the opening chapter. A friend named Valenglard begs him not to tell a newcomer what passed between them, and Casanova promises silence.

Valenglard wishes him a prosperous journey and asks for constant letters, since both men care about the fate of Mademoiselle Roman. The volume moves at travel speed, with money, love, and discretion always in play.
2967-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Genoa, Tuscany, and Rome carry Casanova through this Return to Italy volume. He translates plays, teases Rosalie, and watches his world change. A play, a Russian, Petri, and Rosalie at the convent head the chapters. Casanova translates the Ecossaise for Genoese actors while Rosalie, vexed that Veronique is prettier, draws his teasing comfort. Later passages reflect, with unsettling frankness, on evidence and reputation, and spend two hours of delight with a small, delicate companion.

The volume's candor matches the rest of the memoirs, mixing theatre work with private life. It shows Casanova back in Italy, translating, loving, and watching his world change around him.
2968-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Cardinals, dukes, and gossip fill this Return to Naples volume. Casanova travels through Rome, Naples, and Bologna, with Machen translating. Cardinal Passionei receives him in a vast hall where the cardinal writes, occupying the only chair in the room, and promises to tell the Holy Father of the visit. The chapter then turns to the pope, Masiuccia, and arrival at Naples. Casanova spends a long winter night with lovers, then tells a duke he will leave Naples the next day.

The duke warns that such haste will make people talk and invites him to broth, treating the marriage project as one more prank. The volume shows Casanova navigating cardinals, dukes, and gossip with practiced ease.
2969-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Paris again, imperfect yet the only true town, greets Casanova in this Back Again volume. At ten in the morning he calls on Madame d'Urfe, who receives him with open arms and reports the young Count d'Aranda quite well. Paris, Strasburg, Munich, and Augsburg follow in the chapter headings. Misfortunes at Munich and a sad visit to Augsburg balance the Paris homecoming.

A billiard room scene has d'Ache asking Casanova to lay ten louis he owes against a Swiss officer named Schmit. Men ready to draw cold steel for a yes or no force Casanova to forget a girl rather than quarrel with her father. The volume closes his southern adventures on a note of weary return.
2970-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Milan beckons in this volume, after Casanova gives up Agatha to Lord Percy. The road runs through Pavia, with theatres and gaming tables ahead. An actress, Countess A, a disappointment, Marquis Triulzi, Zenobia, and two marchionesses named Q fill the chapter headings, with the Venetian Barbaro closing the list. Casanova notes that Count d'Aglie encouraged the Corticelli rather than punishing her, and he did not mind, so long as she troubled him no more.

A gambling scene shows a woman losing on three cards in succession, then winning a paroli, pocketing three hundred and sixty sequins for her father weeping with joy. Casanova dances one minuet with her before moving on. The volume shows his Italian years as a round of theatres, gaming tables, and new attachments.
2971-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Genoa and the Mediterranean coast carry Casanova through this South of France volume. At Genoa, a man called Pogomas, known there to all, introduces Casanova to his wife and daughter, whom Casanova leaves on a trifling pretext to dine with his new niece. Rosalie, Signora Isola-Bella, a cook, and a game called biribi fill the chapters. A prince's magnificence shows in an innkeeper's refusal of payment, with orders to serve Casanova in everything and take no money.

His niece laughs as an officer makes love to Marcoline, who understands not a word. The volume shows Casanova moving through southern France as a guest of princes and a maker of his own fortune.
2972-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Toward England goes Casanova in this To London volume. He meets Venetian ambassadors at Lyons before the road carries him on. He meets the Venetian ambassadors at Lyons and Marcoline's uncle, parts from Marcoline, and sets out for Paris on an amorous journey. Freed from the slanders of Possano, he gives himself to his fair Venetian's happiness, as if foreseeing their separation.

Money changers cheat him on guineas for louis, and the young Count d'Aranda, restored to his humble name of Trenti, rides post to show his knowingness. The party sits down to table well pleased with one another when a loud conversation interrupts them. The volume carries Casanova from French roads toward the London adventures that follow.
29722-the-baron-s-yule-feast-a-christmas:
Thomas Cooper, known as the Chartist, printed this Christmas rhyme in London in 1846. He dedicates it to the Countess of Blessington in a sonnet that praises her pity for suffering and her zeal to plead for toil. Cooper asks her to let England hear her plead, in eloquent tongue, that toil be freed from wrong. The dedication sets the tone for a poem that joins old cheer with new conscience.

Cooper says several pieces in the rhyme were written years before, from boyhood scenes above Gainsborough. He loved Coleridge's Christabel by heart and repeated it to his playmate Thomas Miller on woodland rambles. The Baron's Yule Feast itself is a verse tale of a lord's Christmas board, told with old ballad color and a reformer's heart.
29728-cookery-and-dining-in-imperial-rom:
Joseph Dommers Vehling made the first English rendering of the ancient Roman cook book known as Apicius de re Coquinaria. His volume gives a bibliography, a critical review, and a full translation, with a dictionary of technical terms, many notes, and facsimiles of originals. He also drew views and sketches of ancient culinary objects himself. Frederic Starr introduces the work.

The Latin title page names the ten books of Apicius on victuals and condiments, or the art of cookery. Vehling keeps the old recipe numbers, marked with the prescription sign, and preserves the quirks of the text. The result is both a cook book and a work of scholarship. It lets a modern reader taste, or at least study, the dining of imperial Rome.
2973-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
English eccentricity gets Casanova's sharpest treatment in this volume. He studies London's betting clubs, schools, and drawing rooms with an outsider's eye. Chapters cover Castelbajac, Count Schwerin, Sophie at school, a reception at the betting club, and the Charpillon. Casanova wakes after a nightmare night, sad and savage, feeling he could kill a man on the smallest provocation.

The beautiful house he once admired now hangs about his neck like a millstone, and he goes out in traveling clothes to escape it. Later passages show his passions running high and his relief at calming them alone. The volume gives Casanova's sharpest portrait of London society, admiring its freedom while chafing at its coldness.
2974-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Flight drives this London to Berlin volume, as Casanova flees creditors and enemies northward. An avenging parrot and a robber named Pocchini crowd the chapters. Bottarelli, a letter from Pauline, an avenging parrot, Pocchini, and Guerra the Venetian crowd the chapter headings. The comedy's first act ends, and the second begins the next morning with a noise at the street door. Casanova looks from his window to see Pocchini, the scoundrel who robbed him, and the flight gathers speed from there.

A later passage gives Gabrielle twenty guineas and a handsome ring, then prepares riding habits for the next day's journey. The volume shows Casanova escaping creditors, enemies, and entanglements across northern Europe.
2975-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Riga and St. Petersburg await Casanova in this Russia and Poland volume. Prince Charles de Biron, younger son of the Duke of Courland and major-general in Russian service, gives him a distinguished reception after reading his father's letter. The prince is thirty-six, pleasant-looking, and well placed at court. Casanova leaves Riga for St. Petersburg, sees society, buys a slave named Zaira, and entertains the empress for more than an hour with remarks on things of note in the capital.

A conversation about statues and an aunt imposed upon shows his courtly tact. The volume gives his fullest Russian chapters, from Baltic ports to the imperial presence.
2976-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
An order to leave Vienna opens this Spain volume, softened but not annulled by the empress. Casanova then crosses Munich, Augsburg, and Louisburg toward France. Casanova passes through Munich, Augsburg, Louisburg, and Aix-la-Chapelle, reflecting that the greatest mistake in punishing a knave is to leave the rogue alive, since vengeance will follow. A den of thieves without his sword sharpens the lesson.

The narrative turns political as Casanova laments France under revolution, contrasting lettres de cachet and corvees with the whims of the mob and the fancies of the Republic. He calls the people the most brutal and tyrannical sovereign in the world. The volume mixes travel, intrigue, and political complaint from a man who loved the old order.
2977-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Expulsion from Spain drives Casanova's flight in this volume. Manucci's vengeance sends him from Madrid toward Barcelona and the French frontier. A mistake makes Manucci his mortal foe, whose vengeance drives Casanova from Madrid through Saragossa and Valentia to Barcelona. Casanova writes that the memoirs console him in the dreadful weariness killing him in Bohemia, though his spirit and desires stay as young as ever. Danger sharpens on the road, as a messenger warns at ten o'clock that assassins wait near the French frontier.

The man drank with the killers at Casanova's expense and learned they planned murder on the approach. The volume shows the adventurer old in body, quick in mind, and still outrunning enemies.
2978-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Rome receives Casanova again in this volume of Spanish Passions. Roman society, polished rooms, and old trouble await him. Chapters list an actor's punishment, Lord Baltimore, Naples, Sara Goudar, the departure of Betty, Agatha, Medina, Albergoni, Miss Chudleigh, and the Prince of Francavilla. The narrative opens in medias res, with Casanova falling over an Englishman and cutting his left hand on a nail. Betty binds the bleeding finger with a handkerchief while Sir B reads a letter with great attention.

Garden walks, warnings, and involuntary passion follow, as the memoir moves between Roman society and private adventure. The volume shows Casanova older, still restless, and still finding trouble in the most polished rooms.
2979-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
From Florence to Trieste, Casanova travels as exile and petitioner. He seeks asylum from a young grand duke and trades wit before princes. Madame Denis, Dedini, Zanovitch, and Zen head the chapters, with an enforced departure and arrival at Bologna under General Albergati. Casanova asks a young grand duke for asylum in his dominions for as long as he cares to stay. He tells the duke his reasons for exile from his native land and promises to ask nothing for his necessities.

Later reflections weigh a marquis whose writings offended Rome, noting that in theology one is only in the right when Rome says yes. The volume shows Casanova as exile and petitioner, trading on wit before princes.
2980-the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-:
Old age and death close the memoirs in this final volume. Appendix and supplement fragments carry Casanova from pardon to Dux. The editors admit uncertainty over whether Casanova died before finishing, whether he destroyed the concluding volumes, or whether the manuscript fell into bad hands. What survives is fragmentary. The fragments show Casanova at last obtaining his pardon from the Venetian authorities and writing letters from Dux, including one of April 1784 about a balloon carrying six persons at Vienna.

Another letter notes his usual ailment with wry patience. The volume serves as an epilogue, letting the adventurer's voice fade through letters rather than grand scenes.
29917-old-fashioned-ethics-and-common-se:
William Thomas Thornton, author of a treatise On Labour, published Old-Fashioned Ethics and Common-Sense Metaphysics in London in 1873, with Macmillan and Company. A Berkeley passage from Hylas and Philonous fronts the book, praising a revolt from metaphysical notions to the plain dictates of nature and common sense. Thornton says his preface was pieced from fragments shown him by a frequent companion of his solitude.

Six chapters carry the argument: Anti-Utilitarianism, History's Scientific Pretensions, and David Hume as a Metaphysician. Huxleyism, Recent Phases of Scientific Atheism, and Limits of Demonstrable Theism follow. Thornton writes against fashionable doubt and grand systems alike, in favor of old-fashioned moral sense. The book is a sturdy, combative work of Victorian philosophy.
30047-aircraft-and-submarines-the-story-:
Willis J. Abbot wrote Aircraft and Submarines, the story of the invention, development, and present-day uses of war's newest weapons, printed in New York and London in 1918 by G. P. Putnam's Sons. Eight color plates and a hundred other pictures fill the book, with a frontispiece, Fighting by Sea and Sky, painted by John E. Whiting. Abbot also wrote The Story of Our Army and The Story of Our Navy.

Seventeen chapters split the subject in two. The air half runs from the earliest flying men through Santos-Dumont and Count von Zeppelin to the airplane, the aviator's training, and methods and incidents of war in the air. The sea half runs from the beginnings of submarine invention through steam and electricity to John P. Holland and Simon Lake, the modern submarine, life aboard, submarine warfare, and the future of the submarine. The book is a full wartime survey.
30306-religion-sex-studies-in-the-pathol:
Chapman Cohen studies religion and sex as a pathology of religious development, in an Open Mind Library volume published by Foulis in London, Edinburgh, and Boston in October 1919. The series presents questions as handled by different schools of thought in religion, ethics, philosophy, and psychology, and Cohen opens with Tylor's minimum definition of religion as belief in spiritual beings. Religious belief, he says, occupies a larger share of conscious life and energy than any other single subject.

Chapters move from science and the supernatural through the primitive mind and its environment to the religion of mental disease. Sex and religion in primitive life, sexual and pathologic states and belief, conversion, religious epidemics, and the witch mania follow, with a summary and conclusion. Cohen argues, in freethought terms, that faith grows from mind, body, and social pressure together.
30382-say-hello-for-me:
Frank W. Coggins tells Say Hello for Me, a short tale of twenty years lived in anticipation, until the twenty years are up. This is to be the day, though Pettibone has no way of knowing it. He rises as he has for twenty years, dons his space suit, and goes out into the open on Mars. Standing erect and bronzed, facing Earth, he recites a childhood rhyme.

The childhood rhyme, still remembered, guards his power of speech. Having walked to the closest canal for roughly a bushel of dried Martian moss, he sets to buffing the shiny outside of the wrecked space ship. It must glitter if it is to guide a rescue ship as a beacon, and Pettibone has known that a ship will come. With his task half done, he quickens toward the berry bushes before the sun dries the night's crop.
30384-the-day-of-sir-john-macdonald-a-ch:
Sir Joseph Pope, K.C.M.G., chronicles The Day of Sir John Macdonald, first prime minister of the Dominion, in a Toronto and Glasgow volume from Brook and Company in 1915. A frontispiece shows Sir John Macdonald crossing the Rockies over the constructed Canadian Pacific Railway in 1886, from a colour drawing by C. W. Jefferys. Pope writes as the centenary of the statesman's birth approaches, half a century after he laid the foundations of Canada.

For almost twenty years Macdonald guided the destinies of the Dominion. Nearly as long has passed since Pope's Memoirs of Sir John Macdonald appeared, little more than three years after his death, subject to many limitations and restrictions. Pope's earlier connected narrative made no claim to carry events past 1873. Nor has the time arrived for its continuation on the same lines, so Pope offers a résumé of the features of his career.
30770-the-right-time:
Walter Bupp wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in December 1963, about prophets and the price of being right. Its narrator, who calls himself Billy Joe and is called Lefty by others, brings a young woman named Pheola Rountree to a penthouse office. Pheola claims the power of prophecy and the remarkable gift of healing, and she hopes the Lodge will train her.

The head of the Lodge, Maragon, tests her with doubt and rough jokes, while clairvoyants in his outer office show off their own powers. The story asks a neat riddle: if a prophet is right, the news may come too late to help, and if wrong, the prophet is of no use. Bupp answers with humor, a tense interview, and a twist on what true foresight might mean.
30820-if-your-baby-must-travel-in-wartim:
Issued by the United States Children's Bureau in Washington in 1944, this short wartime guide speaks straight to parents who must take a baby on a train. Its opening asks whether the reader has been on a train lately, and warns that wartime trains are crowded, hard work for all aboard, and far from a holiday trip. The guide is practical, not sentimental, and it comes from Children's Bureau publications numbered 303 to 308.

Inside, it pictures soldiers and sailors on leave, business travelers, and mothers squeezed into single seats with toddlers on their laps. Lines for the diner can last two hours, and food may mean sandwiches from a porter or a paper bag. Parents learn what to expect, what to carry, and how to plan, so a needful trip with a small child goes as safely as wartime travel allows.
31041-the-day-of-sir-wilfrid-laurier-a-c:
Oscar D. Skelton's 1916 volume, published in Toronto, presents Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Canada as history of a day rather than a life story, a point its preface states plainly. Fourteen chapters follow Laurier from his making as a Canadian through politics in the 1860s, his first years in Parliament, long stretches in opposition, and his leadership from 1887 to 1896.

Later chapters turn to Washington, an empire in transition, prosperity, foreign powers, and fifty years of union, with a frontispiece showing Laurier speaking in the open air at Sorel in 1911. The book remains a clear, contemporary chronicle of Canada's political coming of age under its most famous French-Canadian premier.
3119-what-is-your-culture-to-me:
Warner gave this address to the alumni of Hamilton College at Clinton, New York, on 26 June 1872. He opens by recalling a voice that called him to the platform twenty-one years earlier. It was President North, speaking in language borrowed from Cicero and Julius Caesar. The classic tag, Warner jokes, clings to a graduate long after he has forgotten the gender of a Latin noun.

From that memory he presses his title question: what is culture to a working man of affairs? The speech weighs book learning against the demands of real life. It argues that college training should show its worth in conduct and judgment, not merely in tags and phrases carried from the classroom.
31370-mistress-nell-a-merry-tale-of-a-me:
George C. Hazelton Jr.'s Mistress Nell is subtitled a merry tale of a merry time, twixt fact and fancy. It tells the story of Nell Gwyn, the king's favorite, with illustrations from the Famous Players photo-play of the same name. Published by Grosset and Dunlap, with copyright in 1901 by Charles Scribner's Sons, the book draws on Hazelton's play and on the film scenes reproduced in this edition. Nell Gwyn, the actress who won Charles II, is its sparkling center.

Hazelton mixes history with invention, keeping the tale light and romantic. Court intrigue, wit, and affection carry the story, rather than strict biography. Readers who enjoy Restoration color and theatrical romance will find a cheerful, old-fashioned novel, where a merry heroine holds the stage and history bends, openly, toward fancy.
3143-sir-walter-raleigh-and-his-time:
Kingsley meditates on Walter Raleigh in this essay from his 1890 collection. Truth is stranger than fiction, he begins, yet few readers believe it when they meet it. Faced with heroic times and heroic men, we explain wonders away, credit accident, and cut great deeds down to common size. The habit spoils history even as it claims to sober it.

Raleigh gives Kingsley his test case: courtier, sailor, writer, and plotter in one life. The essay asks readers to take such a career as it stands, strange and all. It defends wonder as a proper response to the past, and warns against a criticism that makes every hero smaller to make itself look wise.
31630-hand-loom-weaving-a-manual-for-sch:
Mattie Phipps Todd of the Motley School, Minneapolis, wrote Hand-Loom Weaving, a manual for school and home, with an introduction by Alice W. Cooley, formerly supervisor of primary schools in Minneapolis. Rand, McNally, and Company published it at Chicago, New York, and London, with copyright in 1902, and it carries fifty-seven illustrations. Its frontispiece shows weaving on a hand loom, with a little girl's rug of heavy carpet wool in golden brown, striped in deep blue and green.

Todd's manual teaches hand-loom weaving for classrooms and homes, from the first positions to finished work. It belongs to the school handicraft movement, and it treats weaving as a useful art children can learn by doing.
31652-conquest-over-time:
Michael Shaara's science-fiction story Conquest Over Time opens with a radiogram arriving at 10:28 ship's time, when old 29 sat exactly 3.4 light years off Diomed III. Travis throws her wide open and hopes for the best. By 4:10 that afternoon, with three generators burned out and a warped ion screen, old 29 touches the atmosphere and begins homing down. A Mapping Command ship sits in an open field below, sending up the beam that guides them, but what matters now, the story insists, is to come in second.

The headnote explains the world Travis finds: a planet called Mert, where people live in houses strictly from Dickens, with carriages, no sewers, and narrow streets. Travis, reaching Diomed III before others, wages a one-man fight against a strange way of life, and against a secret that almost costs his life.
31663-the-six-fingers-of-time:
R. A. Lafferty's story The Six Fingers of Time, illustrated by Gaughan, opens with a man who began by breaking things that morning. He shatters a tumbler on his bedside table, knocking it wildly against the opposite wall, yet it breaks slowly. He had wakened not to his alarm but to a weird, slow, low booming, though the clock reads six, alarm time.

The story's epigraph plays on time as money, time as healer, and time as the giver of all possibility, and says he now had endless time. Lafferty's tale follows a man whose morning runs slow, as if time itself had loosened its pace around him.
31665-skin-game:
Charles E. Fritch's short science-fiction story follows two Earth con men, Harding and Sheckly, who travel among the peoples of the outer planets and live by cheating them. Harding argues that every being can be fooled, while the more cautious Sheckly dislikes the alien cultures they visit and fears the risks of their game.

The pair's scheme turns on them when they meet natives who take the idea of skinning a sucker literally, and the joke at the heart of the story becomes a real danger. Readers get a brisk, comic tale about greed, confidence tricks, and what happens when a swindle meets a culture that reads it in a wholly different way.
31679-north-american-yellow-bats-dasypte:
E. Raymond Hall and J. Knox Jones, Jr., writing for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History in 1961, survey the North American yellow bats grouped under Dasypterus and list the named kinds of the genus Lasiurus Gray. The paper opens with the tangled naming history of these hairy-tailed bats, sorting older names such as Nycteris against later usage.

Its business is careful classification: which names stand, which are homonyms, and how the yellow bats fit among their kin. Readers get a specialist museum paper, dense with synonymy and type specimens, that settles bat names for later field and museum workers.
31723-cecilia-a-story-of-modern-rome:
F. Marion Crawford's 1902 novel Cecilia, a story of modern Rome, opens in early spring in the Arcadian Society's forgotten garden, beyond the Tiber in a hollow of the Janiculum. Two men sit together on a stone bench in a lonely and beautiful spot few Romans or strangers ever find.

Crawford pauses to explain the Arcadians: people who loved poetry in an artificial age, took shepherds' names, and met in pleasant places to recite verses. Readers get a novel of modern Rome that sets a contemporary love story against an old city and its literary ghosts.
31915-an-artist-in-crime:
Rodrigues Ottolengui's 1903 novel An Artist in Crime, copyrighted in 1892 by G. P. Putnam's Sons, opens with a gentleman who believes he can commit a crime and escape undetected. Jack Barnes, a detective who controls a private agency in New York and counts himself among its shrewdest, boards a midnight express out of Boston with a porter's help.

Barnes has just completed what he considers a most satisfactory piece of work after a large robbery, and though tired, his brain is specially active and sleep impossible. Readers get a detective novel of evidence, alibis, and clever criminals, from an author who also wrote A Conflict of Evidence and Final Proof.
32243-confidence-game:
James McKimmey, Junior's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in September 1954, is a satire on efficiency pushed too far. Its tagline says Cutter kept demanding greater efficiency, and received it, yet enough is enough, and excess is another matter. George H. Cutter wheels his big convertible into his own space in the company lot with a flourish, under a bright California sun.

Cutter strides toward the square, four-square and confident, a company man in his element. Readers get a corporate science-fiction fable, where a demand for ever greater efficiency delivers exactly what was asked, and then more. The story's joke is the old one with a new edge: getting what you demand, in full, can be worse than falling short.
32256-the-big-time:
Fritz Leiber's The Big Time, illustrated by Finlay, opens with a war fought over its soldiers' live and dead bodies. Its two sides hide it. Its tagline warns that you cannot know there is a war on. Snakes coil and Spiders weave so you never learn the fight rages above you. Its first chapter quotes Macbeth, Enter Three Hussars, and introduces Greta Forzane, twenty-nine, born in Chicago of Scandinavian parents.

Greta operates outside space and time. She is not in Heaven or Hell, if there are such places, nor in the cosmos or universe readers know either. Her job is to nurse roughed-up soldiers back to health and sanity, in the biggest war going. It is the Change War of time travellers, called being on the Big Time. Readers get a time-war novel, told by a nurse outside time.
32472-food-in-war-time:
Graham Lusk's small book, published in Philadelphia and London in 1918, gives wartime food advice from a professor of physiology at Cornell University Medical College. Lusk had studied in Munich in 1890. He notes that Americans before the war lived in higher comfort than Europeans, with hard times in America often better than the best times in Europe. His chapters cover a balanced diet, calories in common life, and rules of saving and safety.

Much of the volume first appeared as articles in the Scientific Monthly under the title Food in War Time. Lusk explains calories, food values, and waste in plain terms, urging readers to eat wisely and save for the war effort. The book remains a clear, period guide to nutrition, rationing, and household economy during the First World War.
32482-the-introduction-of-self-registeri:
Robert P. Multhauf's paper, number 23 in Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology, traces self-registering meteorological instruments from their first forms to working systems. Multhauf is head curator of science and technology at the United States National Museum. He notes that such instruments began soon after scientific weather observation itself, yet only became a real factor in meteorology in the 1860s, two centuries later.

The delay, he argues, lay less in instrument-making than in the organisation of meteorology. Only when well-financed, well-directed observatories appeared in the 1860s, mostly as adjuncts to astronomical observatories, could self-registering systems serve science. The paper covers first instruments, systems, and conclusions, and suits readers in history of science and weather measurement.
32588-a-problem-in-modern-ethics-being-a:
John Addington Symonds's A Problem in Modern Ethics, printed in London in 1896 in only one hundred copies, asks how doctors and jurists should understand sexual inversion. Symonds surveys Christian opinion from the age of Justinian, common errors, and a wide literature, from pornographic and descriptive writing to medical, forensic, and historical studies.

Chapters also treat Karl Heinrich Ulrichs's polemical work and Walt Whitman's idealistic writing. An epilogue and suggestions upon legislation close the inquiry, which addresses medical psychologists and jurists directly. The table of contents lists books consulted, from Gibbon's history to studies by Krafft-Ebing, Lombroso, and Burton.
3270-the-jerusalem-sinner-saved-or-good-:
John Bunyan preaches good news for the vilest of men in this work, from Luke chapter twenty-four, verse forty-seven. Repentance and remission of sins, the verse says, should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. Bunyan takes that beginning as his text: grace starts with the worst, in the very city that rejected Christ.

The 1845 Nelson edition, with a picture of Bunyan, presents the sermon-treatise in full. Bunyan argues that no sinner stands beyond pardon, and that Jerusalem's sinners prove the point. A single verse becomes a wide door, open first to those who think themselves shut out.
32783-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, volume eight, runs alphabetically from Drama to Dublin. It opens with the drama, ancient and modern, then moves through Dravidian languages, drawing, dredging, and the Drente, to entries on Drew, drift, and the city of Dublin.

Longer articles treat figures such as Alfred Dreyfus, seized in October 1894, accused of selling military secrets, degraded, transported to Devil's Island, and rehabilitated in 1906, and Anthony J. Drexel, whose library held thirty-five thousand volumes. Each entry gives the concise, scholarly treatment that made the eleventh edition famous.
32805-the-impossible-voyage-home:
F. L. Wallace tells of the limits of space travel, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of August 1954, illustrated by Dick Francis. Training director Marlowe reports that space life expectancy has risen to twenty-five months and six days, a gain of a full month.

Radiation still contaminates the air spacemen breathe and the food they eat, and it reaches the reproductive system. On Mars, old Ethan and Amantha long for a real grandchild, not a picture or a robo-doll. When a runaway boy flees a ship, their homely knowledge of canalberries gives them the answer the experts missed, and a way home.
33020-english-costume:
Dion Clayton Calthrop's English Costume surveys what English men and women wore across the centuries. It was painted and described by the author and published in one volume in 1907 after appearing in four volumes during 1906. Its pictures, many in color in the original edition, show figures from early times to the age of George IV. The coat we still wear in evening dress came into fashion with top-boots in 1799, then called a Jean-de-Bry.

Calthrop writes for readers who want to see dress change, not merely read dates, and each figure pairs a picture with notes on cut, cloth, and custom. The book traces fashion as social history, showing how rank, work, and taste shaped what people put on. For costume designers, historians, and lovers of illustrated books, it remains a charming and useful survey of English dress.
33524-the-belief-in-immortality-and-the-:
James George Frazer's Belief in Immortality and the Worship of the Dead, volume two, continues his great study of how peoples face death. Published by Macmillan in London and New York, the volume gathers Frazer's vast learning on souls, ghosts, and rites for the dead across cultures. Frazer, a fellow of the Royal Society, writes with a scholar's breadth and a storyteller's gift.

The book's value lies in its comparative sweep, moving from tribe to tribe to show how belief in life after death shapes worship. Its tone is learned yet readable, suited to students of anthropology and religion. For readers of The Golden Bough, this volume is a rich, essential companion on humanity's oldest hope.
33578-comments-on-the-taxonomy-and-geogr:
E. Raymond Hall and Keith R. Kelson comment on the taxonomy and geographic distribution of several North American rodents in this 1952 paper from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. While preparing maps of mammal distribution, they found conflicting statements in the literature about the subspecific identity of various rodents, and wherever possible they examined the specimens themselves.

Their results, given in this paper, resolve a number of those conflicts by direct comparison of material from many localities and collections. Support came from a Navy research contract and a Kansas University Endowment Association grant for fieldwork. The paper is a useful, workmanlike contribution to mammal geography, showing how maps depend on getting the underlying specimens and names right.
33691-sandman-time:
Ilsien Nathalie Gaylord writes bedtime verse for small children in this 1915 Boston book, published by Richard G. Badger at the Gorham Press. Six poems fill its pages: Flower Babies, The Little Sand-Men, Star Babies, The Fairies' Ball, The Little Sleepy Song, and Little Sunset Ship of Dreams. Each poem speaks directly to a child listener, in a gentle, lulling voice suited to the hour before sleep.

In Flower Babies, flowers asleep in a long straight row are sung to by a big pine tree while little stars listen. The Little Sand-Men tells of queer elfin men in peaked caps and tight grey suits who sprinkle sand on children's eyes, though the speaker admits she has never seen one herself. Star Babies turns white clouds and shining stars into infants of the sky, and later poems add fairies, sleepy songs, and a sunset ship of dreams.
33703-olof-krarer-the-esquimaux-lady-a-s:
Albert S. Post tells the life story of Olof Krarer, an Inuit woman from Greenland, in this 1887 Ottawa volume. Post aimed to make the book as nearly as possible an autobiography, giving Krarer's own thoughts and words while smoothing small errors from her imperfect English. Her word vouches for the facts from beginning to end. He hoped the story might help her accomplish a cherished purpose.

Krarer, youngest of eight children, was born on Greenland's east coast. She lived near the seashore in a round snow house some sixteen feet across, lined with fur and carpeted double, and later lived in Iceland and Manitoba. Her mother died in Iceland when Krarer was sixteen. The book preserves a rare nineteenth-century Inuit life narrative, told in her voice and framed by a sympathetic editor, and should be read with attention to its period language.
33710-comments-on-the-taxonomy-and-geogr:
E. Raymond Hall and Keith R. Kelson comment on the taxonomy (naming and grouping of living things) and geographic distribution of North American marsupials, insectivores, and carnivores. The paper comes from the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History and dates to 1952. While preparing distribution maps, they found conflicting statements and questionable identifications in the literature, and examined the specimens concerned with the results set out below.

The paper opens with an opossum specimen from Cuernavaca, Morelos, listed on purely geographic grounds as one subspecies and re-examined by the authors. Similar specimen-based corrections follow for other groups, supported by a Navy research contract and by access to several mammal collections. The study shows how careful museum work steadies the maps on which biogeography depends.
33728-believe-you-me:
Nina Wilcox Putnam writes a comic novel of show business in this 1919 book, narrated by a dancing star. She insists she was not going to make any statement about the affair until her publicity man woke her from her first good sleep since Jim floored her. Her companion Musette, once her partner in a big-time act, presses the telephone into her hand, and Roscoe demands a statement about her split with Jim.

Six chapters, from Ladies Enlist through Pro Bonehead Publico, Holy Smokes, Anything Once, Now is the Time, and The Glad Hand, follow the dancer's career. They follow her romances and publicity battles in slangy first-person voice. Putnam, author of Adam's Garden and The Impossible Boy, writes with theatrical sparkle. The novel suits readers who enjoy Jazz Age show-business comedy told in period slang.
33872-nine-men-in-time:
Noel Loomis writes a time-travel science-fiction story in this 1953 tale from Science Fiction Stories. The narrator, Mr. Shane, manages the Imperial Printing Company, his first big job. Shane, who believed the firm was doing a nice business at a profit, is stunned and cannot make sense of it.

From that business crisis, Loomis builds a production manager's fantasy turned uneasy. These include sending a man back in time to redo a botched job so a deadline can still be met, and duplicating a man so two do the same work at once. Readers of golden-age science fiction will enjoy its brisk office opening, its clever time paradox, and the way a dream of efficiency shifts toward nightmare.
34018-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of volume two of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica runs from Anjar to Apollo. Articles in the slice range from Anjar, Anjou, Ankerite, and Antigua through Ankle, Antilia, and Ankylosis. They continue to Anna Comnena, Annapolis in Maryland and Nova Scotia, Ann Arbor, and Anne, queen of Great Britain. Anne of Brittany, Anne of Cleves, and Anne of Denmark follow.

Later entries treat annealing and tempering, Annelida, and the long run of Anti- articles toward Apollo. The slice shows the Britannica's alphabetical method at work. It serves as a handy cross-section of the reference work's second volume.
34109-sister-dolorosa-and-posthumous-fam:
James Lane Allen's 1892 Edinburgh volume pairs two Kentucky tales, Sister Dolorosa and Posthumous Fame. Allen, writing from Lexington, dedicates the book to his mother and notes his Scots, Irish, and English forebears in a preface dated Christmas Eve 1891.

Sister Dolorosa opens with a nun on a hill road, looking back over grey fields toward the farmhouse she has left for the convent. The second tale turns to fame after death, and both pieces show Allen's care for Kentucky land, faith, and the costs of a life set apart. Allen calls these tales Kentucky tales in his preface to the British edition.
34218-hildegarde-s-home:
Laura E. Richards's 1892 novel Hildegarde's Home follows its heroine to a large, low, old-style house with a wide verandah, a sweep of lawn, and tall elms above the roof. Sixteen chapters trace her days there, from first arrival to farewell.

Cousins, callers, and small plots fill the book: gossip, walks, a picnic, jam-pots, and the doings of Jack, Hugh, and Colonel Ferrers. Richards writes for young readers with warmth and humour, and the house itself stands as the book's true centre. Richards, already known for Captain January, writes here in the same warm key.
34230-sweethearts-at-home:
S. R. Crockett's Sweethearts at Home is a family book built from a daughter's diary, with help from Sweetheart herself and the children named on the title page. Crockett found at Neuchatel, by the lake, that Sweetheart had kept a full record of their days.

Editor's chapters turn that record into tales of home life: sleepy Sundays, small quarrels, and the play-names Hugh John, Sir Toady Lion, Maid Margaret, and Miss Elizabeth Fortinbras. The book reads as a fond, comic portrait of a household told in its children's own terms. Crockett's editor chapters frame the diary, telling how the record came to light at Neuchatel.
3606-antonina-or-the-fall-of-rome:
Wilkie Collins writes a historical romance set in Rome during its fall to the Goths in the fifth century. Collins explains in his preface that he did not feel bound to draw his chief characters from historical persons, since invention would serve his story better than strict fact. His heroine Antonina moves through a city of siege, famine, and invasion, caught between Roman pride and Gothic power.

The novel mixes love, intrigue, and the collapse of an empire, with the research Collins prized for verisimilitude behind the romance. Readers should treat it as fiction built on history, not as a chronicle. The book suits those who enjoy Collins before his famous sensation novels, in a grand tale of Rome's last days.
3720-returning-home:
Anthony Trollope opens this tale with a plain essay on home, arguing that those who live far from England prize the word most. Settlers who eat their bread on distant soils, he writes, keep their true home across blue waters, in a small northern island they may never see again. The feeling, he claims, can only be known by those who have felt the flat absence of interest that exile brings.

The essay then gives way to a colonial journey, as a riding party picks its way through straggling trees toward Greytown. Mrs Arkwright, tired and plaintive, begs to rest in a shed by the track, but the pace must hold if the town is to be reached. The tale pairs reflection with travel, and it suits readers who like Trollope in a thoughtful, roving mood.
3813-the-lady-of-blossholme:
H Rider Haggard sets this Tudor tale among the ruins of Blossholme Abbey, above a tidal estuary in the days of Henry the Eighth. The village, built of grey stone, has scarcely changed since, with no railway, mine, or factory to spoil its aspect. Into this still place comes a struggle over a young woman sheltered in the nunnery, while abbots, prioresses, and spies watch every door.

Emlyn, a loyal nurse figure, tries to smuggle a letter past the walls. A deaf gardener fails her, a foolish maid hands the note to the prioress by mistake, and the prioress burns it before her eyes. Monks bearing provisions are met by three sisters set to spy on each other. The tale mixes history with adventure, and readers who like Haggard's romances will find a heroine worth rescuing.
3855-memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-a:
This complete text gathers the secret memoirs of Madame Elizabeth-Charlotte of Bavaria, Duchesse d'Orleans, mother of the Regent. The preface traces nearly eight hundred of her letters, found among the papers of the Duchess of Brunswick in 1767 and extracted by a privy councillor for the court of Brunswick. A French edition of 1788, mutilated by prudence and censors, lost the piquant traits, with bold German softened and names suppressed.

The memoirs themselves show Liselotte comforting the aged Louis the Fourteenth in his evenings, when daughters on both sides thought only of amusement. Maintenon told her plainly that Madame was the only one who did not abandon the king. Readers who want the whole Liselotte will find a frank, funny, and often furious witness to the Sun King's court and its long sunset.
3856-memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-a:
Madame Elizabeth-Charlotte of Bavaria, Duchesse d'Orleans and mother of the Regent, speaks with unusual bluntness in this second book of her secret memoirs. The contents list Philippe the First and Second of Orleans, the affairs of the Regency, the regent's consort, and two dauphines, with the Duke of Burgundy among them. One passage explains why Mazarin kept the king's brother from study, lest a clever brother refuse implicit obedience.

The king, tall and fair, and Monsieur, small and dark with bad teeth, could hardly differ more in looks, the duchess notes. Later pages touch Cardinal de Polignac translating Lucretius in his abbey and a Spanish manifesto too violent to harm her son. Readers who like court gossip without varnish will find Liselotte an incomparable witness.
3857-memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-a:
Madame Elizabeth-Charlotte of Bavaria devotes her third book to the Orleans circle and its neighbors. The contents list Henrietta of England, the Duke and Duchess de Berri, the illegitimate children of the Regent, the Chevalier de Lorraine, Philip the Fifth of Spain, and Mr Law, the financier. Henrietta, she writes, was extremely unhappy, confiding in people who betrayed her, more to be pitied than blamed, surrounded by coquettes in the pay of her foes.

A grim note records a man suspected of poisoning the king's sister-in-law, who died of apoplexy at ombre and held four abbeys to fund his debaucheries. Louis wept when his grandson set out for Spain, and Liselotte wept with him as far as Sceaux. Readers who like the duchess at her most candid will find this volume full of pity, malice, and family feeling.
3858-memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-a:
Madame Elizabeth-Charlotte of Bavaria turns in her fourth book to a gallery of later figures. Victor Amadeus of Sicily, the Duke and Duchess du Maine, Louvois, and the young Louis the Fifteenth all appear. Victor Amadeus, she reports, is always in ill humor and always quarreling with his mistresses, though devotion has softened his temper and his virtuous queen loves him with constancy. Madame de Verrue, his former mistress, stole gold medals from him, and Liselotte bought a share of the loot.

Court etiquette fills other pages, from the grand cordon placed on a royal child at birth to the tabouret privilege of chancellors' wives, a custom dating to Marie de Medici. The book suits readers who want Liselotte's later years, with gossip, manners, and history in one frank voice.
3860-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
The Duke of Saint-Simon opens his memoirs with his birth, family, and early wish to join the army. The first volume follows him into the musketeers and the campaign at the siege of Namur, through dreadful weather, gentlemen carrying corn, and monks of Marlaigne. It then turns to the king's natural children, the proposed marriage of the Duke of Chartres, and the influence of Dubois at court.

Later chapters record his father's death, anecdotes of Louis the Thirteenth, Cardinal Richelieu, and the Duke of Bellegarde, with duels, libels, and gratitude in the old style. A promotion lost on hard terms and the death of the Grande Mademoiselle, richest private princess in Europe, close the volume's news. Readers who start Saint-Simon here will meet the great memorialist as a young soldier learning the court.
3861-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's second volume opens in August 1695 with the death of Harlay, Archbishop of Paris, from epilepsy at Conflans. Harlay, a prelate of profound knowledge and gallant manners, had lost favor with king and Maintenon for opposing the declaration of her marriage, of which he was one of three witnesses. His garden at Conflans, kept so clean that gardeners raked away footprints behind the walkers, stands as a portrait of fallen grace.

Other anecdotes follow, as Charnace wins a free avenue by a trick his neighbors laugh at, and a gaming dispute at Meudon sets the Prince de Conti against a proud Grand Prieur. The volume shows a court where favor decays like health. Readers who like Saint-Simon's vignettes will find this book full of small falls from greatness.
3862-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
The Duke of Saint-Simon devotes his third volume to the crisis over the Spanish succession. The king of Spain, childless and long in weak health, leaves a vast empire to dispute, and William the Third of England proposes a partition to prevent war. Spain, the Indies, and the Low Countries would go to the Archduke, while France gained Guipuscoa, Naples, Sicily, and Lorraine, and the Milanese compensated Lorraine. Louis, tired of war, accepts with few difficulties.

Court news fills the margins, as Monsieur grieves that his son Chartres has no army command, and Chartres, passed over for the king's illegitimate children, gives himself to youthful excess. Saint-Simon watches both the map of Europe and the map of favor shift together. Readers who like high politics with court gossip will find this volume essential.
3863-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's fourth volume delights in court jokes that reveal character. Canaples, brother of Marshal de Crequi, wishes to marry Mademoiselle de Vivonne, no longer young but talented and virtuous, and penniless.
