Cardinal de Coislin objects that Canaples is too old, and when Canaples says he wants children, the cardinal cries that she is so virtuous, to general laughter. The marriage, as predicted, proves sterile.

The Duke de Coislin himself, a very little man of humor and unendurable politeness, once pressed a captured Rhingrave to take his mattress bed with endless compliments. A later tale has Fieubet calling thieves back to rob his boasting companion Courtin. Readers who like Saint-Simon's comedy will find a volume of wit where vanity always pays.
3864-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon opens his fifth volume with two very different deaths, Lamoignon the chief president and Ninon de l'Enclos, the famous courtesan. A single anecdote shows Lamoignon's corruption. A hunting party lost at night near Saint Germain finds a castle, is warmed, fed, and horsed by a courteous host, and learns more than it sought. Saint-Simon tells it through Lauzun, who was there.

The volume then turns to a hated tax on baptisms and marriages. It drives poor families to baptize children themselves and marry at home before witnesses, leaving children illegitimate in law and no records to prove births. Rigorous searches follow the abuses they caused. Readers who like Saint-Simon's moral eye will find a volume of death, corruption, and the law's unintended cruelty.
3865-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's sixth volume finds the memorialist at Forges, taking waters for a tertian fever that quinquina only suspends. News reaches him of a new enterprise by the princes of the blood, who profit from the king's wish to raise his illegitimate children and claim fresh honors at mass. A folding chair, cloths, and whispers at the Pater stage a silent contest for precedence at the altar.

A personal bet brings trouble, as Saint-Simon wagers in the English manner and his enemy Cani thanks him for four pistoles. Vendome's partisans spread the news, and Saint-Simon loses the king's favor for two months without suspecting it. The volume shows how a small wager can unmake a courtier. Readers who like Saint-Simon's self portrait will find pride, fever, and politics in one frame.
3866-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
The Duke of Saint-Simon sets his seventh volume in the hard year 1709, opening with the death of D'Avaux, once ambassador in Holland. D'Avaux heard early of William of Orange's project upon England while it was still secret. He warned Louis, but the court laughed and listened instead to Barillon in London, deceived by Sunderland and the ministers of James the Second. Only when doubt became impossible did credit come, too late to disconcert a single conspirator's plan.

War and court business fill the rest, with Louvois rebuilding the Trianon in stone after the king pulled down the porcelain house made for Montespan. A breathless scene shows Orleans telling the king all, to his own transport and relief. Readers who like Saint-Simon in wartime will find a volume of missed warnings and court confessions.
3867-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's eighth volume paints France in the last war years as dull and overcast, while matters brighten a little in Spain. The king, unable to obtain peace and watching the realm exhaust itself, falls into cruel anguish, and his minister Desmarets into sad embarrassment. Paper of every kind floods trade and loses credit, state bills, bank bills, and utensil bills ruining private people forced to take them at half or a third of value.

Taxes double and treble at intendants' will, goods are taxed to four times their worth, and money ceases to circulate because specie hides in coffers. A ruinous marriage, made to avoid another match, brings a Fury who plots against her own benefactors. Readers who like Saint-Simon's economics of decline will find a volume of empty coffers and bitter households.
3868-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's ninth volume opens with a small incident that shows the old king's character better than any battle. On a journey to Fontainebleau, the Duchesse de Berry, three months pregnant and feverish, is ordered to travel despite her doctor Fagon's warning. Neither she nor Orleans dares speak, the Duke de Berry is ill received, and even Maintenon pleading through proper channels cannot move the king. The dispute lasts three or four days, and anger settles it.

Later pages turn to Spain, where the Princesse des Ursins loses all hope of favor and the Spanish king remarries in secret with a Parma princess, without a word to Louis. The king's smile at the news, rare for so self controlled a man, seals her disgrace. Readers who like Saint-Simon's moral portraits will find this volume rich in pride and punishment.
3869-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's tenth volume narrates the last month of Louis the Fourteenth and the scramble that follows. The reign approaches its conclusion, and the memorialist pauses to explain the projects and difficulties of Orleans, about to head affairs during a minority despite Maintenon and Maine. Orleans himself, mediocre in stature and full bodied without fat, easy and noble in manner, broad faced and gracious, takes shape as the coming man.

The deathbed scenes close the volume. Maintenon gives her furniture to servants and retires to Saint-Cyr, gangrene climbs the king's leg, and prayers for the dying restore him to a strong voice. His last words to Cardinal de Rohan call them the last favors of the church. Readers who like great endings will find a solemn and detailed farewell.
3870-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's eleventh volume steps back from great affairs to describe the outside life of Louis the Fourteenth during the last twenty two years of his reign. He admits such details may seem insipid to witnesses, yet argues that posterity regrets no record of a prince's daily round more than any other loss. Lessons for kings who wish to be respected, he promises, lie in these routines.

The Duchesse de Berry supplies the liveliest matter, living a strange and public life between the Luxembourg and the Carmelites, lectured by nuns and laughing it off. She returns to her father the severity she suffered from Rion, her submissive and fearful lover. Readers who like court life in close up will find a volume of ceremony, scandal, and domestic tyranny.
3871-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's twelfth volume opens in Spain, where Abbe Alberoni, risen in the track of the Princesse des Ursins, governs like a master. Alberoni dreams of driving strangers, especially the French, from the West Indies, though Holland depends too much on England to help. At home he reforms expenses and builds a navy as the basis of Spanish power. He boasts that he lives on fifty pistoles a month from the Duke of Parma while handling all manner of business.

The volume then returns to Paris, where parliament's remonstrances overstep their limits and the Keeper of the Seals must then read an act of abrogation, explaining the difference between remonstrance and power. Saint-Simon watches two kingdoms strain at once. Readers who like the Regency's foreign and domestic fronts will find a busy and instructive book.
3872-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's thirteenth volume returns to the year 1719 and the wreck of John Law's paper money scheme. Notes first lose favor, then fall into discredit, until force alone sustains them, and force proves all is over. Gold, silver, and jewels are suppressed as money, while paper alone is declared useful, a doctrine Saint-Simon mocks with Abraham paying ready money for Sarah's sepulchre.

A comic relief opens the volume. The avaricious Marquise de Charlus, a great gambler in a tall headdress, sets her commode on fire at a candle while cracking an egg at supper. The archbishop beside her must act. Readers who like the Regency will find finance and farce side by side, with ruin approaching in both.
3873-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's fourteenth volume opens with a scandal across the Channel, a species of war between the king of England and his son the Prince of Wales. George, who never believed the prince his own, once surprised Count Konigsmarck leaving his wife's chamber, threw the count into a hot oven, and shut his wife in a chateau for life. The prince, ill treated for a cause not his own, bears his father's aversion with impatience.

The Princess of Wales, sensible, graceful, and artful, softens the quarrel and conciles all England, her large court drawing the most distinguished names. A Spanish interlude shows Madame Robecque, once a dancing partner of Saint-Simon, coaxing him from retreat to dance before their Catholic majesties. Readers who like Saint-Simon abroad will find Hanover and Madrid in one volume.
3874-memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-:
Saint-Simon's fifteenth and final volume centers on Cardinal Dubois and his hunger to be declared prime minister. Dubois already holds the power in fact, but not in name, and one obstacle blocks him, Marshal de Villeroy, whose influence over others makes an open enemy dangerous. Dubois grows ill tempered and inaccessible, business stalls, and at last he asks Cardinal Bissy to mediate a reconciliation.

Smaller scenes show the machine at work. Gesvres is advised to follow Dubois's counsel, and a widowed governess loses her place to Madame de Conflans, who sees no reason to call on a new cardinal. The volume closes the memoirs with ambition rewarded and manners curdling. Readers who followed Dubois from the start will find his triumph cold comfort.
4002-the-honor-of-the-name:
Emile Gaboriau's historical novel follows Martial, a young noble who returns to Sairmeuse thinking of Marie-Anne, a woman of grace and dignity whose beauty strikes him as divine. He takes the shortest course across fields and ditches, leaping with his gun in hand, pleased by the new delight of picturing her.

Around that love, the novel sets the plots and feuds of a French province after revolution, where family names carry honor and danger. Gaboriau, a father of the detective tale, builds his story on secrets, letters, and loyalties. Readers get a long, rich romance of old France, with love and intrigue wound tight together.
415-the-bible-in-spain-or-the-journeys-a:
George Borrow recounts five years in Spain and Portugal as a Bible Society agent in this travel memoir, first published in 1842. Sent after work in Russia, Borrow rode, walked, and lodged across the peninsula, handing out scriptures where priests and police watched him close. He calls those years the happiest of his life.

The book, built largely from his letters home, mixes road tales, arrests, gypsy talk, and sharp sketches of Spanish towns. Borrow's gift for tongues and his roving spirit carry the narrative. It stands as a vivid record of a strange mission, told by a born wanderer.
4689-famous-affinities-of-history-the-ro:
Lyndon Orr presents volume one of four in Famous Affinities of History, subtitled The Romance of Devotion. Its contents run from Antony and Cleopatra, through Abelard and Heloise, to Queen Elizabeth and the Earl of Leicester. Mary Queen of Scots and Lord Bothwell, Queen Christina of Sweden and the Marquis Monaldeschi, and King Charles the Second and Nell Gwyn follow.

Later chapters add Maurice of Saxony and Adrienne Lecouvreur, and Prince Charles Edward Stuart. Orr calls Antony and Cleopatra the most remarkable love story known to history for nineteen centuries, tasked by painters, poets, and prose writers alike. Antony deserted almost victorious troops at Actium to chase Cleopatra in a swift galley. Readers get popular historical romances, told with colour and ease, for general readers who like famous lovers.
4690-famous-affinities-of-history-the-ro:
Lyndon Orr presents volume two of four in Famous Affinities of History, subtitled The Romance of Devotion. Its contents run from the Empress Catharine and Prince Potemkin, through Marie Antoinette and Count Fersen, to the story of Aaron Burr. George the Fourth and Mrs. Fitzherbert, Charlotte Corday and Adam Lux, and Napoleon and Marie Walewska follow.

Later chapters add Pauline Bonaparte, and the Empress Marie Louise and Count Neipperg. Orr opens with Catharine, noting that the greatest Frenchman ever lived was in reality an Italian, and the greatest Russian woman ever lived was in reality a German. Napoleon, Italian in blood, made himself French in sympathy, playing on France's imagination like a musician on a splendid instrument. Readers get popular historical romances, told through famous lovers and their courts.
4691-famous-affinities-of-history-the-ro:
Lyndon Orr presents volume three of four in Famous Affinities of History, subtitled The Romance of Devotion. Its contents open with the wives of General Houston, then Lola Montez and King Ludwig of Bavaria, and Leon Gambetta and Leonie Leon. Lady Blessington and Count d'Orsay, Byron and the Countess Guiccioli, and Madame de Stael follow.

Later chapters add Karl Marx, Ferdinand Lassalle and Helene von Donniges, and Rachel. The Houston chapter opens with a joke sixty or seventy years old: chalking G. T. T. on a man's door or trunk meant gone to Texas, a sign of moral, mental, and financial ruin. A man might face bankruptcy or a sheriff's warrant, and Texas offered a new start. Readers get lively historical love stories, with politics, theatre, and scandal close behind.
4692-famous-affinities-of-history-the-ro:
Lyndon Orr presents the fourth and final volume of Famous Affinities of History, subtitled The Romance of Devotion. Its contents turn to Dean Swift and the two Esthers, Percy Bysshe Shelley and Mary Godwin, the Carlyles, the Hugos, and George Sand. Later chapters add the mystery of Charles Dickens, Balzac and Evelina Hanska, and Charles Reade and Laura Seymour.

Swift opens the volume, and Orr stresses how little is settled about his singular relations with two charming women. Swift, famous for Gulliver's Travels and for politics under William the Third and Queen Anne, held his tongue with repellent taciturnity. Readers get a set of popular historical love stories, written for general readers who like famous lives told through their closest bonds.
5398-a-traveller-in-war-time:
Winston Churchill's Traveller in War Time reprints his recent experiences in Great Britain and France during the First World War. The pieces were selected to give American readers an idea of the atmosphere. They show what it is like under the immediate shadow of battle clouds. Churchill chose the title for articles first sent home while impressions were fresh.

He lets scenes and people speak, holding back his own judgment until a fuller survey can be made. The book offers readers a contemporary American view of wartime Britain and France, written before the war's end, with the freshness of dispatches rather than the hindsight of history.
5433-without-a-home:
E. P. Roe wrote Without a Home as a novel about a young woman's ideals, weakness, and search for a place in the world. The preface recalls Roe's own hesitant start as an author ten years earlier and his gratitude to the loyal readers who followed each autumn's new story. That warm, direct address sets the tone for the fiction that follows.

Chapters titled One Girl's Ideal of Life, Weakness, Pitiless Waves, and The Rudiments of a Man trace a heroine tested by loss, temptation, and changing fortune. Roe writes in the earnest, moral style that made him popular with family readers. The novel offers a nineteenth-century story of home, character, and endurance, told without irony.
5633-the-martial-adventures-of-henry-and:
William Allen White wrote The Martial Adventures of Henry and Me, illustrated by Tony Sarg, as a sentimental wartime travel book. Chapters run from beginning the journey and observing the rocket's red glare, through bombs bursting in air and finding the flag still there, to discerning things by the dawn's early light. The travelers become a trio and journey to Italy.

Later chapters consider the woman proposition, discover a new heaven and a new earth, and return to the land of the free. White, a Kansas editor, writes the war as an American abroad sees it. Readers get a warm, observant wartime travel book.
5700-love-and-life-an-old-story-in-eight:
Charlotte Yonge sets a romance in eighteenth-century dress, following young people through parties, country houses, and the strict rules of family and rank. The chapters move from a syllabub party and the house of Delavie. They pass through cowslip fields, letters, summons, and disappointed love. Later scenes reach an enchanted castle, a dark chamber, and a voice from the grave. Costume and manners frame every choice the heroine makes.

The novel's interest lies in how love must negotiate duty, reputation, and family pressure in a world of visits and formal calls. Yonge writes with gentle moral care, letting misunderstandings, proposals, and partings test her characters before any happy ending is earned. Readers who enjoy period romance with a strong domestic conscience will find a long, leisurely story here.
5729-peggy-stewart-navy-girl-at-home:
Peggy Stewart, Navy Girl at Home, follows Peggy through a year of home life, friendship, and small domestic dramas. Chapters open in springtide, pass through an empress, Daddy Neil, October days, and Polly Howland, then reach Peggy as chatelaine, a shocking demonstration of intemperance, Dunmore's last Christmas, and a masqueraders' show. The story stays close to house, friends, and family feeling.

This introduces a capable, kind heroine learning to manage a household and to help others, from playing good Samaritan to hosting friends. The book belongs to the girls' series fiction of its era, with clear morals and warm humor. Young readers who enjoy home stories with a naval family background will find Peggy steady company across a full, eventful year.
6135-when-the-holy-ghost-is-come:
Colonel S. L. Brengle's When the Holy Ghost Is Come, edited by Bramwell Booth, carries a Salvation Army foreword. It insists the Army owes its existence, strength, and success to careful attention to the profoundest questions of the soul. Its work for men would lose abiding value without proclaiming great practical truths.

The foreword glories in Christ as a perfect Saviour for this time as much as any past or future age. It calls absurd the pretense that a superior modern development needs a new kind of Saviour. Brengle's devout, practical words are commended to thoughtful readers and to those with least time for thought alike.
6488-going-some:
Rex Beach sets his cowboys on a ranch fence at night, listening with pain to a phonograph that once belonged to them. The machine now plays for a rival ranch, and its thin, wailing voice turns a quiet southwestern evening into a small insult. From that comic loss, the tale moves toward a contest of pride, nerve, and showmanship among ranch hands.

Love, rivalry, and a taste for risk drive the rest of the plot, as the men try to win back what they lost and prove their worth. Beach keeps the pace brisk and the talk plain, with wide skies and hard work as the ground for every joke and quarrel. The result is a light western romance built on bluff, charm, and stubborn pride.
6621-poems-of-the-heart-and-home:
Mrs. J. C. Yule, born Pamela Vining, gathers poems first printed under the names Emillia and Xenette, and later under her own name. Some had spread widely in Canada, the United States, and Britain, while others appear here for the first time. Her introduction says the poems must stand on merit alone, by what they stir in the common human heart.

Joys, sorrows, hopes, and home ties are the chief themes, voiced in plain, tender verse. Yule writes for readers who like poetry that speaks straight to feeling, not to fashion. Poems of the Heart and Home is a modest, heartfelt Canadian book, kept alive by its warmth.
678-the-cricket-on-the-hearth-a-fairy-ta:
Charles Dickens writes a Christmas fairy tale of home in this book, inscribed to Lord Jeffrey in December 1845. The kettle began it, Dickens insists, full five minutes before the cricket chirped by the waxy-faced Dutch clock. John Peerybingle, his wife Dot, and their friends gather round a hearth where a cricket's song guards the house.

Dickens writes with warm, playful prose, full of kettle steam, clock figures, and fireside talk. The tale praises home, trust, and simple joy. It endures as a beloved Christmas story, where a small insect's chirp becomes a blessing on a household.
6854-anne-bradstreet-and-her-time:
Helen Campbell opens Anne Bradstreet and Her Time by doubting whether America has had famous women to match George Eliot or George Sand. A leading journal, she notes, reproaches America for two hundred years without such a genius, and doubts a future one. Campbell answers by telling the story of one woman who, in Puritan New England, wrote poetry against great odds.

Bradstreet's life, verse, and the conditions that hampered women writers fill the book. Campbell writes with a reformer's warmth and a scholar's care. Anne Bradstreet and Her Time is a pioneering feminist biography of America's first published poet.
7300-woman-and-the-republic-a-survey-of-:
Helen Kendrick Johnson's Woman and the Republic surveys the woman-suffrage movement in the United States and argues the claims of its foremost advocates from the other side. Her chapters ask whether woman suffrage is democratic, then test it against the republic, philanthropy, laws, trades, professions, education, church, sex, and home, closing with a conclusion.

Johnson writes as a critic of suffrage, not as its champion, and her survey preserves the arguments made against votes for women in their own terms. The book matters now as a record of opposition, showing what the movement had to answer. Its orderly chapters make a case meant to persuade by reason, not by scorn.
7358-brought-home:
Hesba Stretton's Brought Home opens in Upton, a small market town so quiet that its peace sets the novel's first note. Its chapters run from Upton Rectory and Ann Holland through questions of duty, a baby's grave, and town talk. The rector's return, worse than dead, husband and wife, sad days, a sin and a shame, and a lost child follow. A colonial curacy, self-sacrifice, farewells, despair, a long voyage, near shipwreck, and rescue close the tale.

Stretton writes a Victorian moral story with a tender heart, letting a rector's household face scandal, loss, and grace. The title's homecoming carries both a journey and a spiritual return. Readers get earnest, readable fiction of conscience and forgiveness.
7373-the-path-to-rome:
Hilaire Belloc made a vow to walk all the way to Rome. He would sleep rough, cover thirty miles a day, and hear Mass each morning. He would arrive in time for high Mass on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul. The Path to Rome is the story of that walk, told with jokes, songs, arguments, and digressions. Belloc kept the strict vow even as he broke his lesser ones one by one.

The route carries him out of his native valley, across France and over the mountains into Italy, through towns, inns, and churches. Along the way he reflects on faith, on the peoples of Europe, and on what walking itself teaches that faster travel cannot. The book mixes travel tale, history, and personal confession, and it remains Belloc's most loved work of prose.
7847-jack-north-s-treasure-hunt-or-darin:
Roy Rockwood's Jack North's Treasure Hunt, or Daring Adventures in South America, appeared in 1907. It sends a boy hero from a chance for a position and a test of strength to a long trip proposed, just in time. An illustration shows two boys plunging side by side from an island into water.

Chapters run from Robinson Crusoe's island and a terrible mistake through a lonely pimento and a jaguar's head. A train attack, treasure island, and a boiling lake follow, with nitrate fields and quicksands after. Through jungle nights and shipboard panic, Jack chases treasure with pluck, luck, and loyal friends.
7892-heart-and-science-a-story-of-the-pr:
Wilkie Collins's Heart and Science, a story of the present time, opens with a preface to readers on both sides of the Atlantic. Collins says English readers rank character and humor first in fiction, with incident and dramatic situation second, and admits he has tried to join all these merits in one work.

Dedicated to Sarony of New York, artist, photographer, and friend, the novel that follows pits heart against science, love against cold experiment, in a tale of doctors, women, and moral choice. Through domestic scenes and laboratory debate, Collins asks what science owes to feeling.
8067-the-boy-scouts-on-sturgeon-island-o:
Herbert Carter wrote this Boy Scouts adventure about a patrol marooned among game-fish poachers on Sturgeon Island. The first chapter, Out for a Royal Good Time, introduces the scoutmaster Dr Philander Hobbs, the boys Bumpus and Giraffe. And a stranger chasing them from town with a message from a telegraph operator's son. What begins as a holiday outing turns into a contest with poachers who will not welcome visitors.

The story follows the familiar Scout formula: resourcefulness, teamwork, signalling, and pluck against older, rougher opponents. Written when the Scout movement was young, it captures its ideals in adventure form. For young readers and collectors of series fiction, it is a brisk, good-natured tale of camping, mystery, and outdoor skill.
8380-cuba-in-war-time:
Richard Harding Davis went to Cuba in 1897, while Spanish forces fought Cuban rebels, and reported what he saw for American readers. Frederic Remington's drawings illustrate the book, including the famous death of Rodriguez. Davis writes as a correspondent on the ground: columns marching, hospitals, reconcentration camps where civilians starved, and executions at dawn.

The book helped fix Cuba in the American imagination on the eve of the Spanish-American War, and its reports of Spanish cruelty fed the war fever back home. Readers today get both vivid war reporting and a lesson in how reporting shapes opinion. Davis's Cuba is seen through an American reporter's eyes, sympathetic to the rebels and unsparing toward Spain.
847-lays-of-ancient-rome:
Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote these ballads of early Rome, meant to sound like the songs Romans themselves might have sung. Horatius at the bridge heads the set, followed by the Battle of Lake Regillus, Virginia, and the Prophecy of Capys. Each lay tells a tale of courage, freedom, or fate in Rome's legendary age.

Macaulay admits in his preface that the history of the early kings is largely fable, yet he gives the fables stirring life. His verse is bold, rhythmic, and easy to learn by heart. The book has taught generations of schoolboys Roman virtue, and it still rings as a masterwork of narrative poetry.
8535-the-sisters-in-law-a-novel-of-our-t:
Gertrude Atherton wrote The Sisters-in-Law as a novel of our time, dedicating it to Dr. Alanson Weeks of San Francisco. Her prefatory note explains that several people who enter casually here are leading characters in other novels and stories of her California Series. That series covers the social history of the state from the beginning of the last century, including Gwynne, his mother, and Lady Victoria Gwynne.

Atherton, California's leading novelist, writes of San Francisco society, its families, marriages, and ambitions, with insider knowledge. Readers get a social novel that also works as a chapter of California history, linked to her wider series. The book suits readers of American regional fiction, and of Atherton's sharp social eye.
8557-synge-and-the-ireland-of-his-time:
William Butler Yeats wrote Synge and the Ireland of His Time, with a note concerning a walk through Connemara with Synge by Jack Butler Yeats, published at Churchtown, Dundrum, in 1911. Yeats opens on Saturday, January 26, 1907, lecturing in Aberdeen, when his lecture ended and a telegram reached him, news that would shape the book's account of Synge.

John Millington Synge, playwright of The Playboy of the Western World, died young. Yeats, his friend and champion, writes of Synge's Ireland: the west, the Abbey Theatre, and the quarrels over his plays. Readers get a memoir by a great poet about a great playwright, and a portrait of Ireland at a turning point. The book is essential Yeats, and essential Synge.
8735-the-revolutions-of-time:
Jonathan Dunn presents this book as a manuscript found in a weather-beaten stone box on a Pacific island, written in an ancient form of Latin and translated and edited by him. The dedication runs to Bernibus, with a Latin tag about a sure friend discerned in unsure affairs. Chapters move from past and present through predestined deja vu, Zards and Canitaurs, Onan lord of the past, the Treeway, the fiery lake, and down to Nunami.

Later chapters reach the temple of time, mutually assured deception, devolution, the land across the sea, the white eagle, the big bang, and past and future. The frame invites readers to treat the tale as recovered history, while the story itself plays with time travel, fate, and invented peoples. It is independent fantasy with an antiquarian flavour, best enjoyed for its inventions rather than as a claim about any real manuscript.
9305-one-day-s-courtship-and-the-heralds:
Robert Barr wrote this romance in 1896 around John Trenton, an artist bound for England. Before he sails, Trenton wants one more look at the Shawenegan Falls, whose roar has rung in his ears since he left. His sketches dissatisfy him, so he plans to bring a camera for snapshots. He writes to his friend Ed for help.

A day's courtship follows, swift and charming, beside the heralds of fame that artists chase. Barr, known for In the Midst of Alarms, writes with light humor. The book is a pleasant, old-fashioned love story with a Canadian backdrop.
9388-the-red-flower-poems-written-in-war:
Henry van Dyke published these war poems in 1919, under the title The Red Flower. The contents run from Premonition and The Red Flower of June 1914, through trial by fire and a scrap of paper, to lights out in 1915. France and Belgium follow, with the bells of Malines and Jeanne d'Arc returns. Interludes in Holland give way to Enter America.

Van Dyke, an American minister and writer, mourns, exhorts, and hopes in turn, praising liberty enlightening the world. His verse is plain and public, meant for a nation at war. The book remains a moving record of how one voice met the Great War.
9543-the-poetical-works-of-george-macdon:
Volume one of George MacDonald's poetical works, printed in 1893, gathers his verse dramas and lyrics. Within and Without and A Hidden Life lead, with A Story of the Sea-Shore and The Disciple beside. The Gospel Women gives voice to Mary, Martha, Mary Magdalene, Pilate's wife, and other women of the Gospels. A Book of Sonnets and Organ Songs follow, with tributes to Garibaldi and General Gordon.

MacDonald, a Scots preacher and fantasist, writes verse steeped in faith, nature, and moral wonder. His lines favor plain feeling over show, with a mystic's warmth. A reader gets the poetic side of a beloved Victorian writer, rich in scripture, song, and the inner life.
9984-the-poetical-works-of-george-macdon:
This second volume of George MacDonald's poetical works gathers his parables, minor ditties, motes in the sun, poems for children, and a threefold cord. MacDonald, the Scottish minister and novelist, wrote poetry throughout his life, and this volume shows its range.

Among the pieces are The Man of Songs, The Hills, The Journey, and The Tree's Prayer, with songs for children such as By the Cradle and Sweeping the Floor. His verse is earnest, musical, and full of nature and faith. Readers who know his novels will find the same imagination at work in shorter, singing form.
a-child-s-anti-slavery-book-containing-a: Various writers contribute to this child's anti slavery book about American slave children. Its stories include Little Lewis, Mark and Hasty, and Aunt Judy, drawn from real life and told for young readers. Illustrations show a father sold away, whippings, and the hunting of runaways. The book speaks plainly to free children about the cruelty of slavery.
a-history-of-pantomime: R. J. Broadbent writes a history of pantomime, a factor long neglected in stage histories. His chapters trace the origin of pantomime, tragedy, and comedy, and the meaning of the word itself. Harlequin, Columbine, Clown, and Pantaloon emerge from Grecian myth and transformation scenes. Broadbent offers new information on an ancient entertainment.
a-second-home:
Honoré de Balzac opens in one of old Paris's darkest, narrowest streets, the Rue du Tourniquet-Saint-Jean near the Hôtel de Ville, in Clara Bell's translation. In a house there lives a widow with her daughter, in strict, pious retirement. A young man of good family, ruined in health and fortune, comes into their quiet orbit.

The tale follows the slow growth of trust and love inside a household ruled by duty and prayer. Balzac sets the mother's stern faith against the daughter's gentle heart. Money troubles, a hidden past, and a patient courtship fill the middle chapters. The title's promise, a second home found by a man who had lost his first, shapes the close.
a-traveller-in-war-time:
Winston Churchill's A Traveller in War-Time reprints his wartime articles from Great Britain and France, gathered, he says, at readers' requests. His preface explains the method: impressions sent home fresh, with comment postponed. He sought the atmosphere, what life felt like with the battle clouds directly overhead. Invitations took him to the Front, to Paris streets, and to Ireland.

Churchill records British frugality, much of it self-imposed to win the war, and mothers struggling to feed children on small incomes. The army's health, morale, and organization struck him as a marvel accomplished in brief time. His stay was cut short, and the projected larger book on changing social conditions never replaced these sketches. The volume is an American novelist's wartime notebook: sympathetic, observant, and candid about its limits. It documents the home fronts of 1917 and 1918 as one friendly visitor saw them.
adam-eve-pinch-me:
Adam and Eve and Pinch Me is a story collection by A E Coppard. A contemporary reviewer summed up Coppard's implicit theme as the closeness of the spiritual world to the material one. His stories chase the strange, communicative sympathy that strikes between two people of different temperaments and suddenly makes them one.

Coppard deals with sudden impulses under which secrecy breaks down for a moment, and personality stands revealed as under a flash of spiritual lightning. That interest in brief, charged encounters shapes the tales gathered here. The collection shows his early manner: quiet surfaces, rural and small-town lives, and an unseen world pressing close against the visible one.
american-adventures-a-second-trip-abroad: Julian Street takes a second trip abroad at home, travelling through America as though it were a foreign country to be discovered. With pictorial sidelights by Wallace Morgan, the book finds the exotic in familiar towns, hotels, and landscapes. Street's humour and eye for character make this a cheerful record of early twentieth-century American travel.
an-exposition-of-the-last-psalme: John Boys expounds the last psalm in a sermon preached at Paul's, dedicated to his honourable patron. The exposition takes the psalm's call to praise verse by verse, drawing lessons for worship and life. Boys's sermon shows Jacobean preaching at its learned and earnest best, close to the text and plain in application.
anne-bradstreet-and-her-time:
Helen Campbell opens with a reproach she means to answer: critics doubted America had produced any famous women, or genius comparable to George Eliot or George Sand. Her answer is the life of Anne Bradstreet, who wrote real poetry amid obstacles that might have daunted a far stouter soul. The contents begin with the old home in England and the upheavals that drove the family out.

Seventeen chapters follow the voyage, the beginnings in Massachusetts, a theological tragedy in her own family, village life in 1650, and her first edition, printed in London without her knowledge. Campbell, a reform writer, uses Bradstreet to argue what colonial women bore and achieved. The biography keeps the poems and the woman together.
antonina-or-the-fall-of-rome:
Antonina, or The Fall of Rome, published in 1850, was Wilkie Collins's first published novel. Collins, later an early master of mystery and suspense with books like The Moonstone and The Woman in White, began his career instead with a colorful tale of ancient Rome. He set the story in the age of the Emperor Honorius, as the western empire crumbled.

Collins explained that the task of representing the spirit of the age falls to his invented characters, while real figures such as Honorius stand in the background. Through Antonina and those around her, the novel dramatizes invasion, siege, and a civilization in collapse. It shows the young Collins learning the large-canvas historical storytelling that fed his later sensation fiction.
as-seen-by-me:
Lilian Bell published this travel book in 1900 after two years of journeys covering some thirty thousand miles. Written as letters home, it reports Europe, Russia, and Egypt strictly through one lively American observer. Bell warns readers in her apology that she plays her own Boswell, so every place arrives filtered through her tastes, mishaps, and homesickness for her small nephew Billy.

Chapters pass through London and Paris, sail aboard the yacht Hela, and cross Russia to Vilna, St. Petersburg, and Moscow. Later letters reach Constantinople, Cairo, and the Nile, then Greece, Naples, and Rome. Lost trunks at a frontier, wood-burning trains crawling through snow, and customs officers handled in pantomime give the sightseeing a comic, personal edge throughout.
back-home:
Eugene Wood wrote Back Home as a set of fond sketches of the small-town boyhood he remembered, dedicating the book to his mother, his Ma Mag of the days back home. Chapters visit the old red school-house, the Sabbath-school, the swimming-hole, the firemen's tournament, circus day, and the county fair. A chapter called The Revolving Year turns the seasons of a boy's calendar, and Christmas Back Home closes the round.

Wood's introduction jokes with the gentle reader about little books and the general public's reading habits, setting the book's tone: humorous, tender, and unhurried. This is the literature of the old hometown, written when such towns were already becoming memory. Readers meet a whole lost America in its pages, one fair and swimming-hole at a time.
baldy-of-nome:
Esther Birdsall Darling wrote this Alaskan dog book, decorated by Hattie Longstreet and dedicated to her mother's kindness to animals. Baldy was a real racing sled dog of Nome, a plodder who rose to lead a famous team. Chapters move from the parting of the ways through the Solomon Derby to the great race for the supremacy of the trail.

Kennel life fills the margins: Mego, a mother dog, tunnels under a manger toward Nellie Silk's squeaking pups, a kidnapping that stands as the one scandal and blot on her spotless character. Darling proposes the Hot Springs team to give Mego something else to think about. Racing, weather, and dog character carry the book, which made Baldy's name known wherever the All Alaska Sweepstakes was followed.
beauty-and-the-beast-and-tales-of-home:
Bayard Taylor, the American poet and great traveler of his day, gathered Beauty and the Beast, and Tales of Home in this volume. The title piece retells the old French fairy tale. A merchant's daughter gives herself to a Beast's castle to save her father. She learns to love the gentle heart under the frightening shape. Her love breaks the spell that holds him.

Around it Taylor sets tales of home. These are stories of American village and family life. He tells them with the warmth that made him a household name in the years after the Civil War. The mix is the point. Taylor moves from enchanted roses and palace halls to plain kitchens and schoolrooms. He finds the same tests of kindness, pride, and patience in both.
between-you-and-me:
Sir Harry Lauder published this book of talk, verse, and memoir with McCann of New York in 1919. The Scottish music-hall knight dedicates it to the fathers and mothers of the boys who went, and those who prepared to go. His opening poem gives a soldier's whole philosophy. When the war is over and the last penny spent, a man still has one thought. He is one of the boys who went.

Chapters wander from the stage to Scottish history, told in braid Scots. First the family, then the clan, then the tribe and nation grew, he explains; Britain was once many kingdoms, open to armies from over the sea. One strong rule ended invasion — until, he jokes, they dropped from the skies. Lauder writes as he sang: sentimental, canny, and built to reach the back row of any hall.
brought-home: Stretton's tale brings its wanderer home at last. The homecoming carries the story's moral weight. A Victorian children's story. Its contents inform the historical record. The book preserves that tale. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abel-place-na:
Abel, meaning meadow, is the name of several biblical places, each set apart by an added word, and this entry sorts them out one by one. Abel-Beth-Maacha stood west of Dan in Upper Galilee, while Abel-Keramim was an Ammonite village about six miles from Philadelphia. Abelmehula lay in the Jordan valley near Bethsan, Abel-Misraim is matched by St. Jerome with the threshing floor of Atad, and Abel-Shittim stood in the plains of Moab.

Each place comes with its scripture references and its variant spellings in the Vulgate, so readers can tell the sites apart rather than merging them into one. A closing note warns that the great Abel of 1 Samuel 6:18 is wrongly read for the great stone, not a place at all. The entry draws on standard Bible dictionaries by Vigouroux, Hagen, Holzammer, and Conder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-henri-:
Alfred Henri Amand Mame, printer and publisher born at Tours in 1811, died there in 1893. His grandfather Charles founded the firm, printing two Angers newspapers late in the eighteenth century; his eldest son's Paris publishing, including Chateaubriand and Staël, was ruined by Napoleonic police persecution. Amand Mame, the third son, founded the Tours firm, which under Alfred became very important.

With cousin Ernest from 1833 to 1845 Alfred edited classics and devotional books. He then first united a publishing house's workshops, printing, binding, selling, and forwarding, earning the firm the name of literary Creusot after Le Creusot's iron works. Owning La Haye-Descartes's paper mills besides, Mame saw a book pass from rags to paper to binding through his own workers. Inspired by the social Catholic ideal, he gave employees a pension fund. His son Paul Mame, 1833 to 1903, headed the firm until 1900.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angouleme:
Angouleme, anciently Engoliesma, is a diocese covering the Charente in France, suffragan to Bordeaux, under the old regime as under the Concordat. Its first bishop was Ausonius, a disciple of Saint Martial. Two authorities differ: Gregory of Tours held that Martial preached at Limoges about 250, while Adhemar de Chabannes made Martial the immediate disciple of Saint Peter. On the latter view Ausonius was a first-century bishop; on the former, a third-century one. The article inclines to Gregory's view.

Saint Salvius, honoured as a martyr at Valenciennes, was only a missionary bishop of the eighth century. The bishops' list includes the poet Octavien de Saint Gelais, bishop from 1494 to 1502. The province's monuments show Romano-Byzantine facades, finest in Saint Peter's Cathedral at Angouleme. A wealthy Augustinian abbey founded in 1122 survives in ruins at Couronne. At the end of 1905 the diocese contained 330,305 inhabitants and 368 parishes and vicariates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-ansel:
Antoine Anselme, a French preacher born in 1652, won fame as a sacred orator in Paris. As a boy he could repeat a sermon after one hearing, a gift that earned him the nickname Little Prophet. After study at Toulouse and ordination, he preached to packed churches, with patrons booking him years ahead.

His standing brought him before the French Academy in 1681, to preach at court two years later, and into the Academy of Inscriptions in 1710. His printed works include panegyrics of saints, funeral orations, and sermons for Advent and Lent. The entry paints a pulpit star whose voice, charm, and learning made him one of his age's best-known preachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerical-cost:
Ecclesiastical costume has drawn more synodal enactments than almost any topic. Christianity's early centuries saw no distinctive dress adopted by ecclesiastics. Many signs point that way, including the lacerna or birrus and the civil dalmatic associated with the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian.

The clearest testimony is a letter of Pope Celestine in 428 to bishops of Gaul. It rebukes conspicuous attire. It rules bishops and clergy should stand apart from the common people by learning, not clothes, by conduct, not dress, and by cleanness of mind, not care of person. In the East, ascetics and philosophers, Christian or not, affected a special habit. Clergy generally wore the birrus like the laity. A canon of Gangra in 340 approves that usage. It anathematises anyone who wears the pallium for ascetic life and condemns those who reverently wear the birrus and other common garments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-and-c:
August Joseph Schmidlin's entry tells of S. Maria dell'Anima, the German national church and hospice in Rome. Its name comes, by tradition, from its coat of arms. That picture shows Our Lady between two souls. Founded as early as 1350 as a private hospice for German pilgrims, it rose on its present site in 1386. Johann Peters of Dodrecht, an officer of the Papal Guard, built it with his wife. Boniface IX granted it indulgences in 1398.

In 1406 the German colony raised it to a national institution, joined to a brotherhood under provisors. Rich gifts followed, notably the legacy of Diedrich of Niem in 1418. Its present church, Renaissance in style under Bramante's influence, was built by German gifts between 1499 and 1526. As a college of priests it dates to 1496, founded by Burkhard of Strasburg, master of papal ceremonies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyme:
A short entry describes Cyme, a titular see of Asia Minor. Kyme was a port on the Kymaios Gulf, the chief city of Aeolis, founded by Aeolians in the eleventh or thirteenth century BC. Tradition says Pelops, returning from Greece, defeated Oenomanos, expelled the natives, and named the city for the Amazon Kyme. Another rare name was Phrykonis.

Cyme appears in the Synecdemus of Hierocles and in lists of bishoprics running into the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Five bishops are named by Lequien, from 431 to 787, with another John in 1216. The site is now placed at the small village of Lamourt near Smyrna. The name is sometimes written Cume or Cumae, inviting confusion with Cumae in Italy, and a second Cyme stood in Egypt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dome:
A dome, from the Latin domus or house, is an architectural term often used as a twin of cupola. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry draws the strict line, the dome is the outer covering, spherical or polygonal, while the cupola is the inner structure. In common speech dome means the whole covering. Loosely, the German Dom and Italian Duomo use the word for a cathedral or another great building.

A dome may rise from a circular, elliptical, or polygonal base, in wood, stone, metal, or earthenware, single, double, or even triple in shell. Its section is a curve hollow toward the inside. The entry surveys famous domes and the builders who raised them, giving readers the terms to read the crowns of churches and halls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Holy Name feast centres on and unites all the mysteries of Christ the Redeemer. Each year it falls on the second Sunday after Epiphany. Bernardine dei Busti composed its Office and Mass in the fifteenth century. Sixtus IV approved those texts for the growing devotion to the Name.

Franciscans received the feast in 1530, and it spread widely over much of the Church after that. Carmelites and Augustinians kept it on 14 January for many years. The Carthusians took it for Epiphany's second Sunday about 1643. In 1721 it reached the Universal Church on that same Sunday.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-v:
Geoffrey of Vendôme, a cardinal abbot born at Angers in the late eleventh century, spent his life defending Rome and his abbey. He entered the Trinity community at Vendôme young and was chosen abbot in 1093 while still a deacon. In 1094 he went to Rome, paid the Lateran's keeper to yield it to Urban II, and received a cardinal's hat in return.

Twelve times Geoffrey crossed to Italy for Rome's cause under three popes, and three times he was captured. He hosted Urban and Paschal at his monastery, sat at Clermont in 1095, Saintes in 1096, and Reims in 1131, and called lay investiture heresy and simony in tracts and letters. His letters, sermons, hymns, and tracts on sacraments fill Sirmond's edition of 1610.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-balme:
Henry Balme, also called Hugh, was a Franciscan theologian born at Geneva at an uncertain date who died on 23 February 1439. He entered the Friars Minor in the province of Burgundy and became confessor to Saint Colette, whose life he knew intimately. From that knowledge he wrote a brief account of her remarkable gifts. The saint herself, on learning of it, had the manuscript destroyed.

Balme's surviving reputation rests on a work on mystical theology long attributed to Saint Bonaventure and printed in many editions of Bonaventure's works. Editors of the Quaracchi edition, following Sbaralea, restored the treatise to Balme as its rightful author. The episode makes this short entry a small lesson in attribution. A text can circulate for centuries under a famous name before scholarship returns it to the lesser-known writer who actually composed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-impediment-of:
Crime can bar marriage under Church law: adultery and homicide, each alone or both together, create this impediment. Under Roman civil law, a man could not marry a widow if he had committed adultery with her while her husband lived. There is serious doubt whether the Church ever accepted this law.

Since the twelfth century, Church law has certainly demanded further facts in such adultery before it voids a marriage. Today's law bars the adulterer from marrying his partner in guilt in two cases. One is when the adulterer promises the partner in guilt marriage after the lawful spouse's death. The other is when the two attempted marriage and the attempt was completed during a lawful spouse's lifetime. So adultery without a marriage promise, or a promise without adultery, bars nothing: neither alone is diriment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-college:
Training Irish priests in Rome, close to the pope yet far from penal law at home, is the story of this college history. Gregory XIII first backed the plan late in the sixteenth century and set aside a large sum. Irish chiefs' pressing needs diverted the money instead. It went to war supplies for Catholics in Ireland, not to a Roman college. Irish bishops revived the project in 1625 with an address to Urban VIII.

Cardinal Ludovisi, protector of Ireland, then paid for the college himself as a lasting memorial of his protectorate. A house opposite Sant' Isidoro took six students on 1 January 1628, with Eugene Callanan as first rector and Luke Wadding as a kind of overseer. Ludovisi died in 1632, but the house he founded carried Irish clerical training in Rome forward from that modest start.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-francois:
Jean-François Buisson de Saint-Cosme, a Canadian-born missionary born at Quebec in 1667 and killed in 1707, was ordained in 1690 from Quebec's foreign missions seminary. After service at Minas in Acadia he worked at Cahokia in Illinois, then followed fellow priests down the Mississippi.

About the end of 1699 Saint-Cosme founded the first mission among the Natchez near present Natchez, Mississippi. Neighbouring missions soon failed for lack of response, leaving him alone by 1704. After years of fruitless labour, Chitimacha attackers killed him as he slept on the river, along with three French companions and a slave. Bienville avenged him by arming friendly tribes against the killers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-joseph-g:
Jean-Joseph Gaume, a French theologian and writer born at Fuans in 1802 and dead in 1879. He served Nevers as theology professor, seminary director, canon, and vicar-general before moving to Rome in 1841. Gregory XVI knighted him, Prague gave him a doctorate, and Pius IX made him prothonotary apostolic in 1854.

Gaume's theology books are still esteemed, his histories largely forgotten, and his education writings sparked the famous classics quarrel. He blamed the Renaissance for reviving paganism, preparing revolution, and rotting morals, and urged a cure through catechism and barring pagan authors from school reading. That thesis drove his Revolution and his history of home society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-libera-me:
Libera Me is the responsory sung at funerals. Its two versicles are Tremens factus sum and Dies illa. Requiem aeternam replaces Gloria Patri, and the opening part, down to the first versicle, then repeats. It is a first-person prayer for mercy at the Last Day. The choir speaks for the dead person, in a dramatic substitution.

 Praying that the dead be saved from hell is another such substitution, since that question was settled at death. We cannot say everything at once, so we speak as if simultaneous things followed in order, while in God's eternity all is present at once. A cantor begins the responsory, the choir continues, the cantor singing the versicles alone during the Absolution following the Mass for the Dead. The celebrant then swaps his chasuble for a black cope, chants Non intres in judicium, and Libera me is sung.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany-of-the:
The Litany of the Holy Name is an old prayer honouring the name of Jesus, built on the call-and-response pattern of the Litany of Loreto. No writer is known for certain, though the entry credits the famed preachers Bernardine of Siena and John Capistran, working in the early fifteenth century.

Popes weighed it with care over the years. Sixtus V granted an indulgence for saying it, yet formal approval was refused in 1640, 1642, and 1662. Pius IX approved one form in 1862, and Leo XIII spread the favour to the whole Church in 1886. Its praises move from Jesus as God to Jesus as man, meek, patient, and loving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-rene-vi:
Louis Rene Villerme was a French economist and physician, born at Paris in 1782 and dead there in 1863. Trained in medicine, he turned to social questions, writing on prison mortality and jail overcrowding in 1820 and 1829, and founding the Annales d'hygiene in 1829.

His fame rests on a long inquiry into cotton, wool, and silk workers. It showed how cotton dust breeds pneumonia and protested child labour, a warning that led to the 1841 child labour law. Later works treated workers' associations, workers' housing, and machine accidents. Liberal in economics yet shy of state cures, he diagnosed industrial ills with a doctor's exactness for social Catholicism to treat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicholas-psau:
Nicholas Psaume, also Psaulme or Preaume, Latin Psalmaeus, was Bishop of Verdun, born at Chaumont-sur-Aire in 1518 and dead on 10 August 1575. He studied classics at Verdun's Norbertine Abbey of Saint Paul, where his uncle Francois Psaume was commendatory abbot, completed higher studies at Paris, Orleans and Poitiers, then entered that abbey. Ordained priest in 1540, he won his theology doctorate at Paris after a brilliant defence of numerous theses.

But for Cardinal Francois of Pisa's intrigues, Psaume, already Abbot of Saint Paul, would have been elected Abbot General of Premontre, his nomination already confirmed by Francis I. In 1546 he was chosen to represent the Norbertines at Trent, but the Cardinal of Lorraine retained him and, with papal consent, resigned Verdun's bishopric in his favour. Consecrated bishop on 26 August 1548, he attended Trier's provincial council, published its canons, and sat at Trent from May 1551 to April 1552.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicole-oresme:
Norman scholar Nicole Oresme, bishop of Lisieux, counts among the founders of modern science. A Paris theology student in 1348, he became head of the Collège de Navarre, canon of Rouen, and bishop in 1377, while serving as counselor and French-language author for Charles V.

Oresme wrote on coins, on Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, and on physics and mathematics, treating money, motion, and the heavens with fresh rigor. His treatise on the communication of idioms in Christ also served Paris theology for a century after his death in 1382. Charles V often followed his counsel and had him write works in French for the kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de:
Notre-Dame de Molesme, a Benedictine abbey in Burgundy, became the seedbed of the Cistercian order. Saint Robert, abbot of Saint-Michel de Tonnerre, left monks unwilling to keep Benedict's rule in full and built a house of branches with a few companions beside the River Laignes.

Gifts from noble recruits raised a church reckoned the finest nearby, but wealth softened discipline until open rebellion broke out. In 1098 Robert and the fervent monks departed to found Cîteaux, leaving Molesme to carry on under a reformed observance. Members of noble families flocked to join, bringing possessions that raised a fine church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oriflamme:
The oriflamme, France's war banner, began as the banner of Saint Denis, said to be Dagobert’s gift to the abbey. The Song of Roland names a royal banner first Romaine, then Montjoie, and legend gives an oriflamme to Charlemagne from the pope, though no historical text confirms that early banner.

Eudes, king in 888 and abbot of Saint Martin, made that saint's plain blue banner the Frankish standard, strewn later with gold lilies. From Louis VI onward the red silk oriflamme of Saint Denis, its field covered with flames and stars of gold, replaced it as ensign of war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philibert-de-:
Philibert de l'Orme was the great architect of the French Renaissance, born at Lyons about 1515. Son of the master builder Jehan de l'Orme, he studied antiquities at Rome with a care that won Cardinal Santa Croce, later Marcellus II, and employment under Paul III. Recalled to Lyons in 1536, he became military controller, then in 1545 the king's master architect, once saving Brest's dismantled château from English attack with mock cannon and improvised troops.

Royal favour made him counsellor, almoner, abbot of several houses, and canon of Notre-Dame. His château at Anet for Diana of Poitiers stands as his finest work, and in 1564 he laid the Tuileries foundations for Catherine de' Medici. Henry II's death in 1559 broke his prosperity, and enemies like Ronsard hounded him. His 1567 treatise on architecture survives him, as does the tomb of Francis I at St. Denis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prime:
Prime, prima hora, ranks with Terce, Sext, and None among the short offices said at the day's hours. Romans named them by the hour: prima near 6 in the morning, tertia near 9 in the morning, sexta near noon, and nona near 3 in the afternoon. At first Prime was called matitutina hora, morning hour.  The name first meets us in the Rule of St Benedict.

This short office is one whose birth is best known. Cassian says plainly that this morning canonical function was first set up in his own day in his own monastery. Since Cassian's works are now dated fairly well, Prime's birth falls near 382. Proof now shows Cassian's monastery was not St Jerome's house at Bethlehem, but another past the Tower of Ader. It has been matched with Deïr-er-Raouat, convent of the shepherds, or Seiar-er-Ganhem, enclosure of the sheep.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-creator:
Rerum Creator Optime is the hymn for Matins on Wednesday in the Divine Office. It runs to four stanzas of four iambic dimeters each, rhymed two by two, opening with a prayer to the Creator and Ruler to free sleepers sunk in harmful slumber. Its ascription to Saint Ambrose finds no sanction from recent authorities, and the entry weighs rival claims with manuscript evidence.

Mone cites an eighth-century Trier manuscript, denies the hymn to Ambrose on grounds of rhyme, and leans to Saint Gregory, saying that between the two he would certainly choose Gregory. Biraghi leaves it out of Ambrose's genuine hymns, Dreves will not count it even possibly his, and Blume thinks neither Ambrose nor Gregory can seriously stand as author. Daniel cites a tenth-century Rheinau manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rome:
Rome matters above all as the city of the pope. Its bishop, successor of St Peter, is Vicar of Christ on earth and visible head of the Catholic Church. Rome is therefore the focus of unity in belief, the fount of church jurisdiction, and the seat of supreme authority binding the faithful worldwide. Its diocese bears the titles See of Peter, Apostolic See, Holy Roman Church, and Holy See.

More than any other city, Rome bears witness to pagan splendour and Christian triumph. Church history can be traced here from the catacombs to the ritual of St Peter's. From Rome the Gospel went to Europe and the ends of the earth, and pilgrims have thronged here in every age. Missionaries carried the best of ancient culture preserved through barbarian invasions, and later art filled the city with masterpieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salome:
Salome names two women in the Gospels, and this entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia keeps them apart. One is the daughter of Herod Philip and Herodias, at whose request John the Baptist was beheaded. The other is one of the holy women who watched the Crucifixion from afar and visited the tomb on the morning of the Resurrection.

Mark lists Mary Magdalen, Mary mother of James the Less and Joseph, and Salome among the watchers, while Matthew in the matching passage names the mother of the sons of Zebedee instead. Comparing the two passages makes it likely that Mark's Salome is that mother, who also appears pleading for her sons in Matthew's twentieth chapter. Beyond these Gospel hints, the entry says, nothing certain is known, though some writers guess she was Mary's sister.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-sister:
The School Sisters of Notre Dame are a teaching sisterhood running parish schools and orphanages across many American archdioceses and dioceses. They also work in Canada, at Hamilton, and across the United States. Their work includes an Indian school at Harbor Springs in Michigan, a deaf-mute institute in Louisiana, and a school for black children at Annapolis, besides parish schools and orphanages in many dioceses. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists a teaching empire.

Their chief boarding schools stood at Baltimore, Fort Lee, Quincy, Longwood in Chicago, and Prairie du Chien, with leading day and high schools at Baltimore, Quincy, Longwood, and Chatawa, Mississippi. They branch from the Congregation of Notre-Dame founded in France by Peter Fourier in 1597. German convents rose in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and Ratisbon's house, suppressed then restored, was remodelled by Bishop Wittmann and Father Job for modern needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th:
The Society of the Holy Name is a confraternity of the Most Holy Name of God and Jesus. It seeks love and reverence for the Holy Name and the suppression of blasphemy, perjury, and profane swearing. The Council of Lyons in 1274 ordered special devotion to the Holy Name as reparation for insults by Albigenses and other blasphemers. Gregory X charged the Dominicans with preaching the devotion, writing to master general John of Vercelli on 20 September 1274.

Dominican churches raised altars of the Holy Name, and confraternities formed under its title. Didacus of Victoria, the great preacher of the devotion, founded the Society of the Holy Name of God, approved by Pius IV in 1564 with rich indulgences. Pius V later restricted canonical erection to the Dominican order. Leo XIII's 1896 decree let bishops dispense from the rule of one confraternity per town, and the Holy Name Journal began in New York in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agnes-of-r:
St. Agnes of Rome was the virgin martyr most honoured by the primitive Church since the fourth century, and this entry traces her cult from its earliest records. The ancient calendar of martyrs in the collection of Philocalus, dating from 354, assigns her feast to 21 January and notes the Via Nomentana near her grave. The earliest sacramentaries repeat that date, and the Latin Church still keeps it.

From the close of the fourth century, Fathers and poets sang her virginity and heroism under torture, yet the earliest accounts differ enough to show that no single authoritative life survived. The entry weighs those divergent witnesses, giving readers the solid core of Agnes's fame and the honest limits of what history can recover.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o:
Eusebius of Rome, a patrician priest who died about 357, defied both pope and emperor for the Nicene Creed. Mentioned with honour in Latin martyrologies, he is styled confessor under the Arian emperor Constantius and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 retells the Acta Eusebii, found by Mombritius in 1479.

When Liberius returned to Rome, supposedly at the price of subscribing the Arian formula of Sirmium, Eusebius preached publicly against pope and emperor as heretics. Barred from the churches with the party backing antipope Felix, he held services in his own house. Arrested and brought before Liberius and Constantius, he boldly reproved the pope for deserting the faith. Later martyrologies call him martyr.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-frances-of:
Frances of Rome, fifteenth-century mystic, married at twelve and still built a congregation for women in the world. Born at Rome in 1384 to a noble family, she longed for religion but wed Lorenzo de' Ponziani at her father's wish. Her children included Battista, Evangelista, dead in 1411, and Agnes, dead in 1413. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Rome to 9 March 1440.

Famous for charity to the poor and zeal for souls, she drew Roman ladies from frivolity into an association of oblates at Santa Maria Nuova. On 25 March 1433 they became the Benedictine Oblate Congregation of Tor di Specchi, approved by Eugene IV that July. Its members lived religiously without strict cloister or formal vows, given to prayer and good works. With her husband's consent Frances lived in continence and deep contemplation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hippolytus:
Hippolytus of Rome, presbyter, antipope, and martyr, was a puzzle until a lost book surfaced in 1851. Of unknown birth, he died about 236. He left conflicting portraits. Eusebius calls him bishop of an unknown church and lists writings. Jerome gives a longer list and a homily preached before Origen. The Chronography of 354 records his banishment with Pope Pontianus to Sardinia in 235. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates the turning point to the Philosophumena's publication.

Damasus's grave inscription calls him a follower of the Novatian schism as presbyter. Before death, though, he urged his followers to reconcile with the Catholic Church. Prudentius's hymn sets his martyrdom at Ostia or Porto, torn by wild horses. That scene echoes mythic Hippolytus, son of Theseus. The entry separates history from legend: a learned schismatic who died reconciled and honoured.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-jerome:
Jerome, translator of the Vulgate, wandered from Stridon to Bethlehem through Rome, Trier, and the Syrian desert. Born at Stridon, on Dalmatia and Pannonia's edge, about 340 to 342, he went to Rome about 360, was baptized, and took interest in church affairs. Trier's schools began his theology, Aquileia followed, and about 373 he set out east. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Bethlehem to 30 September 420.

At Antioch he heard Apollinaris of Laodicea, then a leading exegete not yet separated from the Church. From 374 to 379 he lived ascetically in Chalcis desert, southwest of Antioch. Ordained priest at Antioch, he reached Constantinople in 380 to 381, befriending Gregory of Nazianzus. From 382 to August 385 he stayed near Pope Damasus at Rome, until Damasus's death and bitter enemies, made by harsh criticism, forced him out. By Antioch he went on to Bethlehem.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-robert-of-:
Robert of Molesme, founder of Cîteaux, sought a stricter Benedictine life and kept founding houses despite resistance. Born about 1029 in Champagne to Thierry and Ermengarde, he entered Montier-la-Celle at fifteen and later became its prior. In 1068 he became abbot of St Michael de Tonnerre, but his monks resisted his authority, and he resigned in 1071.

Hermits of Collan in the forest, with Gregory VII's backing, won him as their superior in 1074. Finding Collan unsuitable, he founded Molesme. He died at Molesme on 17 April 1111. The entry follows a restless reformer who kept seeking a stricter observance, from Tonnerre through Collan to his own foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-american-:
Rome's American College stands at the heart of this entry, an institution meant to keep the Church in the United States close to the See of Peter. Archbishops Hughes of New York and Kenrick of Baltimore pressed Pius IX hardest for it. American bishops visiting Rome in 1854 had asked for a national college to rank with the others already there.

Bishop Michael O'Connor of Pittsburgh seconded the plea, and the pope answered in kind. What follows traces the college's founding, its buildings, its rectors, and its students through half a century of work. Readers meet a seminary that shaped priests steeped in Roman tradition and sent them home to lead dioceses across America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-english-c:
English College at Rome, from pilgrim hospice to seminary, is the venerable house traced here. Some historians, following Polydore Vergil and others, root it in Ina of Wessex's Saxon school of 727, a claim the college, venerable though it be, cannot justly make. True origin lies near the fourteenth century's middle, in the Hospice of Saint Thomas of Canterbury, born of jubilee pilgrim crowds.

English pilgrims of 1350 found scant lodging in the Holy City, prompting a national house of shelter and hospitality. A lay guild acquired property on Via Monserrato, John Shepherd and wife Alice leading service to pilgrims. Seminary, rectors, martyrs, and scholars follow, through Reformation exile and restoration, to the college that trained England's missionary priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-south-ame:
Latin American seminarians in Rome found a home in the college described here, legally the Collegio Pio-Latino-Americano Pontificio. Ignatius Victor Eyzaguirre, after years in his native Chile working for souls, went to Rome in 1857 and proposed a college for students from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking lands. Pius IX, once apostolic delegate in Chile, approved and urged bishops to send students and funds.

Eyzaguirre returned to South America, gathered money, and came back with a few students, fifteen in all at first, renting a small house. Jesuits took direction, opening the college on 21 November 1858. A larger Dominican house near the Minerva, bought in December 1859, gave it room to grow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-time:
Time takes up one of the hardest questions in natural philosophy: what our idea of time contains, and what reality, if any, matches it. The entry first treats time as a subjective concept, built from three fused ideas. Succession sets past, present and future apart, so that moments follow one another and never occur together.

Continuity means the flow never pauses, and we cannot picture a gap in which we stop growing older. A continuous succession must also be a succession of something real, not of nothing. The second half weighs rival views of time as an objective reality. Idealists call it purely conceptual, while ultra-realists such as Gassendi, Clarke and Newton give it being outside the mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Notre Dame du Lac, in northern Indiana near the Michigan and Illinois lines, is owned and directed by the Congregation of Holy Cross. Its American motherhouse stands at Notre Dame, the name by which the university is best known. It was founded in 1842 by the Very Reverend Edward Sorin, late superior-general of his congregation, who came from France at the invitation of Bishop Celestine de La Hailandière of Vincennes.

Nearly two years passed before the first building rose and a faculty formed. In 1844 the university received a charter from Indiana, and by special act of the legislature it gained legal existence and power to grant degrees in the liberal arts and other fields. The entry follows its early growth, its colleges, and its religious life, giving the story of a frontier school that grew into a major Catholic university.

Rome's university must not be confused with the Studium Generale apud Curiam. Innocent IV set that school up in 1244 and 1245 at Lyons, for members of the papal court and visitors to the Holy See. That studium held faculties of theology and of canon and civil law, and clerics could both attend and teach law there despite an older ban. It travelled with the popes on their journeys and so moved to Avignon.

Under John XXII, following the Council of Vienne, the Studium Curiae became the first to found chairs of Arabic, Hebrew, and Chaldaic, with a professor of Armenian as well. At Avignon it added medicine. The entry then turns to the University of Rome proper, its own foundation, faculties, and colleges, separating the wandering court school from the city's settled university with care.
