elinor-wyllys-or-the-young-folk-of-longb:
Susan Fenimore Cooper set her first novel at Wyllys-Roof, the comfortable old house of Elinor Wyllys and her family at Longbridge. Her father, James Fenimore Cooper, supplied a preface dated 1845, gently warning readers that the fashions described were already ten years old. Elinor and the young folk around her fill the first volume with visits, summer excursions, and courtship in a settled American neighborhood.

Cooper watches manners the way she later watched nature: closely, patiently, and with dry amusement at folly. Suitors come and go, characters form slowly, and nothing explodes. Readers who enjoy Austen-like social comedy in an American key will find the pleasure here, in talk, character, and the small stakes of a country circle.
everyday-foods-in-war-time:
Rose's Everyday Foods in War Time guides home cooks through wartime food choices. Mary Swartz Rose taught nutrition at Teachers College, Columbia University. The book is dated 1918. A comic verse about calories and cabbages opens the contents.

Eight chapters cover the core foods of the wartime table. Milk comes first, then cereals, meat saving, and potatoes with substitutes. Fruits, vegetables, fats, and sugar each get a chapter. The last chapter joins economy with patriotism. An appendix adds wartime recipes. The first chapter calls the milk pitcher the one item no bill of fare can spare. Rose writes plain nutrition science for households under strain.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History, volume two of four, collects famous love affairs of rulers and rebels. The Romance of Devotion, his subtitle, promises stories where love outweighs thrones. This volume opens with the Empress Catharine and Prince Potemkin. Catharine, German-born, is praised as the greatest woman who ever ruled a nation.

Marie Antoinette and Count Fersen follow, with the story of Aaron Burr. George IV and Mrs. Fitzherbert bring secret marriage into the set. Charlotte Corday and Adam Lux join revolution to devotion. Napoleon appears twice, with Marie Walewska and through his sister Pauline. The Empress Marie Louise and Count Neipperg close the volume. Orr writes fluent popular history, more storyteller than scholar, and his affinities are chosen for drama rather than doubt.
footsteps-on-the-road-to-learning-or-the:
An anonymous picture alphabet teaches the letters in rhyme, three or more words to a letter. A is for Ass, for Ape, and for Ark, as well as for Ant and for Ann. B is for Boy, for Bat, and for Bark. The verses run through the whole alphabet with woodcut pictures.

M is for Mask, for Mary, and Mail, and N is for Nose, for Net, and for Nail. A child in the opening lines shows off a new book full of fine pictures. The little volume is dated 1850.
for-name-and-fame:
Henty follows a lost child turned foundling through a smackman's life at sea and into the Afghan war. The chapter list runs from the castaways and a fight with prahus to the advance up the Khyber. The Peiwar Kotal, the massacre at Cabul, and the battle of Maiwand mark the campaign's turns.

In one fight Will is shot through the leg and struck down by a tulwar blow on the shoulder. He wakes being carried by his captors, then again in a small room where an old woman bandages the sword cut. G. A. Henty published this tale of the Afghan passes in 1886.
going-some:
Rex Beach's Going Some is a western romance suggested by the stage play Beach wrote with Paul Armstrong. It opens on the rivalry between two southwestern ranches, the Centipede and the Flying Heart, where a lost foot-race has cost one side its phonograph and much of its pride.

Four cowboys set the tone, staring across a barbed-wire fence into a summer night thick with stars, while the prized phonograph wails from the neighbours' side. From that comic grievance the story builds toward courtship, horseplay and the strenuous affection of its subtitle, as ranch hands scheme to win back standing and sweethearts. Mark Fenderson's illustrations punctuate the action. The book suits readers who like light, fast-moving western fun rather than grim frontier realism.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADomesticInte:
Covert Action: Threat to the Constitution came from the Center for National Security Studies, a project of the Fund for Peace. The Center had been founded to watch the watchers, and this publication states its core argument in its title.

It holds that secret operations abroad corrode constitutional government at home, the thesis the oversight movement pressed through the 1970s. The Center's staff worked the fights over domestic spying, and its publications armed congressional reformers with arguments and documents. The piece is advocacy literature from the Church Committee era, preserved complete for readers of that movement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DomesticIntelli:
Joel Sappell reported for the Herald Examiner on a charge with a twist in it. The Citizens' Commission on Police Repression, a group formed to fight police spying, accused the Los Angeles Police Department of spying on the group itself. The department's Public Disorder and Intelligence Division, the charge said, had infiltrated the coalition in 1978.

The case captures the strange loop of domestic intelligence work in that era. A citizens' watchdog said the watched had become the watchers' target. Sappell's article preserves the accusation as the commission made it, part of a wider fight over police intelligence in Los Angeles.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBICrime_FBI_Cr:
James Vorenberg assessed the Nixon administration's war on crime in an article titled The War on Crime: The First Five Years. His review reaches back to the report of the President's Commission on Law Enforcement, whose findings set the terms of the fight. Five years on, he measured what the campaign had actually done.

Vorenberg writes as a legal scholar grading a political promise. Law-and-order pledges had won elections, and his article asks what they bought in practice. It is a period judgment on federal crime policy, made by a writer close to the commission whose work began the era.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OswaldsGameJean:
Jean Davison's book 'Oswald's Game' is preserved here as a full-text scan. Davison studied Lee Harvey Oswald's writings, politics, and movements, and built her account from that record. The scan's front matter, including the ISBN page, is garbled in the character recognition, but the book itself is present in full.

Davison's title borrows Oswald's own habit of treating politics as moves in a game. Her book stands apart from both the lone-gunman briefs and the conspiracy literature in one way: it takes Oswald's stated beliefs seriously as motives. Readers get a complete study of the accused assassin as a political actor, written from his papers and the testimony of people who knew him.

heart-and-science-a-story-of-the-present: Heart and Science, a story of the present time by Wilkie Collins. The heart versus science. This book preserves that novel. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
key-out-of-time:
Key Out of Time is a science fiction novel by Andre Norton, copyrighted in 1963 by the World Publishing Company. Its contents promise eleven chapters, from The Lotus World to Weapon from the Depths. Ross Murdock and his companions face storm menace, ancient mariners, and a time wreck. Loketh the Useless and witches' meat appear among the chapter titles.

Norton's Time Traders books send agents into alien worlds and lost pasts. Here the crew lands among free rovers and baldies on a watery planet. A lair of Mano-Nui and death at Kyn Add raise the stakes late in the book. This copy is a second printing, cleared under a noted textual rule. Norton builds fast adventure on time travel and first contact.
lays-of-ancient-rome:
Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote the ballads in Lays of Ancient Rome. Famous lays include Horatius, Virginia, and the Battle of Lake Regillus. A long preface argues that early Roman history is largely fable.

Public records perished when the Gauls burned Rome, Macaulay notes. Poets, not clerks, kept the old stories alive after that loss. His ballads rebuild those lost songs in bold English verse. Horatius holding the bridge became a schoolroom favorite for generations. The lays mix scholarship, patriotism, and stirring storytelling. Schoolchildren once learned Horatius by heart across Britain. Its ringing refrain helped fix Rome's heroes in common memory.
led-astray-and-the-sphinx-two-novellas-i:
Octave Feuillet's two novellas, Led Astray and The Sphinx, share one volume. Street and Smith copyrighted this edition in 1891. Feuillet had won fame with Romance of a Poor Young Man.

Led Astray opens with a letter from George to Paul in Paris. George writes at nine in the evening from Rozel. His friend has just arrived home from Germany. A graphic description, the chapter title promises, will follow. Feuillet builds refined French society tales from such letters and confessions. Two novellas let Feuillet contrast two kinds of love. Both turn on letters, secrets, and wounded pride.
lha-dhu-or-the-dark-day-the-works-of-wil:
William Carleton's tale Lha Dhu, or The Dark Day, appears in his collected works. The story opens by praising Ireland's softly shaded landscape. Valleys, glens, meadows, and hamlets scatter across the green island, he writes.

Each valley holds some tearful memory of humble calamity, he says. The proud world never hears those small sorrows. Carleton devotes his fiction to exactly those hidden griefs. His peasants are moved by mirth and sorrow in equal force. The Dark Day tells one such humble, haunting Irish story. Carleton knew Irish peasant life from his own youth. That knowledge gives even his legends a lived weight.
libretto-la-bohe-me:
Giacomo Puccini's opera La Bohème rests on this libretto by Giacosa and Illica. W. Grist and P. Pinkerton supplied the English version printed here. The story comes from Henri Murger's book about bohemian life in Paris. Four acts follow poor young artists around the Latin Quarter near 1830.

Rudolph the poet and Marcel the painter share a freezing attic studio. They burn a rejected manuscript for warmth and joke through their poverty. Mimi and Musetta bring love, and later sorrow, into their circle. The libretto lets English readers follow every word of the famous opera.
love-and-life-an-old-story-in-eighteenth:
Love and Life, printed in 1880, is a novel by Charlotte M. Yonge in eighteenth-century dress. Its chapters open with a syllabub party at the House of Delavie. A summons follows, then an enchanted castle and a dark chamber. A voice from the grave deepens the mystery at the heart of the tale.

Yonge tells an old story of love tested by strangeness and separation. Her heroine must trust a husband she rarely sees plainly. Windsor clergy, a queen of beauty, and country manners fill out the world. The book mixes fairy-tale wonder with the rules of real society. It rewards readers who like gentle, old-fashioned romance.
madame-chrysanthe-me:
Madame Chrysanthème is Pierre Loti's diary-novel of a summer in Japan. Laura Ensor translated this Modern Library edition into English. Loti swears he changed nothing in his diary, not even the dates. He names the three chief persons: myself, Japan, and Japan's effect on me.

Loti was a French naval officer stationed at Nagasaki. There he entered a temporary marriage with a young Japanese woman. Chrysanthème, his bride, shares his house for one season. His pages record temples, fans, boats, and his own restless moods. The book charmed Europe and fed the later Madame Butterfly story. It remains a famous, uneasy portrait of Japan through foreign eyes.
making-the-house-a-home:
Making the House a Home is Edgar A. Guest's memoir of family life, dated 1922. A verse at the front promises smiles, tears, weal, and woe. Guest says he and his wife have been building a home for fifteen years. A house takes months, he notes, but a home takes years.

They married on June 28, 1906, when he was twenty-five. He had just left his job as a Detroit Free Press police reporter. Page by page he tells of children, work, grief, and small joys. Guest was America's beloved newspaper poet of home and kindness. This plain, warm record shows the life behind his verses.
marjorie-s-maytime:
Marjorie's Maytime is a Carolyn Wells story for girls, dated 1911. It opens with a May party for Marjorie Maynard. A new pet and a trial trip follow in quick order. The children visit a camp and find Marjorie held a captive.

Two grandmothers take their turns: Grandma Sherwood and Grandma Maynard. An escapade, an exciting picnic, and some ancient finery fill the spring. There are calls at the schoolhouse and a merry joke. A ride in May and a trip to the circus crown the season. Little Vivian and a Boston visit close the book. Wells keeps every chapter sunny and brisk.
master-skylark-a-story-of-shakspere-s-ti:
John Bennett wrote Master Skylark, a tale of Shakespeare's time. Reginald B. Birch drew the pictures for the book. A note gives the hero's mother a place of honor at the front.

Nicholas Attwood, the skylark of the title, sings for the Lord Admiral's men. Chapters track him from home to Coventry and the Warwick road. He is disowned, rides for freedom, and reaches London town. At the end he sings before Queen Elizabeth at Christmas time. The Rose play house and the Children of Paul's show London's stage world. A new life and a waning year lead toward the Queen's pleasance.
memoirs-and-historical-chronicles-of-the:
Memoirs and Historical Chronicles of the Courts of Europe joins three royal lives. Marguerite de Valois, wife of Henri IV, leads the set. Madame de Pompadour and Catherine de Medici stand with her.

Marguerite's letters open with tales of her infancy at court. Plots to turn her to the new faith fail, and she stays Catholic. A court progress and a grand festivity break off in sudden confusion. Her brother Anjou's plots and her loss of favor fill the next letters. A picture shows the child Mozart playing for Madame de Pompadour. Court art and court plots stand side by side in the set.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume one of Saint-Simon's memoirs of Louis XIV opens his set. The contents list for all fifteen volumes stands at the front. Chapter one gives his birth, his family, and his wish for the army.

He enters the Musketeers and serves at the siege of Namur. Chapter two treats the King's natural children and a forced royal wedding. The Duc de Chartres weds, and Madame rages at the match. Chapter three turns to his father's death and tales of Louis XIII. Anecdotes of Richelieu and Madame de Hautefort fill that chapter. Family pride and court favor shape the young duke's start.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book two of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs treats Philippe I first. Philippe II, the Regent, and his wife come next in the list. The Dauphine and Adelaide of Savoy stand in the heads as well.

Mazarin, she says, feared the King's brother would grow too learned. He told the tutor to let the boy play, not study. The brothers differed in all things: build, hair, taste, and temper. Monsieur loved dress, dance, and large parties more than the chase. He never rode, save with the army, and feared sun and powder. Her blunt portraits spare no one, kin least of all.
nasa-tm-19660027035-trajectory-optimizat:
Lyle R. Dickey, of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this technical memorandum, dated May 25, 1966. Numbered TM X-53464, it tackles a core flight mechanics problem. It asks how to find the best possible path for a thrusting vehicle using step-by-step numerical methods.

Dickey starts from an assumed history of thrust direction and computes the path it produces. He then solves the linearized equations of motion directly for nearby paths. With that direct solution in hand, a planner can test whether the assumed path is truly the best one. The first and second variations together give a steady repeat-and-improve method for closing in on the optimum. The method keeps working even when the path includes sudden changes or limits partway through.
nasa-tm-19670009723-a-portable-different:
David Cleghorn, William A. Wall, and J. D. Bennight, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on December 5, 1966. It describes a shop tool: a portable gauge for measuring the inside flare angle of MC146 flared tubing. That angle is critical, because the tube must mate correctly with its fitting.

Quality control crews had been measuring the angle with plaster or plastic casts. That method was slow and costly. The new differential ball gauge measures the angle accurately and speedily instead. The memorandum includes the operating theory and the math behind the design, so other shops could build and trust the tool.
nasa-tm-19670022055-closed-loop-doppler-:
Peter E. O'Neill Jr., of the Communications Research Branch at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this paper in June 1967. Based on his thesis at George Washington University, it presents a closed-loop Doppler correction scheme for satellite links. Motion between a satellite and a ground station shifts the received radio frequency, and precise work must remove that shift.

O'Neill's technique reduces the effective Doppler shift to roughly the second order of the velocity ratio, a far smaller error. Experimental data verified the method, matching theoretical predictions within three percent. A ground-controlled satellite clock of very high stability was established in the Relay II satellite using the scheme. Without correction, the frequency error could grow more than a thousand times larger. Analyses cover constant and changing velocity cases, plus a worst-case study for Relay II.
nasa-tm-19680011768-exploring-in-aerospa: Kirby W. Hiller, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, taught this lesson to the Lewis Aerospace Explorers in 1966 and 1967. It is chapter twenty-one of Exploring in Aerospace Rocketry, on biomedical engineering. The catalog record describes the topic as engineering methods put to work in medicine and biology. The hosted sample preserves the cover and series list only, with no readable lesson text.
nasa-tm-19680015962-hanging-chain-impact:
Wilmer H. Reed III of NASA's Langley Research Center describes a simple damper for tall, flexible structures in this paper, presented in Ottawa in September 1967. Wind makes antennas, stacks, and towers sway back and forth. That motion can damage structures or disrupt their work if nothing absorbs the energy.

Reed's damper is a chain covered with a rubber sleeve, hung beside a vertical channel. As the structure sways, the chain strikes the channel and soaks up energy. Tests measured how design choices changed the damper's performance. The results are given as mechanical admittance and related measures. The concept offers a cheap, simple fix for wind-driven shaking.
nasa-tm-19680017374-alloying-principles-:
G. Mervin Ault surveys alloying principles for heat resistant refractory metals in this July 1967 discussion supplement. The notes support a committee report on strengthening mechanisms. Refractory metals such as molybdenum, tungsten, and chromium promise strength at temperatures where normal alloys fail.

Ault reviews emerging alloy trends and the ductile to brittle transition, a key weakness of these metals. He discusses grain size effects and refractory metal fiber reinforced superalloys. Molybdenum alloys had reached transition temperatures below room temperature as produced, the notes state. Tungsten alloys still missed that goal in their strongest forms. The survey maps where alloy design stood and what designers still needed.
nasa-tm-19680024523-automatic-controls-f:
C. R. Nichols and S. J. Obloy of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52427, for a propulsion conference in Cleveland, Ohio. Their topic is automatic control of the test facilities and mercury ion thrusters used in long durability runs. Ion thrusters must fire for months to prove they can last, far longer than crews can watch them closely.

Three years of such tests at Lewis reshaped several vacuum chamber systems, the authors report. New controls allowed automatic shutdown during unattended running, protecting both thruster and chamber. Thruster control circuits let one person per shift keep tests running almost three months without pause. Further changes, they add, now permit fully unattended durability testing.
nasa-tm-19690021372-neutral-atmosphere-c:
Jimmy E. Cooley and Carl A. Reber wrote this June 1969 Goddard preprint, numbered X-621-69-276. They report neutral atmosphere composition measured between about one hundred thirty and five hundred thirty kilometers up. A magnetic mass spectrometer flew on the Geoprobe, a Javelin rocket launched from Wallops Island, Virginia, on March 2, 1966.

The sealed instrument opened to the air by a pyrotechnic device once aloft. Helium and nitrogen readings agreed well with the standard model above two hundred fifty kilometers, they report. Measured oxygen values in the lower thermosphere ran below the model's, however. Working from the nitrogen profile, they place the exospheric temperature near nine hundred degrees for that flight.
nasa-tm-19710024241-discontinuities-in-t:
L. F. Burlaga of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this study in August 1971, numbered X-691-71-327, on discontinuities in the interplanetary medium. These are sharp boundaries in the solar wind where the magnetic field and plasma change abruptly. Burlaga connects them to how cosmic rays spread through space and gain energy.

Recent electron temperature measurements show magnetic and thermal pressures are about equal in the solar wind. That means hydromagnetic theory, not plain fluid theory, must describe these boundaries. Observations show most interplanetary magnetic discontinuities are tangential, lying along the field. Forward and reverse fast shocks and slow shocks have all been observed, and forward fast shocks can raise particle energies several fold. Fermi acceleration of particles trapped between a shock and magnetic fluctuations can explain the observations.
no-name:
Wilkie Collins built No Name in an unusual shape, as its contents page shows. Instead of plain parts, the novel runs in scenes, like a play. Chapters sit inside each scene, numbered fresh as the scene changes. Between the scenes come short interludes with that very title.

The sampled contents run from the first scene through the fourth and beyond. A preface stands before the first scene opens. Collins, known for tales of secrets and schemes, here borrows the stage's frame. Scene changes let time pass and letters or reports fill the gaps. Readers who like his mysteries get the same grip in a new form.
notable-women-of-olden-time:
Written for the American Sunday-School Union, Notable Women of Olden Time was entered at Philadelphia in 1852. No author is named. The union, at 1122 Chestnut Street, printed it under a committee drawn from seven church bodies. No book of theirs could pass if any committee member objected.

The contents sort Bible women by a trait or a role. Sarah is the wife, and Hagar the wife unloved. Rebekah is the partial and intriguing mother. Leah and Rachel are the rival sisters, and Miriam the affectionate sister. Deborah is the prophetess, and Jezebel the artful woman. Sunday school readers got scripture lives as lessons in character.
on-the-sublime:
Longinus is the name attached to this ancient critical treatise. H. L. Havell translated it into English prose. Andrew Lang wrote the introduction to this edition. Macmillan published it in London in 1890. The translator dedicates his attempt to Professor Butcher of Edinburgh.

The treatise asks what makes writing grand and moving. The sublime lifts readers beyond mere persuasion or pleasure. Longinus studies great passages from Greek and Roman authors. He links grandeur of thought with grandeur of style. Scholars still debate who truly wrote the work. It remains a founding text of literary criticism. Havell's version made it plain for English readers.
once-upon-a-time:
Richard Harding Davis gathered these short stories in 1912. Scribner's published the book in New York that year. Davis dedicated the volume to Gouverneur Morris. The contents list eight tales of adventure and society. Titles include The Spy, The Messengers, and A Charmed Life.

Other tales treat latitude, wasted days, and peace maneuvers. The Amateur and The Make-Believe Man close the list. Davis was famed as a war reporter and storyteller. His tales move fast, with polish and charm. Settings range from drawing rooms to foreign posts. The book shows his popular short fiction at its best.
one-day-s-courtship-and-the-heralds-of-f:
Robert Barr wrote these two tales, published in 1896. Artist John Trenton opens the first tale with a letter. He sails for England on the twenty-seventh, he writes. First he must revisit Shawenegan Falls in Canada. Their roar has stayed in his ears since leaving.

Trenton asks his friend to reserve a canoe for Tuesday. Two expert guides must take him up and back safely. His sketches failed, so he will bring a camera. The second tale, The Heralds of Fame, follows it. Barr writes crisp, witty fiction with Canadian color. The courtship of the title unfolds within one day.
one-man-in-his-time:
Ellen Glasgow published this novel in the year 1922. A note says no character was drawn from real people. The title quotes Shakespeare on man playing many parts. Chapter one is called The Shadow, chapter two Gideon Vetch. Corinna of the old print shop enters in chapter three.

Later chapters send Corinna to war and Patty into society. Old walls and a rising tide frame the change. A journey into mean streets tests the characters. Glasgow writes about old Virginia meeting a new age. September roses and magic soften her social satire. The book suits readers of thoughtful American fiction.
patty-at-home: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Patty at Home, the title page, dedication, and table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Carolyn Wells as the author and dates the book 1904. The contents list tea-club meetings, shopping, servants, differing tastes, a play, entertaining relatives, and a sailing party, the stuff of Patty's life once she is keeping house.
pe-lle-as-and-me-lisande-alladine-and-pa:
Maurice Maeterlinck's volume gathers three of his plays in Richard Hovey's English translation: Pélléas and Mélisande, Alladine and Palomides, and Home. Maeterlinck's own preface, printed in French, asks whether his dramas were truly written for a marionette theatre, as he once claimed.

He answers that they were not written for ordinary actors, and argues that poems die when living beings step into them. The preface sets out his symbolist theory of drama before the plays begin. Pélléas and Mélisande, the doomed love story that leads the volume, later became famous through the music it inspired.
peggy-stewart-navy-girl-at-home: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Peggy Stewart, Navy Girl, at Home, the title page, dedication, and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Gabrielle E. Jackson and a frontispiece by Norman Rockwell, and dates the book 1920. The dedication calls it a little story of Annapolis, and the contents list regatta day, a race, a masqueraders' show, and chapters for Daddy Neil and Polly Howland.
pinnock-s-improved-edition-of-dr-goldsmi: William C. Taylor of Trinity College, Dublin prepared Pinnock's improved edition of Dr. Goldsmith's History of Rome, here in its thirty-fifth American printing. The sample held for this entry shows only the title page, so the text itself cannot be described from it. That page promises an introduction to Roman history, added notes on Roman manners, institutions, and antiquities, biographical and historical notes, engravings, and questions for examination at the end of each section.
podcast-dannyjones-rH4xaWqf0ME:
The host known as Gnostic Informant joins Danny Jones to talk about Rome, the Antichrist, and the two beasts of Revelation. He reads prophecy through old Gnostic texts and church lore. The talk is dense with end-times claims.

The guest lays out his map of the last days, with Rome at its core and two beast powers on the rise. He ties the beasts to states and church heads of our own time. Jones asks which signs he thinks have already come true. Listeners steeped in prophecy will find a full system here. The library files the talk as an archive record.
poems-of-the-heart-and-home:
Mrs. J. C. Yule, born Pamela S. Vining, collected her Poems of the Heart and Home from work that had appeared under the pen names Emillia and Xenette as well as her own. Her introduction gives the poems back to the readers who first met them scattered in periodicals across Canada, the United States, and Britain, and adds pieces never printed before. She insists the poems are essentially Canadian, nearly all written on Canadian soil.

Teaching snatched the hours in which they were written, between schoolroom duties and the heavier work of domestic life, and their scenes are Canadian homes, schoolhouses, forests, and waters. Yule argues that true poetry interprets one heart for all hearts, since human experience repeats itself everywhere. The volume preserves a nineteenth-century Canadian woman's voice, devout, local, and determined to be judged on merit alone.
reflections-on-the-decline-of-science-in:
Charles Babbage argued in 1830 that science was falling behind in England, and he set out some causes in this book. His preface, dated from Dorset Street, London, on April 29 of that year, expects the volume to do science some service. He knows the task is thankless and will make enemies.

Babbage insists the book is not about his calculating machine, on which he had long been engaged. The causes of decline, he says, had worked for years and would have borne fruit without his own case. He cites the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana's article on chemistry as high authority for the fact of neglect, though he differs on its cause.
returning-home:
Returning Home opens with a doubt: the people who most value home, its narrator argues, are not those who live there. Good domestic folk by the parlour fire may love home less than those farthest from it. The piece was transcribed from an 1864 Chapman and Hall edition of Tales of All Countries, and no author's name is printed here.

For an Englishman abroad, home lies across the blue waters in the little northern island he may never see again. Life in distant lands, the narrator warns, turns stagnant rather than stirring, despite dreams of adventure. For women left at a foreign post it is ten times worse, he says, with children and talk of home their chief pursuits.
riley-songs-of-home:
James Whitcomb Riley's Songs of Home were published by Grosset and Dunlap of New York in 1910, with pictures by Will Vawter. He dedicates the book to George A. Carr. Its contents run in alphabetical order, with page numbers, in the manner of a family keepsake volume.

As Created and As My Uncle Used to Say lead the list, followed by At Sea and A Backward Look. Poems of home feeling fill the middle: His Room, A Feel in the Chris'mas Air, Honey Dripping from the Comb, and How Did You Rest, Last Night. Jim, John McKeen, and Just to Be Good stand late in the list shown, in dialect and standard verse mixed.
roads-from-rome:
Anne C. E. Allinson, who wrote Greek Lands and Letters with Francis G. Allinson, gathers essays on Rome in this book. Macmillan's New York edition is dated 1922 on its title page, and notes the work was set up in 1913. Three of the papers had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly: A Poet's Toll, The Phrase-Maker, and A Roman Citizen.

A Latin dedication to her father, Lucilio A. Emery, scholar of law and lover of humane letters, stands at the front. The contents add The Estranger, Fortune's Ledger, and A Road to Rome to the Atlantic pieces. A poster of the Roman Exposition of 1911, drawn by Duilio Cambellotti, serves as the title picture.
russell-h-conwell-founder-of-the-institu:
Agnes Rush Burr wrote Russell H. Conwell, Founder of the Institutional Church in America, subtitled The Work and the Man, dated 1905. The volume holds Conwell's two famous lectures as lately delivered, Acres of Diamonds and Personal Glimpses of Celebrated Men and Women. An appreciative introduction by Floyd W. Tomkins opens the book. Burr gives the work to the members of Grace Baptist Church, and to all who worked with self-giving and devotion to build the Temple walls, or who work in like spirit elsewhere.

The opening appreciation argues that the measure of greatness is helpfulness. Men, it says, are now tested not by wealth, birth, or brain power, but by service, in the method of the Master. Wealth is not to be scorned if it is clean and set apart for good ends. Noble birth counts only if the good survives in the heir.
sima-qian-memoires-historiques-chavannes:
Édouard Chavannes spent a decade turning Sima Qian's Shiji into French, and his fifth tome, from 1905, holds chapters forty-three through forty-seven. The Shiji itself dates to about 91 BCE and is the founding work of Chinese history writing. An index and errata close the French volume.

These chapters give biographies, the lives of men whose deeds shaped the early Han world. Chavannes filled his pages with notes on names, places, and rites, drawn from Chinese commentaries. His version was the standard Western Shiji for a century. Readers of French meet the grand historian here with a sure guide at their side.

Chapters thirty-one through forty-two of the Shiji fill the fourth tome of Édouard Chavannes's French translation, printed in 1901. Sima Qian's history, from about 91 BCE, here moves through the great houses and into the lives. The French text carries Chavannes's dense notes throughout.

The hereditary houses tell of the old feudal states and the families that ruled them for the Zhou kings. Then the biographies begin, lives of ministers and men of mark. Chavannes used Chinese commentaries to pin down names and dates. His set remains the fullest Western version of the grand historian made in the public domain era.

The third tome of Édouard Chavannes's French Shiji, from 1898, holds chapters thirteen through twenty-two. Sima Qian compiled the Records of the Grand Historian around 91 BCE. This stretch of the work is its frame: the tables and the first of the hereditary houses.

Chronological tables line up the rulers of the states year by year, so the reader can see who held power when. Then the houses begin, the long family tales of Zhou's feudal lords. Chavannes explains the tables with notes drawn from Chinese scholarship. Dry as they look, these pages are the spine of the whole Shiji.
sir-walter-raleigh-and-his-time:
An essay on Sir Walter Raleigh and his age opens by mocking the habit of explaining away heroical times. Truth is stranger than fiction, all say, yet few believe it, the writer charges. Readers trim heroes to their own level and call Alexander's conquests an accident with a pin.

Heroes, the essay answers, were men of like passions, with the same flesh, spirit, world, devil, and God as their readers. That kinship, not distance, makes their deeds instructive. The piece, drawn from an 1890 Macmillan set of historical essays, defends Raleigh's age against small, doubting readings of great lives.
stamp-collecting-as-a-pastime: Edward J. Nankivell, a member of the Philatelic Society of London, wrote Stamp Collecting as a Pastime for the Stanley Gibbons Philatelic Handbooks. Stanley Gibbons, Ltd. printed the London book in 1902, with a New York house at 167 Broadway. The contents open with stamp collecting as a pastime, its charm, and its staying power. Heads on its world-wide reach, its worth for lands and past events, stamps with a history, and great rarities follow in the list.
synge-and-the-ireland-of-his-time:
W. B. Yeats wrote Synge and the Ireland of His Time at Churchtown, Dundrum, in MCMXI, or 1911, two years after J. M. Synge's early death. A note by Jack Butler Yeats, about a walk through Connemara with Synge, is added to the volume.

Yeats opens on Saturday, January 26, 1907, lecturing in Aberdeen, when a telegram reached him after the second act of The Playboy of the Western World in Dublin: play great success. A second telegram, after one in the morning, reported the audience breaking up in disorder at the word shift. Yeats tells how forty young men acted. They stamped, shouted, and blew trumpets. They meant to silence a slander on Ireland's womanhood. Yeats defends Synge's country people against them. He calls those people poetic, violent, and grotesque, yet true art.
the-ancien-re-gime:
Charles Kingsley's lecture on the old order in France is shown here as printed in his Historical Lectures and Essays by Macmillan in 1902. In his preface Kingsley notes that the rules of the Royal Institution barred talk on faith and politics. Passages on religion, set in brackets in print, were therefore never spoken aloud in the hall.

He also regrets that he could not set France fully beside England, in his own day or in the century before. That contrast, he argues, is worth close study now. Grasping it would calm rich fears of revolt and poor hopes for it, and let a wider vote be seen for what it is: a safe step, not a threat.
the-ancient-regime: A contents list maps Hippolyte A. Taine's The Ancient Regime, first volume of The Origins of Contemporary France. Book One takes up the frame of old French society. It asks where privilege came from and who held it. A further question is what local and public services the privileged owed. Book Two turns to habits and character, with drawing-room life and its harms. Book Three treats the spirit and teaching of the age. Book Four follows the spread of the new teaching through France.
the-bible-in-spain-or-the-journeys-adven:
George Borrow's account of journeys, adventures, and imprisonments in Spain was issued by Cassell in 1908. An editor's note calls Borrow strong in body, firm in faith, gifted with tongues, and cheerful by nature. Son of a militia captain, he grew up roving and disliked being tied to a Norwich law firm at sixteen.

Borrow began Bible Society work in 1832, went to Russia in 1833, and was sent to Spain and Portugal in 1835. Five adventurous years there, which he called the happiest of his life, form the book. Much of it rests on his letters to the Society, written, the note says, with startling vigour.
the-bobbsey-twins-at-home: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins at Home, put out in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with rights dated 1916. The book is part of her long run of tales about the Bobbsey twins. Its first parts are named Tommy Todd's Story, A Sudden Stop, Snap and Snoop, and Home Again. Later parts cover Tommy's Troubles, School Days, The School Play, and Snoop in Trouble. The twin pets Snap and Snoop show up in the part names, but no page of the tale is shown here.
the-boy-scouts-on-sturgeon-island-or-mar:
Herbert Carter wrote The Boy Scouts on Sturgeon Island, or Marooned Among the Game-Fish Poachers. The first chapter is called Out for a Royal Good Time. It opens mid-trip, as a scout comes in from a scout ahead. He asks his mates who the stranger is, deep in talk with their scoutmaster, Dr. Philander Hobbs.

The fat boy Bumpus names the man: the son of the telegraph man in the town where they ate lunch. The troop had set a plan for word to reach them if a message came. Giraffe, the tall, long-necked boy, hopes no recall has come to spoil the fun at the last leg, with the boat a few miles off. A third boy fears the scoutmaster's glum face means just that. The boys praise Thad Brewster, their able assistant scoutmaster of the Silver Fox Patrol, while they wait to learn the news.
the-ceremonies-of-the-holy-week-at-rome: The Rt. Rev. Monsignor Baggs, Bishop of Pella, wrote this guide to the Holy Week ceremonies at Rome, in a third edition sold at Rome in 1854 by Luigi Piale. Only the title page and a contents list added by the transcriber are present here. The chapters promise directions for seeing the ceremonies, then accounts of the Mass, Palm Sunday, and the office of Tenebrae.No pages of the work itself follow the front matter.
the-complete-home: Clara E. Laughlin edited this household guide, published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in November 1906, with a frontispiece showing a $3,400 house. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here. The first two chapters, both by Oliver R. Williamson, treat choosing a place to live, then floors, walls, and windows. Their subheadings weigh renting against buying or building, city against country, schools, churches, transport, and the size and style of the house. No chapter text follows.
the-cricket-on-the-hearth-a-fairy-tale-o:
Charles Dickens calls The Cricket on the Hearth a fairy tale of home. He inscribed the little story to Lord Jeffrey with his affection as a friend, dating the dedication December 1845. Chapter I, Chirp the First, starts with a flat claim about the Peerybingle household: the kettle began it.

The narrator insists on the point against Mrs. Peerybingle's own record. The kettle started a full five minutes, by the little waxy-faced Dutch clock in the corner, before the cricket chirped at all. He pictures the clock's haymaker jerking right and left with a scythe before a Moorish palace, mowing half an acre of make-believe grass. A story, he says, must begin at the beginning, and the beginning here is the kettle, in what looks like a trial of skill between kettle and cricket.
the-game:
Jack London wrote The Game as a short novel of the prize ring, printed at London in 1913. Joe, a young fighter, and his girl stand at the start, shopping for carpets for a home.

The girl begs Joe to say why he loves the fight game and begs him to quit it. Joe vows this bout with Ponta is the very last: the purse will make an even hundred dollars in the bank, a nest egg for their marriage. The last bout with O'Neil cleared the last payment on his mother's house. London, who knew the ring, shows the pull of glory that kind words cannot break.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio: Thomas Babington Macaulay wrote The History of England from the Accession of James II. The record shows Volume I of 5, chapters I to V. Porter & Coates printed it at Philadelphia. The contents give a full outline of chapter one. The outline starts with Britain under the Romans. It runs through the Norman Conquest and the Wars of the Roses. It ends with the Puritans and the doctrine of divine right. Only the title page and contents outline are present here.
the-honor-of-the-name: Emile Gaboriau wrote The Honor of the Name, with a heading in the record dated 1869. The contents list chapters numbered I through XVIII in the pages present, with no titles given for any of them. Only the title page and contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. A second record in the library carries the same title and author, and that record opens with the first chapter itself.
the-iron-puddler-my-life-in-the-rolling-:
James J. Davis called his life story My Life in the Rolling Mills and What Came of It. Joseph G. Cannon supplied the introduction. Cannon marvels at the arc of that life. Davis was only forty-eight at the writing. He had been trapped in a southern peon camp. Hungry men there drank the cup of unpaid toil. In less than thirty years he rose high. He became secretary of labor. Cannon calls that rise a second act, not a beginning.

Cannon credits Davis with fathering Mooseheart. More than a thousand students study at that school. Both sexes and all ages attend it. He repeats the motto Davis learned from his father. No man is greater than his friends. All good in a life comes from friends. Davis can call ten thousand men by their first names, Cannon says. Labor leader and fraternal organizer, he carried others upward with him.
the-jerusalem-sinner-saved-or-good-news-:
John Bunyan's sermon appears here from the 1845 Thomas Nelson edition. Its text comes from Luke. Repentance and remission of sins should be preached among all nations. The preaching begins at Jerusalem. Bunyan rehearses the risen Christ's commission first. Matthew and Mark record it too. He fixes on Luke's special clause. The apostles held a warrant for all the world. Their ministry was still limited at its start. The first proffer of the gospel went to Jerusalem.

Bunyan sets out his method plainly. He will show what Jerusalem then was. Her descent from Abraham comes first. Her preference, exaltation, and decayed state follow. Second, he shows what preaching the gospel to her meant. The title gives the application. Mercy begins with the city that crucified Christ. The Jerusalem sinner saved is good news for the vilest of men.
the-lady-of-blossholme:
H. Rider Haggard opens this novel with the ruins of Blossholme Abbey. They stand on their mount between a tidal estuary and rich marshes. The scene has changed little since Henry VIII's days, he says. The events happened then. No large town has arisen nearby. No mines or factories defile the air. The village population has scarcely varied. Houses of local grey stone still stand with tile roofs. Reeds from the dike once covered them.

His inventory continues through the parish wells. The stocks and whipping-post stand on the Priests' Green. Irons were fitted for man, woman, and child. A weathercock shaped like the archangel Gabriel tops it. On this spot, Cicely Harflete was chained to a stake. She was Lady of Blossholme. Her foster-mother Emlyn stood chained beside her. Both were to be burned as witches. Haggard builds his tale of Tudor persecution on surviving ground.
the-little-shepherd-of-kingdom-come: John Fox, Jr. wrote The Little Shepherd of Kingdom Come, dedicated at Kentucky in April 1898. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The thirty-one chapter titles trace a boy's path. Two Runaways from Lonesome lead to a blab school on Kingdom Come, life with the Major, the Bluegrass, and college. Then comes the choice of the Blue or the Gray. Titles name Morgan's Men, brother against brother, and Pall-Bearers of the Lost Cause, ending with Peace and The Westward Way.
the-man-from-home: Booth Tarkington and Harry Leon Wilson wrote The Man from Home, published by Harper and Brothers in 1908 with illustrations from scenes in the play. Only the title pages and the original cast list are present here, so the play itself does not appear. The cast list records the first production, presented at the Studebaker Theatre in Chicago on September 29, 1907. It ran there for a year before opening in New York at the Astor Theatre on August 17, 1908. William Hodge, to whom the book is dedicated, played the lead, Daniel Voorhees Pike.
the-martial-adventures-of-henry-and-me: William Allen White wrote The Martial Adventures of Henry and Me, a wartime travel book illustrated by Tony Sarg. Only the contents and the list of illustrations are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. The chapter titles borrow phrases from the national anthem, moving from the rocket's red glare to the dawn's early light and the land of the free. One chapter turns the pair into a trio bound for Italy, and the picture captions show shipboard scenes, cigars, and waving crowds.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Jacques Casanova's memoirs continue here in A Cleric in Naples, part of the Venetian Years, drawn from the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters found by Arthur Symons. Chapter Eight opens with Casanova traveling in an ambassador's small retinue toward Chiozza. The steward tells him to lodge where he pleases and report his address to the captain of the boat.

The captain offers a large bed shared with the cook, whose wife stays aboard, and Casanova accepts for want of better. His trunk goes under the bed that fills the room. After dinner at an inn he walks the town, a Venetian sea-port of ten thousand people. The chapter's own summary promises misfortunes at Chiozza, a quarantine station at Ancona, a Greek slave, and a pilgrimage to Loretto. Readers follow the young cleric learning travel's discomforts at first hand.
the-path-to-rome:
Hilaire Belloc wrote The Path to Rome, his account of a pilgrimage on foot. In a greeting headed Praise of This Book, he tells how the vow began. Visiting the valley where he was born, he found its old church, once tumble-down, scraped white and rebuilt. Behind the high altar stood a statue of Our Lady unlike any he had seen.

Moved, he vowed to walk to Rome, taking no wheeled thing, sleeping rough, covering thirty miles a day, and hearing Mass each morning. He meant to reach St Peter's for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul. Belloc admits he broke his lesser vows one by one, but he kept the strict one and entered Rome on foot in time.
the-poetical-works-of-george-macdonald-i: Volume I of The Poetical Works of George MacDonald is dated 1893. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. The contents open with Within and Without, A Hidden Life, and The Disciple. A long Gospel Women sequence follows, treating sixteen figures. Among them are the mother Mary, the Syrophenician woman, the widow of Nain, the woman of Samaria, and Mary Magdalene. A Book of Sonnets begins after them, with titles such as The Burnt-Offering and The Unseen Face.
the-red-flower-poems-written-in-war-time: Henry Van Dyke gathered poems written during the First World War. He issued the volume in 1919. Its title poem is dated June 1914. One section treats trial as by fire. Another treats France and Belgium. The bells of Malines sound there, and Joan of Arc returns. Interludes in Holland follow. America enters in the last section. Liberty enlightening the world gets a poem there. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The poems themselves do not appear.
the-religion-of-ancient-rome: Cyril Bailey, fellow and tutor of Balliol College, Oxford, published his survey with Archibald Constable at London in 1907, thanking W. Warde Fowler for reading proofs and offering hints. Contents open with sources and scope, then turn to antecedents of Roman religion, main features of the religion of Numa, and early Rome as an agricultural community. Here only the title pages, thanks note, and opening of the contents list are present, so the survey itself does not appear.
the-revolutions-of-time:
Jonathan Dunn presents his book as a manuscript found in a weather-beaten stone box on a Pacific island, written in ancient Latin and translated and edited by him. Fourteen chapters promise past and present, predestined deja vu, creatures called Zards and Canitaurs, a lord of the past, a treeway, a fiery lake, and a temple of time.

A quotation from Jehu the Kinsman Redeemer mocks men who claim freedom from superstition while wearing the caps of their own prejudices. Another fragment warns that a physical show of spiritual force is not the force itself. Found-manuscript framing and time lore mark the book as speculative fiction.
the-riddle-of-the-frozen-flame: Mary E. and Thomas W. Hanshew wrote the detective Cleek stories. They set this riddle in a 1929 Burt edition. Doubleday, Page arranged the publication. Contents open with the law and the frozen flames. Sunshine and shadow follow in the list. An evil genius and a spectre at a feast come next. Shots in the dark and watchers in shadow follow. Victims and a secret of the flames close the opening list. Only the title pages are present here. The opening of the chapter list appears with them.
the-rules-of-the-game: Stewart Edward White's novel The Rules of the Game was published in October 1910. Doubleday, Page and Company issued it, with illustrations by Lejaren A. Hiller. The portion preserved here reaches only the author's note and a list of illustrations. The novel's opening chapters do not appear. In his note, White warns that the geography may be recognized by readers familiar with the country. He insists his characters, including Baker and Plant, are not the real inhabitants. Baker's Power Company, he says, has nothing to do with any actual company.
the-silk-hat-soldier-and-other-poems-in-: Richard Le Gallienne's The Silk-Hat Soldier and Other Poems in War Time is represented here by a list of the author's works and a title page. No poem itself appears. The works list names Robert Louis Stevenson: An Elegy and English Poems. The Quest of the Golden Girl and The Romance of Zion Chapel also appear. Readers therefore learn Le Gallienne's range, but none of the war poems' subjects.
the-sisters-in-law-a-novel-of-our-time:
Gertrude Atherton called The Sisters-in-Law a novel of our time. She dedicated it to Dr. Alanson Weeks of San Francisco. A note before book one links its people to her California Series. Several casual figures here lead in other novels, she explains. Gwynne and the Hofers belong to Ancestors, and the Randolphs to A Daughter of the Vine. Rezánov has a novel of his own name.

Book one opens on a long San Francisco street rising and falling toward the fading stars. The street is deserted even by private watchmen. Alexina darts across into the shadows of her avenue. She is breathless and rather frightened, Atherton writes. Her adventurous spirit had led her out before, but never after midnight. It was five o'clock in the morning, the narrator reveals. She had danced at a party given by new people her mother disdained.
the-vehement-flame:
Margaret Deland published The Vehement Flame in 1922, dedicating the novel to Lorin, with whom she had planned the story seven or eight years earlier. Lorin criticised the first chapters, then Deland had to continue alone through darkened years. She assigns all blunders to herself and any merits to that lost collaborator.

Chapter one takes its text from the Song of Solomon: love strong as death, jealousy cruel as the grave, with coals of a most vehement flame. Nineteen-year-old Maurice Curtis lies in blossoming grass at his wife's feet on a June day, embodied joy under a locust tree. Her answering love holds a doubt his lacks. Deland opens on rapture already shadowed by the title's warning.
there-s-pippins-and-cheese-to-come: Charles S. Brooks published There's Pippins and Cheese to Come in 1917, illustrated by Theodore Diedricksen, Jr. Brooks dedicated the volume to his father and mother. His earlier books include Journeys to Bagdad and Chimney-Pot Papers. Eleven essays are listed, on buying old books, roads of morning, Grub Street, spring, and Pepys in the theatre pit. One title promises a plague of all cowards. The title pages and contents are what is present here, so Brooks's essays themselves do not appear.
time-crime:
H. Beam Piper's Time Crime ran in Astounding Science Fiction across February and March 1955, illustrated by Freas. Its headnote calls the case a headache for the Paratime Police. Finding one gang among billions of probability lines dwarfs tracing one man among millions.

Guard captain Kiro Soran watches plantation clerks count gold coins for enslaved people's purchase, his revolver butt in hand. Manager Dosu Golan admits in another language that chattel slavery sickens him despite local custom. Readers get Piper's paratime adventure, where police cross alternate timelines and confront slavery on a colonial sector.
tom-fairfield-s-pluck-and-luck-or-workin: Allen Chapman wrote Tom Fairfield's Pluck and Luck, or Working to Clear His Name, published at New York by Cupples and Leon in 1913. A contents list runs through seventeen chapters. Headings open with an indignation meeting and brazen defiance, move through football and a cross-country run, then turn darker. Poisoned horses, Sam Heller's evidence, Tom's silence, and an empty bottle follow as Tom seeks clues. A contents list alone is included in this record, so Chapman's school story itself is not shown.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Definition of Computer Crime opens the main study in the United Nations manual printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Before law can act, it must know what it is chasing. Experts had argued for years over the words. No single world meaning had won out.

The piece traces the tale back to workers who smashed an early loom in 1801. It notes that theft, fraud, and forgery are old crimes in new dress. Fresh wrongs born of the machines may need fresh bans. A 1989 European list of acts fit for punishment is held up as a guide. The text warns courts to split true crime from mere careless or rude use.
vitality-supreme: Bernarr Macfadden wrote Vitality Supreme, a course in building health and strength. Pages present here hold the contents only, so the lessons themselves are not shown. The list runs from chapter two onward. It names functional activity as the secret of power, and proper posture. Straightening the spine, cleansing the alimentary canal, and exercise for vitality follow. How to breathe, outdoor life, and strengthening the stomach come next. The list adds preserving the teeth, how and what to eat, and hints on bathing.
we-philologists-complete-works-of-friedr: We Philologists forms part of volume eight of the Complete Works of Friedrich Nietzsche. That set was the first complete and authorized English rendering, edited by Dr. Oscar Levy. J. M. Kennedy made this translation. T. N. Foulis of Edinburgh and London issued the third edition in 1911. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only. Contents place the translator's preface at page 105 and the text at page 109. The text is headed Autumn 1874 and marked as published after Nietzsche's death.
what-dreams-may-come:
Gertrude Atherton, writing as Frank Lin, wrote What Dreams May Come. She gave the book to Muriel Atherton. The story opens in Constantinople in August, in the early days of the century. Sunset light falls on domes, minarets, bazaars, and the old palace gardens.

The scene moves to the English Embassy in Pera, where the windows stand open to a weak breeze. Curtains are drawn in one small room lit by wax candles. Beauty and a sense of decay hang over the city at once. Atherton sets romance in a place full of past intrigue. Readers enter a tale of love watched by an old, rich world.
what-is-your-culture-to-me:
Charles Dudley Warner gave the address What Is Your Culture to Me? to the alumni of Hamilton College on June 26, 1872. Warner recalls his own graduation day there, twenty-one years before. He jokes about the Latin words that once called him to the platform. That call, he says, stirred the blood like a trumpet.

Warner then notes how fast the world swallows each class of young graduates. His own class of 1851 slipped into life with scarce a ripple. He hopes the old tongue drills still go on at the college. The speech asks what a lofty, pure culture is worth in a busy world. Humor carries a real doubt.
when-the-holy-ghost-is-come:
Colonel S. L. Brengle wrote When the Holy Ghost Is Come, a Salvation Army book edited by Bramwell Booth. Booth's foreword, dated London, January 1909, opens the volume. He says the Army owes its strength to care for the deepest questions of the soul. Christ, he argues, is a full savior for this age as for any past one.

Booth scorns the claim that modern growth calls for a new kind of savior. He urges readers, busy or thoughtful alike, to study such practical truths. The contents ask who the Holy Spirit is and how his house is prepared. One chapter asks if his baptism is a third blessing. Readers get Army teaching on a devoted, active faith.
when-william-came:
A novel printed by John Lane in 1914, When William Came opens with Cicely Yeovil in a low swing chair. She studies her face in a mirror, then studies the young man at the piano. Both views please her. Her looks came by birth, she reflects, while Ronnie Storre is a prize she won by her own taste and effort.

Cicely has built a full philosophy of life and set out to live by it. She quotes a poet on how little lovers grasp love once it ends. She turns the line toward life itself and those who guard it too much. No author is named on the pages shown. A tale of a beaten, occupied Britain unfolds from this bright, vain start.
without-a-home:
E. P. Roe wrote this novel, and his long preface looks back on ten years as an author. He thanks loyal readers for kind letters. He admits praise and blame both puzzled him. Roe says he never planned to write stories at all. The burning of Chicago changed that. Days spent among smoking ruins gave him his first novel, Barriers Burned Away.

Roe describes stories growing in his mind like plants on his farm. Scenes formed while he worked and while he should have slept. That warm, personal opening frames the fiction that follows. Readers meet the author before they meet his characters.
woman-and-the-republic-a-survey-of-the-w:
Helen Kendrick Johnson wrote this survey of the woman suffrage movement in the United States. She sets out to test the claims of its leading advocates. Chapter one quotes the History of Woman Suffrage, edited by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, and Matilda Joslyn Gage. Johnson then points to contradictions in that claim. Women cannot always have been slaves, she argues, if they now lead thought.

Later chapters test suffrage against democracy, law, trade, and the home. Each pairs the movement with one part of public life. Readers get a sceptical case, built point by point. Johnson writes as a critic, not a supporter.
you-can-search-me: Hugh McHugh wrote these comic John Henry stories, published in 1905 with pictures by Gordon H. Grant. Pages present here hold the title page, a chapter list, a list of illustrations, and the first line of chapter one. Every chapter title starts with John Henry Gets, from a partner to a sufficiency to a setback. The opening line counts seven weeks until wedding bells. The tales themselves barely begin in these pages.
young-folks-history-of-rome:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote this history of Rome for young readers, copyrighted in 1880 at Boston. Her preface sets the span. The sketch runs from early Italy to Charles the Great as head of a new western empire. Yonge says she kept it as brief as interest allowed. Contents open with Italy, Aeneas, and the founding of Rome in 753 B. C.

Kings, Tarquins, and republic follow in short chapters. Yonge wrote matching histories of England and France for the same audience. Readers get Rome's long arc in plain, story-like chapters. The aim is a first map of Roman history that young readers can actually finish.
